p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: ICT stands for Information and Communication Technology . It is the umbrella term for all technologies used to capture, store, process, retrieve, transmit and exchange information in digital form. It is an extended form of Information Technology (IT), with extra emphasis on telecommunications and unified communications : telephony, wireless signals, middleware, audio-visual systems and networks. IT focuses on computing and data processing. ICT adds the communication layer, so a person can send, share and collaborate across distances. ICT tools are hardware, software and networks, such as smartphone, laptop, tablet, projector, smart board, internet, e-mail, LMS and video-conferencing. Chalk and duster are not ICT tools. This is a favourite "which is NOT" question.

p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: Hardware: physical devices, such as computers, phones, routers and projectors. Software: programs that run on hardware. Networks and connectivity: LAN, WAN, internet, wireless. Data and content: text, audio, video, databases. People and procedures: users, trainers, policies.

t: 1.3 Role of ICT in Teaching and Learning
p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: The correct exam answer is that ICT enhances access, interactivity and quality of instruction . It does not replace teachers, remove assessment or reduce learner participation. Key points: Anytime, anywhere learning (flexible access). Multimedia content improves understanding and retention. Supports different learning styles and personalised learning. Enables collaboration (shared documents, discussion forums). Provides quick assessment and feedback (online quizzes). Makes quality content available to remote learners (SWAYAM, DIKSHA). Helps teachers with record-keeping, lesson planning and reuse of resources.

p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: Literature review using online databases (Scopus, Web of Science, JSTOR, Google Scholar) and reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote). Data collection with online surveys (Google Forms) and sensors. Data analysis with software (SPSS, R, Python, NVivo for qualitative data). Plagiarism checking (Turnitin, URKUND/Ouriginal in India through Shodhshuddhi). Publishing and sharing (institutional repositories, Shodhganga, ORCID, preprint servers). Collaboration through cloud tools (Google Drive, Overleaf). A question may ask which is an application of ICT in research. Pick the option involving online databases or software, not hand notes or print-only reliance.

p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: Universities use ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) software for admissions, fees, examination, payroll and student records. The same idea appears as MIS (Management Information System), digital attendance, biometric systems and online grievance portals. If a scenario describes admissions, fees and records, the answer is administration .

p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: The digital divide is the gap between those who have access to ICT and those who do not. Causes include income, location (urban versus rural), gender, age, disability, language barrier and low digital literacy. Types are the access divide (devices and internet), the skills divide and the usage divide. Remedies are BharatNet, Common Service Centres, low-cost devices, regional language content and digital literacy programmes (PMGDISHA). Do not confuse digital divide (gap in access) with digital literacy (skills) or digital library (a collection).

p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: Level Meaning Example Data Raw, unprocessed facts and figures Marks of 50 students Information Processed, organised data with meaning "The class average is 62%" Knowledge Understanding gained by analysing and applying information Knowing which teaching method works best after analysing results Wisdom Judgement to apply knowledge ethically and effectively Deciding which method to adopt for the long-term good of learners Order (lowest to highest): Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom. Exam questions give a scenario and ask you to label the level. Use this trick: a list or number alone is data; a summary or statistic is information; an insight about what works or why is knowledge; a decision with judgement is wisdom. Also remember data is plural of datum , and information needs context.

t: Memory Capsule: Basics of Information and Communication Technology
p: Basics of Information and Communication Technology · ICT
x: ICT = IT + communication. Digital divide = access gap. Moodle and Google Classroom = Learning Management Systems (LMS). DIKW order is a frequent "arrange in order" question.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: A computer is an electronic device that accepts input , processes it under stored instructions and produces output , with the ability to store results. Basic cycle: Input → Processing → Output → Storage . The modern design follows the Von Neumann architecture , in which the program and data are stored in the same memory (the stored-program concept). Characteristics: speed, accuracy, diligence (no fatigue), versatility, storage capacity, no IQ (cannot think on its own), automation.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: Generation Period Key technology Features and examples First 1940–1956 Vacuum tubes Machine language, huge size, heat, high power use, punched cards. ENIAC, UNIVAC, EDVAC Second 1956–1963 Transistors Assembly language and high-level languages ( COBOL, FORTRAN ), smaller, faster, magnetic core memory. IBM 1401 Third 1964–1971 Integrated Circuits (IC) Keyboards and monitors replaced punched cards and printouts, operating systems, multiprogramming. IBM 360 Fourth 1971–present Microprocessors (LSI/VLSI) The Intel 4004 (1971) began this era, personal computers, GUI, networking. IBM PC, Apple Macintosh Fifth Present and future Artificial Intelligence, ULSI, parallel processing Natural language processing, expert systems, robotics, quantum computing research Memory aids: Vacuum → Transistor → IC → Microprocessor → AI (V-T-I-M-A). Machine language was used in the first generation. COBOL and FORTRAN belong to the second generation. Keyboard and monitor arrived in the third. Microprocessor arrived in the fourth. AI is the fifth. Watch for the period traps: the second generation starts in 1956 and the first runs from 1940 to 1956.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: By size and power: Supercomputer: fastest and most powerful. Used for weather forecasting, nuclear simulation, space research and genomics. Speed is measured in FLOPS (floating point operations per second). India's PARAM series was developed by C-DAC under Dr Vijay Bhatkar. Other Indian examples are Pratyush (IITM Pune) and Mihir (NCMRWF). Foreign examples are Cray and Fugaku. Mainframe: large organisations such as banks, airlines and railways. Supports bulk transaction processing and many simultaneous users . Example: IBM Z series. Minicomputer: midsize, between microcomputers and mainframes, multi-user. Microcomputer: built around a microprocessor . Desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, single-user. Supercomputer versus mainframe: a supercomputer solves a few extremely complex scientific calculations quickly. A mainframe handles a vast number of transactions reliably. This is a concept question. By working principle: Analog: processes continuous data (temperature, speed, pressure). Example: thermometer, speedometer. Digital: processes discrete binary data (0 and 1). Example: PC. Hybrid: combines both. Example: ICU patient monitors, which measure analog body signals and display digital readings.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: The CPU is the brain of the computer. Parts: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit): performs arithmetic (add, subtract) and logical (AND, OR, NOT, comparison) operations. Control Unit (CU): directs and coordinates all operations, fetches and decodes instructions and controls data flow. It does not process data itself. Registers: very small, fastest storage inside the CPU that hold data and instructions being processed. Examples: Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction, Instruction Register (IR) holds the current instruction, Accumulator holds intermediate results, MAR holds a memory address, MDR holds data read or written. Instruction cycle: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Store. Clock speed is measured in Hz (MHz, GHz). Other performance factors are the number of cores, cache size and word length. Bus types: data bus, address bus and control bus.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: System Base Digits Binary 2 0, 1 Octal 8 0 to 7 Decimal 10 0 to 9 Hexadecimal 16 0 to 9, A to F (A=10 … F=15) Conversions to remember: Decimal to binary: divide repeatedly by 2 and read remainders bottom to top. Example: 10 = 1010. Binary to decimal: multiply each bit by powers of 2. Example: 1101 = 8+4+0+1 = 13. Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right. Binary to hex: group in fours. Quick values: 1010 = 10, 1111 = 15 = F, 11111111 = 255 = FF, 10000 = 16. Computers use binary because electronic circuits have two states (on and off). Codes: ASCII is 7-bit (128 characters), extended ASCII is 8-bit (256), Unicode supports all world languages (UTF-8 and UTF-16), and BCD and EBCDIC are other codes.

p: Computer Fundamentals · ICT
x: Bit (0 or 1) → Nibble (4 bits) → Byte (8 bits) → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB → EB → ZB → YB. Each step is 1024 times the previous one in the traditional binary convention (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Order from smallest: Bit \< Nibble \< Byte \< KB \< MB \< GB \< TB \< PB. Network speeds are in bits per second (Mbps), and storage is in bytes . A byte stores one character.

p: Hardware and Software · ICT
x: Hardware means the physical, touchable parts: CPU, memory, input and output devices, storage, motherboard, power supply and peripherals. Classes: input, output, processing (CPU), storage and communication hardware.

p: Hardware and Software · ICT
x: Software is the set of programs and instructions that make hardware work. It is intangible. System software manages the hardware and gives a platform for other programs: Operating system (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android). Utility programs: antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup, file compression. Language translators: Assembler (assembly to machine code), Compiler (translates the whole program at once, reports all errors, faster execution, e.g. C and C++), Interpreter (line by line, stops at first error, e.g. Python and JavaScript). Device drivers and firmware (permanent software on ROM chips, e.g. BIOS). Application software performs user tasks: General purpose: word processor (MS Word), spreadsheet (Excel), presentation (PowerPoint), browser, database (Access). Specific purpose: tally accounting, railway reservation, hospital management. Custom (bespoke) versus packaged software.

p: Hardware and Software · ICT
x: Proprietary: paid, source code closed (MS Office). Freeware: free but not modifiable (Adobe Reader). Shareware: free trial, then payment. Open source: source code available, modifiable and shareable (Linux, LibreOffice, Moodle). Free software emphasises freedom (GNU/GPL), not price.

p: Hardware and Software · ICT
x: Hardware Software Firmware Physical Programs Software embedded in hardware Cannot be installed Can be installed and updated Stored in ROM, rarely changed

t: 4.1 Input Devices (send data into the computer)
p: Input and Output Devices · ICT
x: Keyboard (QWERTY), mouse , trackball , joystick , light pen , touch screen , stylus . Scanner: converts paper documents or images into digital form. OMR (Optical Mark Reader): detects marks made in bubbles, used for checking MCQ answer sheets , such as NET and entrance exams. OCR (Optical Character Recognition): converts printed or handwritten text to editable text. MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Reader): reads magnetic ink characters on bank cheques . Barcode reader: reads product codes in retail and libraries. QR code scanner is a 2-D variant. Microphone, webcam, digital camera, biometric devices (fingerprint, iris, face). Trap pairs: OMR is marks and exams, OCR is text, MICR is cheques and banks, barcode is retail.

p: Input and Output Devices · ICT
x: Monitors: CRT, LCD, LED, OLED. Quality depends on resolution (pixels) and refresh rate. Printers: impact (dot-matrix, line printer, daisy wheel, with a physical strike, noisy, can make carbon copies) and non-impact (inkjet, laser, thermal, quiet, higher quality). Laser printers are fast and give high-quality text. Print speed is in PPM (pages per minute), and resolution in DPI . Plotter: large engineering drawings and maps. Speakers, headphones, projector.

p: Input and Output Devices · ICT
x: Touch screen, modem, headset with microphone, multifunction printer (print and scan). Some are classed as input-output devices. Hard disks and pen drives are storage devices, not typical I/O in exam logic.

p: Input and Output Devices · ICT
x: A monitor, printer, speaker and plotter are output. Keyboard, mouse, scanner and light pen are input. Resolution is described in pixels (monitor) and DPI (printer).

p: Memory and Storage · ICT
x: From fastest, smallest and most expensive to slowest, largest and cheapest: Registers → Cache → RAM (main memory) → Secondary storage (SSD or HDD) → Tertiary and offline (optical, tape). The principle is a trade-off of speed, cost and capacity.

p: Memory and Storage · ICT
x: RAM (Random Access Memory): volatile (data lost when power is off), read and write, holds currently running programs and data. SRAM (Static RAM): faster, costlier, used in cache , no refreshing. DRAM (Dynamic RAM): slower, cheaper, needs constant refreshing, used as main memory. ROM (Read Only Memory): non-volatile, holds start-up instructions (BIOS or firmware). Types: PROM (programmable once), EPROM (erased with UV light), EEPROM (erased electrically) and Flash memory (block-erase, used in pen drives and SSD). Cache memory: a small, very fast memory between CPU and RAM that holds frequently used data. Levels L1 (inside CPU, fastest), L2 and L3. Virtual memory: use of disk space to extend RAM.

p: Memory and Storage · ICT
x: Magnetic: hard disk (HDD), floppy, magnetic tape (sequential access, used for backup and archives). Optical: CD (about 700 MB), DVD (about 4.7 GB), Blu-ray (about 25 GB per layer). Solid-state: SSD , pen drive, memory card. No moving parts, faster and more durable than HDD. Cloud storage: Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox. Access methods: sequential (tape), direct or random (disk, RAM).

p: Memory and Storage · ICT
x: RAM ROM Volatile Non-volatile Read and write Mostly read-only Temporary working space Permanent start-up instructions Primary memory Secondary memory Directly accessed by CPU Not directly accessed Fast, costly, small Slow, cheap, large Volatile (RAM) Non-volatile Quick traps: Cache is faster than RAM. Registers are the fastest of all. ROM is non-volatile. An SSD has no moving parts.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: An operating system (OS) is system software that acts as an interface between the user and the computer hardware and manages all hardware and software resources. Without an OS the computer cannot run applications. The OS is loaded into RAM at booting (start-up), when the BIOS or firmware runs a power-on self-test and loads the OS from disk. The kernel is the core of the OS. The shell is the layer the user interacts with.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: Process management: scheduling the CPU, multitasking. Memory management: allocating and freeing RAM, virtual memory. File management: creating, naming, organising, protecting files and folders. Device management: drivers for printers, keyboards and disks. Security and access control: passwords, user accounts, permissions. User interface: CLI or GUI. Error detection, resource allocation and job accounting.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: Type Key idea Example or use Batch Jobs with similar needs grouped and run without user interaction Early mainframes, payroll Multiprogramming Several programs in memory, CPU switches when one waits for I/O Mainframes Time-sharing (multitasking) CPU time sliced among many users or tasks Unix, Windows Real-time (RTOS) Must respond within a strict deadline Air-traffic control, medical devices, missiles Distributed Many computers appear as one system Large clusters Network OS Manages servers and shared resources on a network Windows Server, Novell NetWare Embedded Fixed-function device OS Washing machine, ATM Mobile Touch-based OS Android, iOS Single-user versus multi-user, and single-tasking versus multi-tasking are other classifications.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: Windows (Microsoft): proprietary, GUI-based. Linux: open-source, kernel by Linus Torvalds (1991) . Distributions include Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat. Based on Unix ideas. Unix: multi-user, multi-tasking, developed at Bell Labs in the 1970s. macOS and iOS (Apple) , Android (Google, Linux-based, open source) . BOSS (Bharat Operating System Solutions): Indian Linux-based OS developed by C-DAC . Maya OS is a Linux-based OS developed for the Indian defence sector.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: CLI (Command Line Interface): text commands (DOS, Linux terminal). Fast and powerful, but harder to learn. GUI (Graphical User Interface): windows, icons, menus and pointer (WIMP). Easy and intuitive. Examples are Windows and macOS. Xerox PARC pioneered the GUI.

p: Operating Systems · ICT
x: File extension identifies type: .docx (Word), .xlsx (Excel), .pptx (PowerPoint), .pdf, .txt, .jpg, .mp3, .mp4, .exe. Shortcuts: Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+P print, Ctrl+A select all, Ctrl+F find, Alt+Tab switch windows, Ctrl+Alt+Del task manager options. Folder (directory) versus file . Path shows the location of a file. MS Office suite: Word (documents), Excel (spreadsheets, cell address, formulas such as SUM and AVERAGE), PowerPoint (slides), Access (database), Outlook (e-mail). Traps: Linux is open source and Windows is not. Android is not a Microsoft product. The OS is system software, whereas MS Word is application software.

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: ARPANET (1969): funded by the US Department of Defense (ARPA). It connected four nodes and used packet switching. It is the ancestor of the internet . TCP/IP was formally adopted on 1 January 1983 , creating the internet as a network of networks. 1989 to 1991: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN proposed the World Wide Web, then built the first web server, browser and website (1991). He created HTML, HTTP and URL . Mosaic (1993) was the first widely used graphical browser. Netscape followed. India: ERNET began for academic use, and VSNL launched public internet access on 15 August 1995 .

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Internet World Wide Web Global network of networks (infrastructure) Collection of web pages and resources accessed through the internet (a service) Uses TCP/IP Uses HTTP/HTTPS Older (1969/1983) Newer (1989/1991) Includes e-mail, FTP, VoIP and more Only linked hypertext and multimedia pages The web is one service on the internet . This is among the most repeated concept questions.

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Dial-up: uses telephone line and modem, slow. Broadband: always-on high-speed (DSL, cable, fibre). DSL/ADSL: over telephone line. Fibre optic (FTTH): fastest wired option, light pulses. Leased line: dedicated, for organisations. Satellite and VSAT: remote areas. Wi-Fi and mobile data: 3G, 4G (LTE) and 5G. WiMAX: wireless broadband over a wider area.

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: A protocol is a set of rules for communication. Protocol Full form Use Port TCP/IP Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol Core suite for the internet, TCP splits data into packets and IP addresses them - HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol Web page transfer 80 HTTPS HTTP Secure (SSL/TLS) Secure web 443 FTP File Transfer Protocol Upload and download files 21 SMTP Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Sending e-mail 25 POP3 Post Office Protocol Downloading e-mail 110 IMAP Internet Message Access Protocol Syncing e-mail on server 143 Telnet Terminal Network Remote login (unencrypted, replaced by SSH) 23 DNS Domain Name System Domain name to IP address 53 DHCP Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Assigns IP addresses automatically - IP address: IPv4 is 32-bit (for example 192.168.1.1) and IPv6 is 128-bit. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) has scheme, domain and path: https://www.ugc.gov.in/page. Domain suffixes: .com (commercial), .org (organisation), .edu (education), .gov (government), .net (network), .in (India), .ac.in (academic, India), .gov.in (Indian government).

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Web browser: software to view web pages. Examples: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Safari, Opera. Features include tabs, bookmarks, history, cache, cookies, incognito (private) mode. Search engine: a program that searches web content. Examples: Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo, Baidu. Remember: a browser is not a search engine. Tips: use quotation marks for exact phrase, AND, OR and NOT as Boolean operators, site: and filetype: operators. Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar are academic search engines.

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Version Nature Features Web 1.0 Read-only static web Static pages, few creators, many readers Web 2.0 Read-write , social web User-generated content, blogs, wikis, social media, YouTube Web 3.0 Semantic and intelligent web, read-write-execute AI, machine learning, blockchain-style decentralisation, personalised experience

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Social media includes Facebook, X (Twitter), Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube, WhatsApp, Telegram, Reddit and blogs. Educational uses: class groups, content sharing, collaboration, video lectures, discussion, professional networking (LinkedIn, ResearchGate and Academia.edu for researchers). Risks: distraction, misinformation, privacy violations, cyberbullying, addiction. Other web tools: blog (online journal), wiki (collaboratively edited, Wikipedia), podcast (audio series), RSS (feeds), MOOC .

p: Internet and World Wide Web · ICT
x: Intranet: private network within an organisation using internet technology, accessible only to its members (staff portal). Extranet: an intranet extended to selected outside users such as suppliers, partners or students. Internet: public. Order of openness: Intranet (most restricted) \< Extranet \< Internet.

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: A computer network is two or more connected devices that share data and resources. Benefits: resource sharing (printers, files), communication, centralised data, cost savings and reliability.

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: Type Area Example PAN A few metres Bluetooth between phone and earphones LAN Building or campus College computer lab CAN Campus University network MAN City Cable TV network, city Wi-Fi WAN Country or world The Internet By size: PAN \< LAN \< CAN \< MAN \< WAN. VPN (Virtual Private Network) builds a secure private tunnel over a public network.

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: Bus: one common cable, cheap, a break stops the network, collisions. Star: all devices connect to a central hub or switch. Most common in LANs , easy to add devices, central failure stops all. Ring: circular, data moves in one direction, token passing. Mesh: every node connected to every other, very reliable, costly. Number of links in full mesh = n(n-1)/2. Tree: hierarchical, combination of star and bus. Hybrid: combination of topologies.

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: Simplex: one direction only (keyboard to computer, TV broadcast). Half-duplex: both directions, but one at a time (walkie-talkie). Full-duplex: both directions simultaneously (telephone, mobile call).

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: Guided (wired): twisted pair (UTP and STP, used in LAN cables), coaxial cable (cable TV), optical fibre (light, highest speed, no electromagnetic interference, most secure). Unguided (wireless): radio waves, microwave, infrared, satellite, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi. Bandwidth is the data-carrying capacity, in bits per second. Latency is delay.

p: Computer Networks · ICT
x: OSI model (7 layers, top to bottom): Application → Presentation → Session → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical. Mnemonic from the bottom: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away . TCP/IP model (4 layers): Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access. Client-server: central server provides services to clients (web, e-mail). Peer-to-peer (P2P): all nodes are equal and share resources directly (torrent). Switching: circuit switching (dedicated path, telephone) versus packet switching (data split into packets, internet).

p: Networking Devices · ICT
x: Device Function Key point NIC (Network Interface Card) Connects a computer to a network Has a unique MAC address (48-bit) Hub Connects devices in a LAN, broadcasts data to all ports Unintelligent, shared bandwidth Switch Sends data only to the intended device using MAC addresses Intelligent, replaces hub Bridge Connects two LAN segments Filters traffic Router Connects different networks and forwards packets using IP addresses , finds the best path Connects LAN to internet Gateway Connects networks using different protocols, a translator Entry and exit point Modem Modulator-Demodulator , converts digital to analog and back Used for telephone and cable lines Repeater Regenerates and amplifies weak signals Extends distance Access Point (AP) Provides Wi-Fi to wired network Wireless connectivity Firewall Filters incoming and outgoing traffic by rules Hardware or software security

t: 9.2 Layer Mapping, Addresses and Look-Alike Pairs
p: Networking Devices · ICT
x: Layer mapping: Hub and repeater work at the physical layer, switch and bridge at the data link layer, router at the network layer. Identification: MAC address (hardware, physical, fixed) versus IP address (logical, changes with network). Modem versus router: modem connects to the ISP, router distributes the connection to devices.

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: Bluetooth: short range (about 10 metres), low power, creates PAN, IEEE 802.15. Wi-Fi: wireless LAN, IEEE 802.11 standard. NFC (Near Field Communication): a few centimetres, used in contactless payment and tap-to-pay. Infrared: line-of-sight, used in remotes. RFID: radio tags for tracking, used in libraries and toll collection (FASTag). GPS: satellite-based location. India's regional system is NavIC .

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: Gen Main feature 1G Analog voice 2G Digital voice, SMS (GSM, CDMA) 3G Mobile internet, video calling 4G (LTE) High-speed broadband, HD streaming 5G Very high speed, ultra-low latency, IoT and smart cities. India launched 5G services in October 2022 GSM (Global System for Mobile) uses SIM cards. CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access).

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: Satellites relay signals using uplink and downlink . INSAT and GSAT are Indian communication satellites. EDUSAT (2004) was India's first dedicated educational satellite. Types: geostationary (about 36,000 km altitude, appears fixed) and low-earth orbit. Used in DTH television, VSAT, weather, navigation and distance education.

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: Invention: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network e-mail in 1971 and introduced the @ symbol. Address structure: username@domain.com. The username is the user's mailbox, and the domain identifies the mail server. Parts of a message: To (main recipient), Cc (carbon copy, visible to all), Bcc (blind carbon copy, hidden from others), Subject , Body , Attachment and Signature . Folders: Inbox (received mail), Outbox (mail waiting to be sent), Sent , Drafts (unsent saved mail), Spam or Junk (unsolicited mail) and Trash . Protocols: SMTP sends mail (outgoing). POP3 downloads mail to one device, usually removing it from the server. IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs across devices. Advantages: fast, cheap, global, attachments, searchable record, asynchronous. Limitations: spam, phishing, viruses, overload, no tone or emotion, needs internet. E-mail netiquette: clear subject, polite and concise, do not type in all capitals (it is shouting), proofread, use Reply All carefully, do not forward chain mails, respect privacy, use Bcc for large groups.

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: Audio-conferencing: voice-only communication among multiple locations. Video-conferencing: audio and video in real time, which allows face-to-face interaction at a distance. Types: point-to-point (two sites) and multipoint (many sites). Requirements: device (computer or phone), camera, microphone, speaker, stable internet bandwidth , and conferencing software. Platforms: Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Cisco Webex. Educational uses: virtual classes, guest lectures, thesis viva, remote meetings, webinars and workshops. Advantages: saves travel cost and time, flexible, recordable, reaches remote learners. Limitations: needs bandwidth and power, technical glitches, privacy and security concerns, less personal interaction, "Zoom fatigue". Synchronous means at the same time (live class). Asynchronous means at different times (recorded lecture).

p: Communication Technologies · ICT
x: VoIP (Voice over IP) sends voice using the internet (WhatsApp calls, Skype). IoT (Internet of Things) connects everyday objects to the internet. Cloud computing gives on-demand computing resources over the internet (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS, for example Google Docs, AWS, Azure). AI and ML let machines simulate intelligence, with generative AI producing text, images and code. Big data is characterised by volume, velocity, variety (the 3 Vs). Blockchain is a decentralised, tamper-resistant ledger. AR and VR give augmented and immersive experiences.

p: Digital Learning · ICT
x: Digital learning is any learning that uses digital technology, content or tools to improve the learning experience. It is wider than e-learning, and covers e-learning, blended learning, mobile learning, flipped classrooms, gamification, adaptive and personalised learning, microlearning, simulations, AR and VR, and AI-based tutoring. It also develops digital literacy (skills to find, evaluate, create and communicate information digitally) and digital citizenship (safe, ethical and responsible use).

p: Digital Learning · ICT
x: Learner-centred and self-paced. Anytime, anywhere access. Multimedia, interactive and immersive content. Instant feedback and analytics to track progress. Collaboration through discussion forums and shared documents. Scalable to large numbers at low marginal cost.

p: Digital Learning · ICT
x: Connectivism (George Siemens): learning happens through networks and connections, and it underlies cMOOCs. Called the learning theory of the digital age. SAMR model (Ruben Puentedura): four levels of technology integration. S ubstitution (tech replaces a tool with no change), A ugmentation (tech adds functional improvement), M odification (task is significantly redesigned) and R edefinition (tasks that were previously impossible). The first two are enhancement , the last two transformation . TPACK (Mishra and Koehler): overlap of T echnological, P edagogical and C ontent K nowledge. An effective teacher integrates all three. Bloom's Digital Taxonomy (Andrew Churches): adapts Bloom's levels to digital tasks. Constructivism: learners construct knowledge, supported by collaborative digital tools.

p: Digital Learning · ICT
x: NEP 2020 gives strong support to technology in education: the National Educational Technology Forum (NETF) for exchange of ideas on technology use, expansion of digital infrastructure, online and digital education, digital repositories, virtual labs, content in regional languages, teacher training for technology, and the Academic Bank of Credits for flexible, multidisciplinary learning. When asked about NEP and ICT, remember NETF, ABC, blended learning and the emphasis on equity and access.

p: Digital Learning · ICT
x: Digital divide, poor connectivity and power, limited teacher training, cost of devices, language barriers, privacy and security risks, screen-time and health concerns, lack of motivation or interaction and assessment integrity.

p: E-Learning · ICT
x: E-learning is learning delivered through electronic media, mostly the internet, in which content, instruction and interaction are provided online. It is a form of technology-enhanced learning .

p: E-Learning · ICT
x: Synchronous: live and in real time (virtual class on Zoom, live chat). Asynchronous: at the learner's own time (recorded lectures, forums, e-mail, self-paced modules).

p: E-Learning · ICT

x: Advantages: flexibility, wider reach, cost-effectiveness, personalised pace, updated and multimedia content, record of progress, eco-friendly. Limitations: needs devices and internet, requires self-discipline, low social interaction, dropout rates, assessment and plagiarism concerns, not ideal for practical skills without simulation.

p: E-Learning · ICT
x: Open access: free, immediate online access to scholarly literature. Gold (published open in the journal) and Green (self-archiving in a repository). DOAJ is the Directory of Open Access Journals. The Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002) is a landmark. Open-source software: source code open to all (Linux, Moodle, LibreOffice, Python). Creative Commons (CC): licences such as CC BY (attribution), NC (non-commercial), ND (no derivatives) and SA (share-alike). OER concept was adopted at UNESCO in 2002.

Assessment and evaluation: online tests, auto-graded quizzes, e-portfolios, rubrics, learning analytics and digital proctoring. p: ICT in Education · ICT
x: A teacher should have technological competence, digital pedagogy skills, ethical awareness (copyright, privacy), online communication skills and the ability to evaluate digital resources. ICT does not replace the teacher: it changes the role from information provider to facilitator and guide .

x: SWAYAM (MOOC platform, online courses) versus SWAYAM Prabha (TV channels). A very common trap. e-PG Pathshala (PG, UGC) versus e-Pathshala (school, NCERT). Shodhganga (full theses) versus Shodhgangotri (synopses) versus Shodhshuddhi (plagiarism checker). NAD stores certificates, ABC stores credits, APAAR is the student ID, DigiLocker is the wallet. NDLI is a digital library at IIT Kharagpur, and NPTEL is a course platform by IITs and IISc. p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: Cyber ethics are the moral principles for using computers and the internet responsibly: respect privacy, do not hack, do not pirate software, do not plagiarise, do not spread false information, give credit and be honest. Netiquette (network etiquette) is the set of rules for polite online behaviour: be respectful, avoid ALL CAPS, do not spam, verify before sharing, respect copyright, protect others' privacy and think before posting.

p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: Cybercrime is a crime in which a computer or network is the tool, the target or the place of the crime. Common forms: Hacking: unauthorised access to systems. Ethical (white hat) hackers test security with permission, black hat hackers attack, grey hat lies between. Phishing: fake e-mails or sites to steal credentials. Vishing is by voice call, smishing by SMS, spear phishing targets a specific person, and pharming redirects users to fake sites. Identity theft, cyberstalking, cyberbullying, online fraud, sextortion. Spoofing: disguising as a trusted source. Spam: unsolicited bulk messages. Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed DoS (DDoS): flooding a service to make it unavailable. Man-in-the-Middle (MITM): intercepting communication. SQL injection: attacking databases through input. Zero-day: exploit of an unknown vulnerability. Social engineering: manipulating people rather than machines.

p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: Malware is malicious software. Type Behaviour Virus Attaches to files and spreads when the host file is run Worm Self-replicates across networks without a host file or user action Trojan horse Disguised as useful software, does not self-replicate Ransomware Encrypts data and demands payment (WannaCry, 2017) Spyware Secretly collects information Adware Shows unwanted adverts Keylogger Records keystrokes Rootkit Hides deep in the OS Botnet Network of infected computers controlled remotely Logic bomb Triggered by a condition or date

p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: CIA triad: Confidentiality (only authorised access), Integrity (data is not altered), Availability (data is accessible when needed). Authentication means verifying identity. Authorisation means granting permissions. Measures: strong passwords and a password manager, two-factor or multi-factor authentication (2FA/MFA) , OTP , antivirus and anti-malware , firewall , encryption (converts data to unreadable cipher text, symmetric uses one key and asymmetric uses a public-private key pair), VPN , regular updates and patches, backups, HTTPS sites, careful use of public Wi-Fi, avoiding unknown links and attachments, and digital literacy training. Digital signature uses asymmetric cryptography to give authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation. Digital certificates are issued by a Certifying Authority (CA) . Biometrics are fingerprint, iris and face. CAPTCHA distinguishes humans from bots.

p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: Information Technology Act, 2000: India's primary cyber law, in force from 17 October 2000 , based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on E-Commerce. It gives legal recognition to electronic records, e-contracts and digital signatures , and defines cybercrimes and penalties. Amended in 2008 (added provisions on cyber terrorism, identity theft and data protection). Important sections: 43 (damage to computer or data without permission, compensation), 66 (computer-related offences, hacking), 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation), 66E (privacy violation), 66F (cyber terrorism), 67 (publishing obscene material), 67B (child sexual abuse material), 69 (government interception and monitoring powers), 70 (protected systems) and 72 (breach of confidentiality). Section 66A (offensive messages) was struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) . CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, 2004, under MeitY) is the national agency for incident response. I4C (Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre) and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) and helpline 1930 support reporting. Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023: India's data-protection law covering consent, rights of data principals and duties of data fiduciaries. Rules under it are being implemented in phases. Check the latest status before the exam. National Cyber Security Policy, 2013.

p: Cybersecurity · ICT
x: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR): copyright, patent, trademark, design, geographical indication. Copyright Act, 1957 (amended 2012) protects original literary, artistic, musical and software works. In India, copyright lasts for the author's life plus 60 years. Fair dealing allows limited use for criticism, review, research and education. Plagiarism: presenting others' words or ideas as one's own. Forms: copy-paste, paraphrasing without credit, self-plagiarism, mosaic plagiarism. Tools: Turnitin, Ouriginal, iThenticate, and Shodhshuddhi in India. UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in HEIs) Regulations, 2018: similarity up to 10% is excluded from penalties (Level 0), 10–40% (Level 1), 40–60% (Level 2) and above 60% (Level 3), with increasing penalties. Creative Commons and open licences allow lawful reuse. Software piracy is illegal copying. Digital footprint: trail of data left online. Cookies: small files stored by websites.

p: ICT Applications (E-Governance and Digital India) · ICT
x: E-governance is the use of ICT to deliver government services, exchange information and make administration transparent, efficient and accountable (SMART governance: Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent). Challenges: digital divide, low literacy, infrastructure, cybersecurity and privacy, resistance to change, interoperability and language.

p: Exam Pattern, Recent Trends and Question Formats · ICT

p: Basics: Argument, Statement, Truth, Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Logic is the study of the methods and principles used to distinguish correct reasoning from incorrect reasoning. It does not study how people actually think (that is psychology). It studies the relationship between premises and conclusion .

p: Basics: Argument, Statement, Truth, Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false . Commands ("Close the door"), questions, requests and exclamations are not statements, so they have no truth value and cannot be premises or conclusions. The truth or falsity of a statement is called its truth value .

p: Basics: Argument, Statement, Truth, Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: An argument is a group of statements in which one (the conclusion ) is claimed to follow from the others (the premises ). Every argument therefore has at least one premise and exactly one conclusion in the basic form. Conclusion indicators: therefore, hence, thus, so, consequently, it follows that, accordingly, which shows that. Premise indicators: because, since, for, as, given that, inasmuch as, the reason being. Non-arguments: mere description, report, explanation, command, question, simple conditional statement. An explanation tells why something happened (the fact is already accepted), while an argument tries to prove that something is true.

p: Basics: Argument, Statement, Truth, Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: These three words are the most tested distinction in the unit. Term Applies to Meaning Truth / Falsity Statements (propositions) Agreement or disagreement with fact Validity / Invalidity Deductive arguments Conclusion follows necessarily from premises Soundness Deductive arguments Valid and all premises true Strength / Weakness Inductive arguments How probable the conclusion is, given the premises Cogency Inductive arguments Strong and all premises true Key facts to memorise: Validity depends only on form , not on the actual truth of the statements. A valid argument can have a false conclusion, but only if at least one premise is false. If the premises are true and the conclusion is false, the argument is definitely invalid . A valid argument with a false premise is valid but unsound . An invalid argument can have true premises and a true conclusion. Truth of the parts does not guarantee validity. Propositions are true or false; arguments are valid or invalid. Never say "a true argument" or "a valid statement".

p: Basics: Argument, Statement, Truth, Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Feature Deduction Induction Direction (traditional) General to particular Particular to general Claim Conclusion follows necessarily Conclusion follows probably Conclusion Contained in the premises (no new information) Goes beyond the premises (new information) Evaluation Valid / invalid Strong / weak Effect of added premises Valid argument stays valid Strength can increase or decrease Example All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal The sun has risen every day so far; so it will rise tomorrow Caution: the "general to particular" and "particular to general" rule is only a rough guide. Some deductive arguments move from general to general, and some inductive arguments move from particular to particular (analogy). The real test is whether the conclusion is claimed to follow necessarily or only probably . Types of induction: perfect induction (complete enumeration of all cases, which is really deductive in force), imperfect induction (a sample is generalised, which is the usual inductive method), analogy, causal inference, statistical generalisation and hypothesis. Francis Bacon's Novum Organum championed the inductive method, and J. S. Mill systematised the canons of induction.

p: Categorical Propositions · Logical Reasoning
x: A standard-form categorical proposition has four parts: quantifier (All / No / Some), subject term (S) , copula (is / are) and predicate term (P) . It states a relation between two classes.

t: 2.2 The four forms (A, E, I, O)
p: Categorical Propositions · Logical Reasoning
x: The letters come from the Latin AffIrmo (I affirm) and nEgO (I deny). Form Statement Quantity Quality Subject distributed? Predicate distributed? A All S is P Universal Affirmative Yes No E No S is P Universal Negative Yes Yes I Some S is P Particular Affirmative No No O Some S is not P Particular Negative No Yes Memory rule for distribution: Universals distribute the subject; negatives distribute the predicate. So A distributes S, E distributes both, I distributes neither, O distributes P. A term is distributed when the proposition says something about every member of the class the term denotes.

p: Categorical Propositions · Logical Reasoning
x: The square arranges A, E, I, O at its corners (A top-left, E top-right, I bottom-left, O bottom-right). Relation Between Rule Contradictory A–O and E–I (diagonals) Cannot both be true and cannot both be false. Exactly one is true. Contrary A–E (top) Cannot both be true; can both be false Subcontrary I–O (bottom) Can both be true ; cannot both be false Subalternation A to I, and E to O (sides) Truth passes down (universal to particular); falsity passes up (particular to universal) Inference table (traditional view): If this is... A E I O A is true T F T F A is false F ? ? T E is true F T F T E is false ? F T ? I is true ? F T ? I is false F T F T O is true F ? ? T O is false T F T F (? means undetermined.) The shortcut: contradictories always flip; contraries cannot both be true; subcontraries cannot both be false; "true travels down, false travels up".

p: Categorical Propositions · Logical Reasoning
x: The traditional (Aristotelian) view assumes every class named in a proposition has at least one member, so universal propositions imply the existence of their subject. This makes subalternation, and the contrary and subcontrary relations, valid. George Boole rejected this. On the Boolean (modern) view , universal propositions (A and E) make no existence claim, while particular propositions (I and O) do. Consequences: only the contradictory relation survives on the Boolean square; contrary, subcontrary and subalternation fail; and "All unicorns are white" does not imply "Some unicorns are white". The existential fallacy is committed when a syllogism with two universal premises draws a particular conclusion, which is valid only on the Aristotelian view.

p: Categorical Propositions · Logical Reasoning
x: Immediate inference draws a conclusion from one premise . The three classical operations are conversion, obversion and contraposition. Conversion (interchange S and P, keep quality): Original Converse Type A: All S is P Some P is S By limitation (per accidens) E: No S is P No P is S Simple I: Some S is P Some P is S Simple O: Some S is not P Not valid O cannot be converted Obversion (change the quality, replace the predicate with its complement; valid for all four ): Original Obverse A: All S is P No S is non-P E: No S is P All S is non-P I: Some S is P Some S is not non-P O: Some S is not P Some S is non-P Contraposition (replace S with non-P and P with non-S; equals obvert, convert, obvert): Original Contrapositive A: All S is P All non-P is non-S E: No S is P Some non-P is not non-S (by limitation) I: Some S is P Not valid O: Some S is not P Some non-P is not non-S Memory: O cannot be converted; I cannot be contraposed; A and O are the only forms that contrapose simply; obversion works for everything.

p: The Categorical Syllogism · Logical Reasoning
x: A categorical syllogism is a mediate inference with three categorical propositions (major premise, minor premise, conclusion) and exactly three terms , each appearing twice. Major term (P): predicate of the conclusion. Minor term (S): subject of the conclusion. Middle term (M): appears in both premises, never in the conclusion. Major premise: the premise containing the major term. Minor premise: the premise containing the minor term.

p: The Categorical Syllogism · Logical Reasoning
x: Mood is determined by the types (A, E, I, O) of the three propositions in order (major premise, minor premise, conclusion). Since each of three propositions can be one of four forms, there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible moods . Figure is determined by the position of the middle term in the premises. There are four figures : Figure Major premise Minor premise Middle term position 1 M – P S – M Subject of major, predicate of minor 2 P – M S – M Predicate of both 3 M – P M – S Subject of both 4 P – M M – S Predicate of major, subject of minor With 64 moods and 4 figures there are 256 possible syllogistic forms . Of these, 24 are valid on the Aristotelian view. On the Boolean view only 15 are unconditionally valid (the other 9 depend on existential import).

t: 3.3 Valid moods and mnemonic names (memory heavy)
p: The Categorical Syllogism · Logical Reasoning
x: Figure Valid moods (unconditional) Mood letters 1 Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio AAA, EAE, AII, EIO 2 Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroko EAE, AEE, EIO, AOO 3 Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison IAI, AII, OAO, EIO 4 Camenes, Dimaris, Fresison AEE, IAI, EIO Conditional (Aristotelian only, existential import needed): Barbari (AAI-1), Celaront (EAO-1), Cesaro (EAO-2), Camestrop (AEO-2), Darapti (AAI-3), Felapton (EAO-3), Bramantip (AAI-4), Camenop (AEO-4), Fesapo (EAO-4). Mnemonic reading: the three vowels of each name give the mood. The initial consonant (B, C, D, F) shows the first-figure mood to which it is reduced. Letters inside the name tell the method of reduction: s (simple conversion), p (conversion by limitation), m ( mutare , transpose the premises), c (reductio ad absurdum). Figure-wise features: Figure 1: minor premise must be affirmative; major premise must be universal. It gives conclusions of all four kinds (A, E, I, O) and is called the perfect figure; the only one whose conclusion can be A. Figure 2: one premise must be negative; major premise must be universal; conclusion is always negative (E or O). Figure 3: minor premise must be affirmative; conclusion is always particular (I or O). Figure 4: the Galenic figure (named after Galen, though added later); if the major premise is affirmative then the major must be universal... (rarely asked in detail).

t: 3.4 The rules of the syllogism and their fallacies
p: The Categorical Syllogism · Logical Reasoning
x: # Rule Fallacy if violated 1 Exactly three terms Four terms ( quaternio terminorum ); equivocation of the middle term is a common cause 2 The middle term must be distributed at least once Undistributed middle 3 A term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise Illicit major (major term) or Illicit minor (minor term) 4 No conclusion follows from two negative premises Exclusive premises 5 If one premise is negative, the conclusion must be negative (and vice versa) Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise 6 No conclusion follows from two particular premises (Two particular premises) 7 If one premise is particular, the conclusion must be particular Existential or similar error 8 From two affirmative premises, the conclusion must be affirmative (Corollary of rule 5) Quick test procedure for a syllogism: (1) put it in standard form and name S, P, M; (2) identify the mood and figure; (3) check each rule above in order; (4) the first rule broken names the fallacy. Worked example. All dogs are mammals; no fish are mammals; therefore no fish are dogs. Terms: M = mammals, P = dogs, S = fish. Mood EAE? Arranging: major premise "All dogs are mammals" (A), minor premise "No fish are mammals" (E), conclusion "No fish are dogs" (E). Figure 2 (middle term is predicate of both). Mood AEE-2 is Camestres , which is valid.

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: A hypothetical proposition has the form "If P then Q". P is the antecedent , Q is the consequent . It is false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent false. Form Pattern Status Modus ponens (affirming the antecedent) If P then Q; P; therefore Q Valid Modus tollens (denying the consequent) If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P Valid Affirming the consequent If P then Q; Q; therefore P Fallacy Denying the antecedent If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q Fallacy Pure hypothetical syllogism If P then Q; if Q then R; therefore if P then R Valid

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: "Either P or Q; not P; therefore Q." Valid. If the disjunction is inclusive , affirming one disjunct does not allow denying the other ("Either P or Q; P; therefore not Q" is a fallacy for inclusive disjunction but valid for exclusive disjunction).

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: A dilemma combines a hypothetical and a disjunctive argument. The major premise contains two conditionals (hypotheticals); the minor premise is a disjunction . Constructive dilemma: (P→Q) and (R→S); P or R; therefore Q or S. Destructive dilemma: (P→Q) and (R→S); not-Q or not-S; therefore not-P or not-R. Three ways to meet a dilemma: Escape between the horns: reject the disjunctive premise by showing that other alternatives exist. Grasp (take) it by the horns: deny the truth of one of the conditional propositions. Rebut it: construct a counter-dilemma that proves the opposite conclusion.

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: Sorites: a chain of syllogisms in which the conclusion of each becomes a premise of the next, and all intermediate conclusions are left unstated. Only the final conclusion is given. Enthymeme: a syllogism in which one premise or the conclusion is suppressed (understood but unstated). It is the form in which most everyday arguments occur. Epicheirema: a syllogism in which one or both premises are supported by a reason.

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: Law Statement Symbolic Identity Whatever is, is; A is A A is A Non-contradiction Nothing can both be and not be at the same time and in the same respect not (A and not-A) Excluded middle Everything either is or is not; there is no third possibility A or not-A A fourth, the Law of Sufficient Reason , was added by Leibniz. A statement "P and not-P" violates non-contradiction; "A is B or not B, and a middle option exists" violates excluded middle.

p: Other Forms of Argument · Logical Reasoning
x: Connective Symbol True when Negation ~P P is false Conjunction P ∧ Q Both true Disjunction (inclusive) P ∨ Q At least one true (false only if both false) Conditional P → Q False only when P true and Q false Biconditional P ↔ Q Both have the same truth value Tautology: true under every assignment of truth values (e.g., P ∨ ~P). Contradiction (self-contradiction): false under every assignment (e.g., P ∧ ~P). Contingent statement: true under some and false under others. De Morgan's laws: ~(P ∧ Q) ≡ ~P ∨ ~Q, and ~(P ∨ Q) ≡ ~P ∧ ~Q.

t: 5.1 What a Fallacy Is: Formal and Informal
p: Fallacies · Logical Reasoning
x: A fallacy is an error in reasoning that makes an argument unsound or invalid. Two broad classes exist. Formal fallacies arise from the form (structure) of the argument and can be detected without knowing the subject matter. Examples: undistributed middle, illicit major, illicit minor, exclusive premises, four terms, affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, existential fallacy. Informal fallacies arise from the content, language or context of the argument. They are grouped as fallacies of relevance, ambiguity and presumption.

t: 5.2 Fallacies of relevance (premises are irrelevant to the conclusion)
p: Fallacies · Logical Reasoning
x: Fallacy Latin name Meaning Example Appeal to force Argumentum ad baculum Threat is used in place of proof Accept my view or lose your job Appeal to pity Ad misericordiam Sympathy replaces evidence Pass me, I will lose my scholarship Appeal to the people Ad populum Popularity or crowd emotion is used Everyone believes it, so it is true Argument against the person Ad hominem Attacks the speaker, not the argument (abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque) He is a liar, so his theory is wrong Appeal to improper authority Ad verecundiam Cites an authority outside their field A film star's view on nuclear physics Appeal to ignorance Ad ignorantiam Claims truth because falsity is unproved (or vice versa) No one has disproved ghosts, so they exist Irrelevant conclusion Ignoratio elenchi Proves something other than the point at issue Argues about crime to justify a tax Red herring Diverts attention with an irrelevant issue Straw man Misrepresents the opponent's view so it can be easily refuted Tu quoque "You do it too" (a form of ad hominem circumstantial) Genetic fallacy Judges a claim by its origin It came from a politician, so it is false

p: Fallacies · Logical Reasoning
x: Begging the question ( petitio principii ): the conclusion is assumed in the premises; circular reasoning. Complex (loaded) question: a question presupposing a point not yet granted ("Have you stopped cheating?"). False cause ( non causa pro causa ): treating a non-cause as a cause. Its best-known type is post hoc ergo propter hoc (after this, therefore because of this). Accident: applying a general rule to a special case where it does not apply. Converse accident (hasty generalisation): moving from an exceptional or unrepresentative case to a general rule. False dilemma: presenting only two alternatives when more exist. Slippery slope: claiming one step will inevitably lead to a chain of bad consequences. Naturalistic fallacy (G. E. Moore): deriving "good" from a natural property such as "pleasant" or "natural".

t: 5.4 Fallacies of ambiguity (language is used in shifting senses)
p: Fallacies · Logical Reasoning
x: Fallacy Cause Equivocation A word is used in two different senses in the same argument Amphiboly Ambiguity from loose or faulty grammar and sentence construction Accent Shifting emphasis or stress changes the meaning Composition What is true of the parts is inferred to be true of the whole Division What is true of the whole is inferred to be true of each part Trap: composition and division are opposites. "Each brick is light, so the wall is light" is composition. "The team is excellent, so each player is excellent" is division.

p: Uses of Language, Terms, Connotation and Denotation, Definitions · Logical Reasoning
x: Use Purpose Truth-valued? Example Informative Conveys information; affirms or denies propositions Yes Water boils at 100°C Expressive Expresses or evokes feelings and attitudes No Ouch! What a beautiful sunset! Directive Causes or prevents action (commands, requests, advice) No (but can be right or wrong, effective or not) Submit the form by Monday Some writers add a fourth, ceremonial or performative use ("I now pronounce you..."). Most real sentences mix several uses. Disagreements: a verbal dispute arises merely from different meanings given to a word; a factual dispute concerns an actual matter of fact. Emotive meaning is the feeling attached to a word ("slim" versus "skinny"); cognitive meaning is its informative content.

p: Uses of Language, Terms, Connotation and Denotation, Definitions · Logical Reasoning
x: Denotation (extension): the class of objects to which a term applies. The denotation of "planet" is Mercury, Venus, Earth and so on. Connotation (intension): the set of attributes the term signifies. The connotation of "triangle" is closed plane figure with three sides. Inverse relation (traditional view): as connotation increases, denotation decreases, and vice versa. "Animal" has a wide denotation and small connotation; "Indian male Nobel laureate in physics" has a very large connotation and very small denotation. A term may have connotation but no denotation ("unicorn").

p: Uses of Language, Terms, Connotation and Denotation, Definitions · Logical Reasoning
x: Basis Kinds Number of objects Singular (Delhi), General (city), Collective (committee, army) Nature Concrete (table), Abstract (honesty) Quality Positive (healthy), Negative (non-smoker), Privative (blind, deaf) Relation Relative (father/son), Absolute

p: Uses of Language, Terms, Connotation and Denotation, Definitions · Logical Reasoning
x: The term to be defined is the definiendum ; the words that define it are the definiens . Kinds of definition by purpose: Stipulative: assigns a new meaning for a particular purpose (cannot be true or false). Lexical: reports established dictionary usage (can be true or false). Precising: reduces vagueness of an existing meaning. Theoretical: gives a theoretical account of a subject ("heat is molecular motion"). Persuasive: uses emotive language to influence attitudes. Kinds by method: Extensional (denotative): lists members or points to examples (including ostensive definition). Intensional (connotative): gives the attributes, including genus and differentia ("Man is a rational animal": animal is the genus, rational is the differentia), synonym and operational definition. Rules of a good definition: it should state the essential attributes; must not be circular; must not be too wide or too narrow; must not be obscure, figurative or ambiguous; and should not be negative where an affirmative one is possible.

p: Uses of Language, Terms, Connotation and Denotation, Definitions · Logical Reasoning
x: Predicable Meaning Example (man) Genus The wider class Animal Species The narrower class Man (under animal) Differentia Essential quality that separates a species from others in the genus Rational Property (proprium) Necessary but not essential quality Capable of laughter (risible) Accident Non-essential, separable quality Being tall or fair

p: Induction and Analogy · Logical Reasoning
x: Induction extends from observed to unobserved cases. The conclusion is only probable , and the argument is judged strong or weak . Perfect induction (complete enumeration) is deductive in force; imperfect induction rests on a sample. The inductive leap is justified by the uniformity of nature and the law of causation .

p: Induction and Analogy · Logical Reasoning
x: Method Principle Key idea Agreement If instances of a phenomenon have only one circumstance in common, that circumstance is the cause (or effect) Look for what is common Difference If an instance where the phenomenon occurs and one where it does not differ in only one circumstance, that circumstance is the cause Look for the single difference Joint Method of Agreement and Difference Combines the two to reduce error Double check Residues Subtract the part known to be caused by earlier antecedents; the remainder is caused by the remaining antecedent Look at the remainder Concomitant Variation Two phenomena that vary together in degree are causally connected Look at variation in degree The method of difference is the most reliable (it is the basis of the controlled experiment); agreement is the weakest because common factors may be coincidental. Concomitant variation is used when the cause cannot be removed (the tides and the moon).

p: Induction and Analogy · Logical Reasoning
x: An analogy argues that because two or more things are alike in some known respects, they are likely alike in a further respect. It is an inductive argument; the conclusion is probable ; it is judged strong or weak . Form: A has properties a, b, c and d; B has properties a, b and c; therefore B probably has d. What strengthens an analogy: A larger number of relevant similarities. A larger number and variety of cases compared. Greater relevance of the shared properties to the conclusion property. A more modest (less ambitious) conclusion relative to the premises. What weakens it: relevant dissimilarities , irrelevant or superficial similarities ( false analogy ), and an over-ambitious conclusion. Related points: Paley's watchmaker argument (design implies a designer) is a classic analogy. Refutation by logical analogy shows an argument is invalid by producing a parallel argument of identical form with obviously true premises and a false conclusion. In Indian logic the corresponding pramana is upamana . Verbal and number analogy items ("Pen : Write :: Knife : Cut") test the relationship : part–whole, cause–effect, tool–function, genus–species, synonym, antonym, producer–product, degree, sequence. First find the relation between the first pair, then apply it to the second pair.

p: Venn Diagrams and Testing Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Venn diagrams (John Venn ) represent classes as overlapping circles. They follow the Boolean interpretation. A two-circle diagram has 4 regions (including outside); a three-circle diagram has 8 regions . Shading an area means the area is empty . An X means the area has at least one member . An X on a boundary line means the member is in one of the two regions, but it is unknown which.

p: Venn Diagrams and Testing Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Proposition Diagram A: All S is P Shade the part of S outside P E: No S is P Shade the overlap of S and P I: Some S is P Put an X in the overlap O: Some S is not P Put an X in S outside P

p: Venn Diagrams and Testing Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Draw three overlapping circles labelled S, P and M. Diagram the universal premise first (shading), then the particular premise (X). Do not diagram the conclusion. Check whether the conclusion is already shown. If yes, the syllogism is valid ; if not, it is invalid . When an X can fall in two regions, place it on the line; a conclusion needing the X in a definite region is then not established. Worked example. All A are B; All B are C; therefore All A are C. Shade A outside B; shade B outside C. The part of A outside C is then fully shaded, so the conclusion is already shown. Valid (Barbara). Existential fallacy: because Venn diagrams use the Boolean view, a syllogism needing existential import (for example AAI-1, universal premises with a particular conclusion) shows as invalid on the diagram.

t: 8.4 Euler diagrams and everyday class relations
p: Venn Diagrams and Testing Validity · Logical Reasoning
x: Euler diagrams show only the actual relationship between classes: one circle inside another (all S is P), separate circles (no S is P), overlapping circles (some S is P), identical circles (same members). Standard class-relation patterns (frequent in exams): Dog, Cat, Animal: two separate circles inside a larger circle. Mother, Sister, Woman: two overlapping circles inside the Woman circle (a woman may be both). Doctors, Women, Teachers: the circles overlap each other as the data allow; test each stated relation. Man, Woman, Human: two separate circles inside the Human circle. Tiger, Lion, Carnivore: two separate circles inside the Carnivore circle.

p: Indian Logic: Means of Knowledge (Pramana Theory) · Logical Reasoning
x: Indian epistemology asks how valid knowledge arises. Nyaya names four factors: Term Meaning Pramata The knower (subject) Prameya The object of knowledge Pramana The means (instrument) of valid knowledge Prama (or Pramiti ) Valid knowledge, the result Prama is yathartha anubhava , true (right) experience (Tarkasamgraha). Cognition ( buddhi ) is divided into smriti (memory) and anubhava (experience). Anubhava is prama (valid) or aprama (invalid, covering samshaya doubt, viparyaya error and tarka hypothetical reasoning). Smriti is not counted a pramana because it only reproduces an earlier experience and is not a fresh cognition.
