A statement that equates research with mere data collection, or that says it needs no hypothesis in any form, is a trap. Remember that methodology is broader than methods: every question that asks “the study of methods and the reasoning behind them” points to methodology.

p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Good research is recognisable by a cluster of features that make it trustworthy. It is systematic because it follows ordered steps, logical because conclusions follow from evidence by valid reasoning, empirical because it rests on observation and data rather than speculation, and objective because the personal views of the researcher are kept out of the procedure as far as possible. It is replicable , meaning another researcher using the same method on similar subjects should get comparable results, and cumulative , since each study builds on earlier ones and adds to a body of knowledge. It is problem-oriented , controlled (variables are identified and extraneous influences are minimised), critical (assumptions are questioned) and ethical . Research also aims at generalisation, although action research and many qualitative studies deliberately give that up in return for depth and local relevance. Core features: systematic, logical, empirical, objective, replicable, verifiable, cumulative, precise, problem-focused, ethical. Replicability and objectivity are what separate scientific research from opinion. Research is cyclical: findings raise new questions, which start the next cycle. Reliable tools and valid measures are part of the character of good research. “Research is always completely value-free” is too strong; the realistic position is that objectivity is a goal, and qualitative research openly admits researcher subjectivity. Be careful with an option that says research always aims at universal laws; applied and action research aim at solving specific problems.

p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: The scientific method is the disciplined way of acquiring knowledge: observe a phenomenon, define a problem, form a hypothesis, test it by collecting evidence under controlled conditions, analyse the results, and then accept, modify or reject the hypothesis, which may feed into a theory. Behind the method lies a scientific attitude , which means curiosity, open-mindedness, healthy scepticism, honesty in reporting, objectivity, and readiness to revise beliefs when evidence demands it. Reasoning takes two classical forms. Deductive reasoning goes from general premises to a particular conclusion (all humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal), and the conclusion is certain if the premises are true. Inductive reasoning goes from particular observations to a general statement, and the conclusion is only probable. Modern research usually combines both in the hypothetico-deductive cycle: induction suggests a hypothesis and deduction derives testable consequences. Deduction: general to particular, associated with Aristotle and the syllogism. Induction: particular to general, associated with Francis Bacon. Parsimony (Occam’s razor): among competing explanations, prefer the simplest that fits the facts. Serendipity: a valuable discovery made by accident but recognised through a prepared mind (the term is from Horace Walpole; penicillin is the usual example). Abduction (C. S. Peirce): inference to the best explanation. Do not mix up the directions: if the statement moves from many observed cases to a rule, it is induction. A deductive argument can be valid yet false if a premise is false. Scientific attitude includes scepticism, not dogmatic belief.

p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: A variable is any characteristic that can take different values across persons, objects or occasions, such as age, income or teaching method. The independent variable (IV) is the presumed cause, manipulated or selected by the researcher; the dependent variable (DV) is the presumed effect that is measured. An extraneous variable is any other factor that might affect the DV and must be controlled; when it actually varies together with the IV and muddies the conclusion it is called a confounding variable . An intervening (mediating) variable lies between IV and DV and explains how the effect happens, but it is a hypothetical construct that is not directly observed, such as motivation between teaching method and achievement. A moderator variable changes the strength or direction of the IV–DV relationship, for example gender changing how strongly study hours affect marks. An attribute variable (age, sex, caste) is a characteristic that the researcher can only select, never assign. IV = cause/predictor/treatment; DV = effect/outcome/criterion. Mediator explains how or why ; moderator explains for whom or when . Continuous variables take any value in a range (height); discrete take whole counts (number of children). Control variables are held constant deliberately. The classic confusion is moderator versus mediator versus confounder. Ask: is it in the causal chain (mediator), does it alter the strength of the relationship (moderator), or is it an uncontrolled outside factor spoiling the comparison (confounder)? Also, an attribute variable cannot be experimentally manipulated, which is why such studies are ex post facto.

p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable statement about the relationship between variables, formed before data collection and expected to be confirmed or rejected by evidence. A good hypothesis is clear, specific, testable, consistent with existing knowledge, and expressed in simple terms. The null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no difference or no relationship; the alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha) states that there is. A theory is a more developed body of interrelated concepts, definitions and propositions that explains and predicts a wide range of phenomena; it sits above a single hypothesis, and a well-supported theory is not a guess. A concept is an abstract idea, a construct is a concept deliberately built for research, and an operational definition states exactly how that construct will be measured, such as defining “intelligence” as the score on a named test. Operational definitions are the reason studies can be replicated. Hypothesis → tested; theory → explains; law → describes a regularity that holds without exception in its domain. Operational definition: concept turned into measurable procedure (operationalism is linked to P. W. Bridgman). Parsimony is a desirable quality of a theory; replicability needs clear operational definitions. Hypotheses are never “proved”; we reject or fail to reject H0. Watch the wording “accept the null hypothesis”; the correct statistical language is “fail to reject”. A hypothesis that cannot be tested is not a scientific hypothesis. The conceptual definition is dictionary-like; only the operational one tells you how to measure.

t: 1A.6 Reliability and Validity of Research Tools
p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Reliability means consistency: a tool is reliable if it gives similar results under similar conditions. Validity means that the tool measures what it claims to measure. Reliability is checked by test–retest (stability over time), parallel or alternate forms (equivalence), split-half (internal consistency, usually corrected with the Spearman–Brown formula), Cronbach’s alpha or Kuder–Richardson (KR-20) for internal consistency, and inter-rater reliability when judges score responses. Validity has several types: content validity (the items fairly cover the subject; face validity is a surface judgement of this), criterion-related validity (agreement with an external standard, either concurrent or predictive), and construct validity (the tool measures the theoretical trait, shown by convergent and discriminant evidence). Reliability ≠ validity; reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A valid instrument is necessarily reliable; a reliable instrument may be invalid (a scale that is consistently 2 kg off). Alpha of about 0.70 or above is usually treated as acceptable. Predictive validity: tool today predicts future performance; concurrent: agrees with a present criterion. If an option says a reliable test must be valid, it is wrong. The target analogy helps: tight shots away from the bullseye = reliable but not valid; shots on the bullseye = both.

p: Meaning and Characteristics of Research · Research Aptitude
x: The research process is a sequence: choosing a problem, reviewing literature, formulating objectives and hypotheses, preparing the research design, deciding the sample, collecting data, analysing and interpreting it, and finally writing the report. A pilot study is a small preliminary trial that tests the tools, procedure and feasibility before the main study. The research design is the overall plan or blueprint that specifies what data are needed, from whom, by what method and how they will be analysed. Kerlinger’s MAX-MIN-CON principle says a good design maximises systematic (experimental) variance, minimises error variance and controls extraneous variance. Data are primary when collected first-hand for the present purpose and secondary when collected earlier by someone else for another purpose. Order: problem → literature review → hypothesis → design → sampling → data collection → analysis → report. Pilot study: tests tools and feasibility; not meant to prove hypotheses. Primary data: questionnaire, interview, observation. Secondary data: census reports, journals, records. Design = blueprint; methodology = reasoning behind the methods. Questions on “first step” almost always point to identifying and defining the problem. A pilot study is not the same as a preliminary hypothesis test.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Fundamental research aims to expand knowledge and develop or test theory for its own sake, without immediate concern for practical use. It asks why and how things are, and its findings are meant to be general. Typical examples are studies on the nature of learning, the structure of matter or how language develops. Its value is judged by its contribution to theory, and although it may look useless at first, it often becomes the base of later applied work. Also called pure or basic research; theory-oriented; high generalisability. Done mostly in universities and laboratories with a long time horizon. Example: testing a theory of motivation, formulating a law. If the outcome is an immediate practical solution, it is applied or action research, not fundamental.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Applied research uses existing knowledge to solve a practical problem of a particular group, organisation or society. It tests whether a theory or technique works in real conditions, so it is concerned with usefulness. Evaluating a new teaching method, testing a drug, and market research are standard examples. Its conclusions are valid for the context studied and may be generalised only with care. Aim: solve a problem; users: managers, planners, teachers, policy makers. Example: effect of a remedial programme on learning outcomes. Applied research draws on the theories produced by fundamental research. Applied research is not “less scientific”; it follows the same rigour. The difference lies in aim and use.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Action research is carried out by practitioners (for example a teacher) in their own working situation to solve an immediate local problem and improve practice. The term was coined by Kurt Lewin in the mid-1940s, who described a spiral of planning, action and fact-finding about the result of the action. In education it was popularised by Stephen Corey, and Kemmis and McTaggart gave the widely used cycle of plan, act, observe and reflect. The researcher is a participant, the sample is usually the researcher’s own class or group, and findings are used at once to revise the next cycle. Generalisation to other settings is limited. Participatory action research (PAR) goes further and treats the community as co-researchers for empowerment and change. Coined: Kurt Lewin. Popularised in education: Stephen Corey. Cycle: plan → act → observe → reflect, repeated as a spiral. Features: practitioner-led, local, cyclical, collaborative, immediate application. First step: identify the problem or area of improvement. Options claiming that action research gives universally generalisable results, or is conducted by outside experts only, are wrong.

t: 1B.4 Fundamental, Applied and Action Research Compared
p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: The three types sit on a spectrum from theory to practice. Fundamental research targets knowledge and theory, applied research targets the solution of a problem for a wider group, and action research targets improvement within one specific setting and is done by those who work there. Understanding the contrasts lets you answer match-type and “which is correct” questions without memorising each example. The most immediate local application belongs to action research; the greatest generalisation belongs to fundamental research. Feature Fundamental Applied Action Main aim Knowledge, theory Solve a practical problem Improve local practice Who researches Scholar or scientist Researcher for client or society Practitioner Setting Often laboratory Real-world Own workplace or classroom Generalisation High Moderate Low Time to use Long term Medium Immediate

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: These types are classified by purpose. Exploratory research is used when little is known; it uses a flexible design, literature survey, expert interviews or case studies to gain insight and to generate hypotheses. Descriptive research describes characteristics of a population or phenomenon as they are, answering what, who, where and how many; surveys, fact-finding enquiries and correlational studies fall here, and no variable is manipulated. Explanatory research (causal or analytical) asks why, tests hypotheses about cause and effect, and often uses experiments or advanced statistics. Exploratory: formulates hypotheses; flexible; qualitative leaning. Descriptive: what is; surveys, correlational studies; no manipulation. Explanatory: why; tests causal hypotheses. Correlational research shows association, not cause. Correlation does not imply causation. A survey is descriptive even if it uses statistics.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: A cross-sectional study collects data from different groups at one point in time, for example children of ages 6, 9 and 12 measured this month; it is quick and inexpensive but cannot follow individual change. A longitudinal study collects data repeatedly over a long period. Within it, a trend study samples different people from the same population at different times, a cohort study follows a group sharing a common experience such as birth year, and a panel study follows exactly the same individuals at each wave. Longitudinal designs show true change but suffer from attrition and high cost. Cross-sectional: one time, many groups. Longitudinal: many times, same or similar units. Panel = same individuals every time; trend = different samples; cohort = shared event. Weakness: attrition (dropouts) in panel studies. Different samples at different times is a trend study, not a panel study.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Quantitative research measures variables numerically, usually follows a deductive logic, uses large samples and statistics, and aims at generalisation. Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and context in words, uses inductive logic, small purposive samples and interpretive analysis. Mixed-methods research integrates both, either by running them together (convergent), by following quantitative with qualitative to explain results (explanatory sequential), or by exploring qualitatively first and then testing quantitatively (exploratory sequential), a framework associated with John Creswell. Among qualitative approaches, grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss, 1967) builds theory from data, ethnography studies a culture through long field immersion, and phenomenology (rooted in Husserl) studies lived experience. Quantitative: numbers, deductive, objective, generalisable. Qualitative: words, inductive, contextual, rich description. Grounded theory: Glaser and Strauss, 1967. Ethnography: culture. Phenomenology: lived experience. Triangulation is combining methods or data sources to cross-check findings. Do not label grounded theory as quantitative. Mixed methods is not simply using two questionnaires; it needs integration of both strands.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Conceptual research is based on abstract ideas and reasoning, with no direct data collection; philosophers and theorists develop or reinterpret concepts, and thought experiments such as Einstein’s belong here. Empirical research is data-based, resting on observation or experiment and capable of verification by experience; it is sometimes called experimental type research. In law, the matching pair is doctrinal (study of statutes and cases) and non-doctrinal or empirical research. Conceptual = theory and reasoning; empirical = observation and data. Empirical research tests hypotheses against evidence. A literature-only philosophical analysis is conceptual even if it is long and systematic.

t: 1B.9 Case Study, Experimental, Historical and Ex Post Facto Research
p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: A case study is an intensive investigation of a single unit such as a person, school or community, giving depth rather than breadth. Experimental research manipulates the independent variable, uses a control group and random assignment, and so can establish cause and effect. Historical research studies past events using primary and secondary sources and criticism of those sources. Ex post facto (causal-comparative) research studies a presumed cause after it has already occurred; the researcher cannot manipulate the independent variable, so conclusions about cause are weaker than in experiments. Case study: depth, single unit; Yin is the best-known method writer. Experiment: manipulation + control + randomisation. Ex post facto: “after the fact”; no manipulation; Kerlinger’s definition stresses lack of direct control. If the researcher cannot assign participants to groups (gender, caste, past illness), the design is ex post facto, not experimental.

p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Evaluation research judges the worth or effectiveness of a programme, policy or product. Formative evaluation is done during the programme to improve it, and summative evaluation at the end to judge outcomes (the distinction is credited to Michael Scriven). Other forms include process and impact evaluation. Interdisciplinary research integrates concepts and methods from two or more disciplines to address a problem that no single discipline can handle; it differs from multidisciplinary work, where disciplines work side by side without real integration, and transdisciplinary work, which also involves non-academic stakeholders. Formative = during, to improve. Summative = at the end, to judge. Multi = side by side; inter = integrated; trans = crosses boundaries including society. Do not reverse formative and summative.

t: 1B.11 Content Analysis, Census, Field, Laboratory Research and Meta-analysis
p: Types of Research · Research Aptitude
x: Content analysis systematically codes and quantifies the content of communication such as texts, speeches or media (Berelson is the classic source). A census is complete enumeration of every unit of the population, whereas a sample survey studies a part. Field research is done in the natural setting and has high realism but less control; laboratory research is done in an artificial controlled setting and has high control but lower realism. Meta-analysis statistically combines the results of many independent studies to estimate an overall effect (the term was coined by Gene Glass in 1976). The Delphi technique collects expert opinion through several anonymous rounds with feedback until consensus emerges. Meta-analysis: Gene Glass, 1976. Delphi: expert panel, anonymity, iterative rounds. Census = every unit; no sampling error but costly. A systematic review is not necessarily a meta-analysis; only the latter pools effect sizes statistically.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Positivism is the view that genuine knowledge comes from sensory experience and scientific method, and that social phenomena can be studied like natural ones. It was named and systematised by Auguste Comte (1798–1857) in his Course of Positive Philosophy ; he also coined the word “sociology”. Comte’s law of three stages says that human thought passes from the theological stage (explanations by gods and spirits), through the metaphysical stage (abstract forces and essences), to the positive or scientific stage (observation and laws). Earlier roots lie in the empiricism of Bacon and Hume and in Saint-Simon’s ideas; Durkheim later applied positivist method to sociology. Founder: Auguste Comte; coined “positivism” and “sociology”. Three stages: theological → metaphysical → positive. Sociology as the “queen” of sciences in his hierarchy. The stage order is a favourite match item; keep it in historical sequence, theological first.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Positivism assumes a single, objective, external reality (realist ontology), that the researcher can stand apart from what is studied (objectivist epistemology), and that research should be free of values (value-free axiology). Methodologically it favours experiments and surveys, quantitative measurement, hypothesis testing through the hypothetico-deductive model, and the search for law-like generalisations. Observation is supposed to be neutral, causes are sought through control, and knowledge grows by verification. Ontology: one objective reality. Epistemology: objective, detached researcher. Axiology: value-free. Methods: experiment, survey, statistics; deductive; generalisation. Related ideas: empiricism, determinism, reductionism, parsimony. Statements such as “reality is socially constructed” or “multiple realities” are not positivist; they belong to constructivism.

t: 1C.3 Logical Positivism and the Verification Principle
p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Logical positivism emerged in the 1920s–30s in the Vienna Circle (Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath) and was popularised in English by A. J. Ayer in Language, Truth and Logic (1936). Its central claim, the verification principle , holds that a statement is meaningful only if it is either analytically true (true by definition, as in logic and mathematics) or empirically verifiable. Metaphysical, ethical and theological claims were therefore dismissed as meaningless. The doctrine was criticised because the verification principle itself is neither analytic nor empirically verifiable. Vienna Circle: Schlick, Carnap, Neurath; Ayer in Britain. Verification principle: meaning = verifiability. Criticised by Popper (falsification) and Quine. Verification (logical positivism) and falsification (Popper) are opposites in emphasis; do not interchange them.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Karl Popper rejected verification and induction. In The Logic of Scientific Discovery (German 1934, English 1959) he argued that what separates science from non-science is falsifiability : a scientific theory must make claims that could, in principle, be refuted by observation. No amount of confirming instances proves a universal law, but a single contrary instance (one black swan) can refute it. Science advances by bold conjectures and severe attempts at refutation, a position called critical rationalism . Popper cited Marxist history and Freudian psychoanalysis as theories so flexible that nothing could count against them, contrasting them with Einstein’s risky predictions. His ideas are the starting point of post-positivism. Key concept: falsifiability as the demarcation criterion. Books: Logic of Scientific Discovery ; Conjectures and Refutations ; The Open Society and Its Enemies . Theories are corroborated, never finally proved. If an option says science proves theories true by repeated confirmation, it contradicts Popper.

t: 1C.5 Kuhn, Lakatos, Feyerabend and Paradigm Shift
p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Thomas Kuhn’s The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) argued that science does not grow only by steady accumulation. Mature science works in normal science within a shared paradigm; accumulating anomalies create a crisis , followed by a scientific revolution and a paradigm shift to a new framework, such as the move from Newtonian to Einsteinian physics. Rival paradigms are partly incommensurable . Imre Lakatos offered a middle path with research programmes made of a hard core protected by a belt of auxiliary hypotheses, judged as progressive or degenerating. Paul Feyerabend, in Against Method , defended epistemological anarchism with the slogan “anything goes”. Kuhn: paradigm, normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution. Lakatos: research programmes. Feyerabend: epistemological anarchism. Popper: falsification. Sequence: pre-science → normal science → anomalies → crisis → revolution → new normal science. Keep the pairing of thinker and concept firm; match questions test exactly this.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Post-positivism keeps the aim of studying reality scientifically but admits that humans can know it only imperfectly. It is often described as critical realism : a real world exists, yet our observations are theory-laden, fallible and shaped by the observer’s background. Objectivity is therefore a regulative ideal rather than an achievable state. Researchers use multiple methods and triangulation to approximate truth, accept probabilistic rather than certain conclusions, and hold that hypotheses are not proved but only not yet rejected. Quantitative methods remain common, though qualitative ones are accepted. Influential discussions come from Popper, Kuhn, Guba and Lincoln, Phillips and Burbules, and Roy Bhaskar’s critical realism. Ontology: critical realism (reality exists but is imperfectly apprehended). Epistemology: modified objectivist; knowledge is fallible. Triangulation and falsification are central. Observation is theory-laden. Post-positivism is a modification of positivism, not a rejection of science; it should not be confused with constructivism.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: These three terms define a research paradigm. Ontology asks what exists and what reality is. Epistemology asks how we can know it and what relationship the knower has with the known. Axiology asks about the role of values and ethics in research. The combination determines the methodology, meaning the practical way of studying the problem. Map each statement to its question word: “what is real” is ontology, “how do we know” is epistemology, “what role do values play” is axiology. Paradigm Ontology Epistemology Axiology Typical methods Positivism One objective reality Objective, detached Value-free Experiments, surveys Post-positivism Critical realism Modified objectivity Mostly value-aware Mixed, triangulation Interpretivism / constructivism Multiple socially constructed realities Subjective, co-constructed Value-bound Interviews, ethnography Critical theory Reality shaped by power Transactional Value-laden, emancipatory Participatory, dialogic Pragmatism Reality is what works Practical Both Mixed methods

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: Interpretivism holds that social life must be understood from the meanings people give to it; Max Weber’s Verstehen (interpretive understanding) and the hermeneutic tradition of Dilthey and Gadamer are key sources. Constructivism adds that reality is socially constructed (Berger and Luckmann), so there are multiple realities and the researcher is part of the inquiry. Phenomenology (Husserl, Schutz) studies lived experience. These paradigms prefer qualitative methods and rich description. Critical theory , from the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Horkheimer, Habermas), goes further by examining power and inequality and aiming at emancipation. Hermeneutics is the theory and method of interpretation, originally of texts. Weber: Verstehen. Dilthey and Gadamer: hermeneutics. Husserl: phenomenology. Critical theory: Frankfurt School; emancipation. Constructivism: multiple, socially constructed realities. A statement about the goal of explanation and prediction through laws is positivist; a statement about understanding meaning is interpretivist.

p: Positivism and Post-positivism · Research Aptitude
x: A paradigm, in the sense used by Kuhn and later by Guba and Lincoln, is a worldview that shapes what questions are asked and how they are answered. Pragmatism , drawn from Peirce, James and Dewey, rejects the fight between paradigms and chooses whatever method best answers the question; it is often called the philosophy of mixed methods. Triangulation means using more than one source, method, investigator or theory to cross-check findings. Norman Denzin listed four types: data, investigator, theory and methodological triangulation. Pragmatism: what works; philosophical base of mixed methods. Denzin’s triangulation types: data, investigator, theory, methodological. Triangulation improves credibility and validity. Triangulation is about convergence of evidence, not about increasing sample size.

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: The experimental method is the research strategy in which the investigator deliberately manipulates one or more independent variables, controls other influences, and observes the effect on a dependent variable. Because the researcher decides who receives the treatment, it is the strongest method for establishing cause and effect. A true experiment has three hallmarks: manipulation of the independent variable, control (usually through a control group and constancy of conditions) and randomisation. R. A. Fisher laid the statistical foundations in the 1920s–30s with the principles of randomisation, replication and local control (blocking), and developed analysis of variance. J. S. Mill’s canons (agreement, difference, concomitant variation and residues) are the older logical ancestors of experimental reasoning. Experiments may run in a laboratory (high control) or in the field (high realism). Three hallmarks: manipulation, control, randomisation. Fisher: randomisation, replication, local control; ANOVA and the F-ratio. Experimental group receives the treatment; control group does not, or receives the standard treatment. Laboratory experiment = more control; field experiment = more realism. If the researcher cannot manipulate the independent variable, the study is not a true experiment, however carefully it is analysed.

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: The control group gives the baseline against which the effect of the treatment is judged. For that comparison to be fair, the groups must be equivalent at the start. Random assignment gives every participant an equal chance of being placed in any group, so that known and unknown differences are spread out evenly on average; this is the main safeguard of internal validity. Do not confuse it with random selection , which is the way a sample is drawn from the population and supports external validity. When randomisation is impossible or the sample is small, matching pairs participants who are alike on a key variable such as IQ or age and then splits each pair between groups. Matching controls only the variables that were matched, which is its weakness. Counterbalancing varies the order of conditions across participants to control order effects in repeated-measures designs. Random assignment → internal validity. Random selection → external validity. Matching controls only measured variables; randomisation controls unmeasured ones too. Blocking: group units into homogeneous blocks and randomise within each block. An option that says randomisation guarantees identical groups is wrong; it makes them equivalent only in probability.

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: The placebo effect is an improvement caused by a participant’s expectation rather than by the actual treatment, so many medical and psychological experiments give the control group an inert substance or sham procedure. Blinding prevents expectations from distorting results. In a single-blind design the participants do not know which group they are in; in a double-blind design neither the participants nor the experimenters who deal with them know; in a triple-blind design the data analysts are also unaware. Double-blinding guards against demand characteristics (participants guessing what is wanted) and experimenter bias (the Rosenthal or Pygmalion effect, in which the researcher’s expectations unintentionally influence outcomes). Single blind: participants unaware. Double blind: participants and experimenter unaware. Placebo group controls for expectation, not for the treatment itself. Rosenthal effect: experimenter expectancy. If an option says neither the participants nor the experimenter knows the assignment, that is double-blind, whatever else is added.

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: Following Campbell and Stanley (1963), internal validity is the extent to which the observed change in the dependent variable can really be attributed to the independent variable rather than to something else. External validity is the extent to which the results can be generalised to other persons (population validity), places (ecological validity) and times. Cook and Campbell (1979) added construct validity (are the concepts correctly operationalised) and statistical conclusion validity (are the statistical inferences sound). There is a trade-off: tight laboratory control raises internal validity but may lower external validity, whereas field studies do the reverse. Internal = causal certainty. External = generalisability. Campbell and Stanley (1963) classic list of threats; Cook and Campbell (1979) extension. A study that is not internally valid cannot be externally valid in any useful sense. Do not treat reliability and internal validity as the same thing; reliability is consistency of measurement, internal validity is soundness of causal inference.

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: Threats to internal validity are rival explanations for the observed effect. History is an outside event occurring between pretest and posttest. Maturation is natural change in participants with time (growing older, tired or wiser). Testing is the effect of taking a pretest on the later score. Instrumentation is a change in the measuring tool or the observers. Statistical regression is the tendency of extreme scorers to move toward the mean on retesting. Selection means groups differ from the start. Mortality (attrition) is the loss of participants, especially when dropouts differ between groups. Threats to external validity include pretest sensitisation, interaction of selection and treatment, reactive arrangements such as the Hawthorne effect (behaviour changes because people know they are being studied, from the Western Electric studies associated with Elton Mayo) and multiple-treatment interference. Internal threats: History, Maturation, Testing, Instrumentation, Regression, Selection, Mortality (memory cue: HMTIRSM). Hawthorne effect = awareness of being observed; John Henry effect = control group works harder to compete. Regression to the mean affects groups chosen for extreme scores. Distinguish history (outside event) from maturation (internal change over time) and testing (effect of the pretest itself).

p: Experimental Method · Research Aptitude
x: Pre-experimental designs lack control, for instance the one-shot case study (X then O), the one-group pretest–posttest (O X O) and the static-group comparison; they cannot rule out many threats. True experimental designs use random assignment: the posttest-only control group design (R X O / R O), the pretest–posttest control group design (R O X O / R O O) and the Solomon four-group design (Solomon, 1949), which combines both to detect the effect of pretesting. Quasi-experimental designs, such as the non-equivalent control group design or the time-series design, compare groups without random assignment. Factorial designs study two or more independent variables at once and reveal interaction effects ; a 2 × 3 design has two factors with 2 and 3 levels. A randomised block design controls one nuisance variable, and a Latin square controls two by arranging treatments so each appears once in every row and column. Within-subjects (repeated-measures) designs expose the same people to all conditions, while between-subjects designs use different people for each condition. Solomon four-group: four groups, controls pretest sensitisation. Factorial design: main effects + interaction; analysed by ANOVA. Latin square: controls two extraneous variables (rows and columns). Quasi-experiment: no random assignment. A one-group pretest–posttest design looks experimental but is pre-experimental, because it has no control group.

p: Descriptive Method · Research Aptitude
x: Descriptive research describes things as they are: the present status of a population, the opinions people hold, the conditions that exist, the processes going on or the trends developing. It does not manipulate variables. The main forms are surveys, case studies, developmental or growth studies, correlational studies, comparative studies and observational studies. A survey collects information from a sample or the whole population, usually by questionnaire, interview or schedule; it may be cross-sectional (once) or longitudinal (repeatedly). In a panel study the same respondents are surveyed again and again, which makes change at the individual level visible. Surveys give breadth and are efficient for large populations, but they establish association rather than cause and are open to response bias. Descriptive = what is; no manipulation; includes survey, case study, correlational, developmental studies. Panel study: same respondents repeatedly; trend study: new samples each time. Opinion polls and census-type enquiries are surveys. A statement that a survey can prove causation is wrong; it can only show association.

p: Descriptive Method · Research Aptitude
x: A questionnaire is a set of written questions answered by the respondent without an interviewer. It reaches a scattered sample cheaply and removes interviewer bias, but it needs literate respondents and a mailed questionnaire often suffers from a low return rate. A schedule contains similar questions but is filled in by an enumerator, so it can be used with illiterate respondents and gives higher response, at higher cost. Questions can be closed (fixed options) or open-ended ; they should avoid leading, loaded and double-barrelled wording, and the instrument should be pilot-tested. An interview may be structured (fixed questions), semi-structured or unstructured, and uses probing and rapport. Observation may be participant (the observer joins the group, as in ethnographies) or non-participant, structured or unstructured, and is open to observer bias and the Hawthorne effect. Questionnaire: self-administered; schedule: filled by the investigator. Mailed questionnaire: wide coverage, low response, no interviewer bias. Leading question: suggests the expected answer, so it biases responses. Participant observation gives depth but risks losing objectivity. If respondents are illiterate, the correct tool is a schedule or interview, not a mailed questionnaire.

p: Descriptive Method · Research Aptitude
x: Attitude scales convert opinions into scores. The Likert scale (1932) is a summated rating scale in which respondents mark agreement on a five-point range from strongly agree to strongly disagree and the item scores are added. The Thurstone scale (1929) uses statements pre-rated by judges to be equal-appearing intervals, and respondents agree with those they accept. The Guttman scale (scalogram, 1944) uses cumulative, unidimensional items so that agreement with a stronger item implies agreement with the weaker ones. Osgood’s semantic differential (1957) uses bipolar adjective pairs (good–bad) on a seven-point range to measure the meaning of a concept along evaluation, potency and activity. The Bogardus social distance scale (1925) measures willingness to accept groups at different degrees of closeness. Sociometry , developed by J. L. Moreno (1934), studies social acceptance and rejection within a group and displays them in a sociogram. Likert: summated, five-point agreement. Thurstone: equal-appearing intervals, judges. Guttman: cumulative scalogram. Semantic differential: Osgood, bipolar adjectives. Bogardus: social distance. Sociometry: Moreno; sociogram; stars and isolates. Likert is easy to build because no judges are needed, unlike Thurstone. Sociometry measures group relations, not individual attitudes toward objects.

p: Descriptive Method · Research Aptitude
x: A population is the entire group of interest and a sample is the part actually studied; the list from which the sample is drawn is the sampling frame . In probability sampling every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, which allows estimation of sampling error. The main kinds are simple random, systematic (every k-th unit after a random start, where k = N/n), stratified (random sampling within strata, proportionate or disproportionate), cluster (whole groups are randomly selected) and multistage. In non-probability sampling selection is not random, so sampling error cannot be calculated: convenience (accidental), purposive (judgemental), quota (fixed numbers from categories but chosen non-randomly) and snowball (participants recruit others). Fuller treatment appears in Topic 3E. Probability: simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, multistage. Non-probability: convenience, purposive, quota, snowball. Systematic interval k = N/n; quota is non-random even though it resembles stratified sampling. Quota sampling is a non-probability method, a favourite wrong-option trap in lists of probability techniques.

t: 2C.1 Meaning and Process of Historical Research
p: Historical Method · Research Aptitude
x: Historical research is the systematic collection and objective evaluation of evidence about past events in order to test hypotheses, explain causes and trends, and so help us understand the present and anticipate the future. Unlike experiments, the past cannot be repeated or manipulated, so the researcher works only with surviving traces and must judge how far they can be trusted. The usual sequence is: choose a problem and form a hypothesis; collect sources (called heuristics ); subject them to criticism (external, then internal); synthesise and interpret the verified facts; and finally present the findings in an organised narrative, often chronological. The writing of history and the study of how it has been written is historiography . R. G. Collingwood is associated with the idea that the historian must re-enact past thought in the mind. Steps: problem → heuristics (collection) → criticism → synthesis/interpretation → exposition. Heuristics = locating and collecting sources; chronology = arranging events in time order. Historical research is non-reactive: the researcher cannot influence the past. A question on “collection of sources” points to heuristics, while “testing authenticity” points to criticism. Do not confuse historical method (a research method) with historiography (the study of historical writing).

p: Historical Method · Research Aptitude
x: A primary source comes directly from the time and person under study: eyewitness accounts, diaries, letters, official records, archives, inscriptions, coins, photographs, speeches and artefacts. A secondary source is an account written by someone who did not witness the event, such as a textbook, encyclopaedia, biography or later history. Sources are also divided into records (intentionally preserved evidence, such as minutes and chronicles) and relics or remains (unintentional evidence, such as tools, buildings and skeletons). Oral history collects first-hand testimony through interviews and is treated as primary evidence for recent events. Whether a source is primary or secondary depends on how close the author was to the event and on the research question. Primary: original, contemporary, first-hand. Secondary: interpretation by later writers. Relics/remains give unintended evidence; records are intended to inform. Oral history: interviews with participants; subject to memory distortion. A textbook on the Mughal period is secondary even if it quotes primary documents; a diary of a participant is primary.

p: Historical Method · Research Aptitude
x: Historical criticism asks two questions in a fixed order. External criticism (lower criticism) checks authenticity: is the document genuine, who wrote it, when and where? It examines handwriting, paper, ink, language, style, signatures and seals, and exposes forgeries. Internal criticism (higher criticism) assumes the document is genuine and tests credibility: what does the text mean (positive internal criticism) and is the author reliable, competent, close to the events, honest and free from bias (negative internal criticism)? Corroboration , the confirmation of a fact by independent sources, strengthens credibility. External = genuineness. Internal = trustworthiness of content. Order: external first, then internal. Corroboration: agreement of independent witnesses. A genuine document can still be false; that is why internal criticism follows external criticism.

p: Historical Method · Research Aptitude
x: Historiography traces how historians have understood and written about the past. Herodotus is called the Father of History for his Histories , while Thucydides is admired for his critical, evidence-based approach. Leopold von Ranke, the father of modern scientific history, insisted on archival documents and on showing the past as it actually happened. Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah is a landmark of the philosophy of history, and Kalhana’s Rajatarangini (twelfth century) is a celebrated chronicle of Kashmir. Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre founded the Annales school with its emphasis on long-term social and economic structures. E. H. Carr, in What Is History? , described history as a continuous dialogue between the historian and the facts, and between the present and the past; Arnold Toynbee wrote A Study of History on the rise and fall of civilisations by challenge and response; Karl Marx’s historical materialism interprets history through economic relations. Herodotus: Father of History. Ranke: scientific history. Carr: What Is History? Toynbee: challenge and response. Annales school: Bloch and Febvre. Kalhana: Rajatarangini . Ibn Khaldun: Muqaddimah . Indian schools: nationalist, Marxist (D. D. Kosambi), subaltern (Ranajit Guha). Match each historian with the central idea; options usually swap Carr, Toynbee and Collingwood.

t: 2C.5 Limitations and Errors in Historical Research
p: Historical Method · Research Aptitude
x: The historian cannot observe events, repeat them or control variables, and the surviving record is partial, often written by the powerful and sometimes forged or destroyed. Interpretation is therefore open to subjectivity. Typical errors include presentism or anachronism (judging the past by present values or concepts), selective use of evidence to support a favourite view, hindsight bias, the single-cause fallacy and the post hoc fallacy (assuming that because B followed A, A caused B). Generalisations from unique events are limited, which is why historical conclusions are expressed as probabilities. Presentism = reading present standards into the past. Main limits: incomplete sources, bias, no replication, no experimentation. An option that says historical research can be repeated under controlled conditions is wrong by definition.

t: 2D.1 Nature and Aims of Qualitative Research
p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Qualitative research aims at understanding meanings, experiences and processes in their natural setting rather than measuring and counting. The researcher is the main instrument, the design is flexible and emergent, reasoning is inductive, and data are words, images and observations gathered through interviews, observation and documents. It produces thick description , a term that Clifford Geertz borrowed from Gilbert Ryle for rich, contextual accounts of the meaning of behaviour. Samples are small and purposive, so results are not statistically generalisable; instead Lincoln and Guba speak of transferability to similar contexts. Features: natural setting, inductive, holistic, researcher as instrument, emergent design. Thick description: Geertz. Verstehen: Weber. Not typical of qualitative work: large random samples and statistical hypothesis testing. “Qualitative” does not mean unsystematic; it has its own standards of rigour (see 2D.5).

p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Qualitative sampling is purposive: participants are chosen because they can give rich information. Forms include criterion sampling, maximum-variation sampling, typical-case and extreme or deviant-case sampling, snowball sampling and theoretical sampling in grounded theory, where the next participants are chosen according to the emerging theory. There is no fixed sample size; sampling continues until data saturation , when additional interviews yield no new themes or properties. In grounded theory the equivalent is theoretical saturation . Key informants and gatekeepers help access. Purposive, snowball and theoretical sampling are typical. Saturation = no new information emerging; it decides when to stop. Do not apply a sample-size formula to qualitative studies; adequacy is judged by richness and saturation.

t: 2D.3 Interviews, Focus Groups and Field Notes
p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: The in-depth interview, unstructured or semi-structured, explores a participant’s perspective through open questions and probing. A focus group brings together a small group, commonly six to ten people, under a moderator to discuss a topic; the group interaction produces data that individual interviews cannot, and the technique grew from Robert Merton’s focused interview. Field notes record what is observed, with descriptive notes (what happened) kept separate from reflective notes (the researcher’s thoughts); interviews are usually audio-recorded and transcribed. Rapport, probing and a reflexive journal improve quality. Focus group: 6–10 participants, moderator, interaction. Field notes: descriptive + reflective. Probing: follow-up questions for depth. Emic = insider’s view; etic = outsider’s view. Focus-group data are group-level; individual opinions may be shaped by dominant members.

p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Analysis begins during data collection and moves from raw text to themes. In thematic analysis , Braun and Clarke (2006) describe six phases: familiarisation with data, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and writing up. In grounded theory, coding proceeds from open coding (breaking data into labelled parts) to axial coding (relating categories) to selective coding (integrating around a core category), using the constant comparative method and memo writing . Other forms are content, narrative and discourse analysis. Software such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA (CAQDAS) helps organise data but does not do the interpretation. Braun and Clarke: six-phase thematic analysis. Open → axial → selective coding (Strauss and Corbin); constant comparison (Glaser and Strauss). CAQDAS: NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA. Software supports analysis; the researcher still codes and interprets.

p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Lincoln and Guba (1985) replaced the quantitative criteria with four parallel ones. Credibility parallels internal validity, transferability parallels external validity, dependability parallels reliability and confirmability parallels objectivity. Credibility is strengthened by prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative-case analysis and member checking (asking participants to verify the interpretation). Dependability and confirmability rest on an audit trail , a documented record of decisions. Reflexivity means the researcher critically examines their own influence on the study, and thick description supports transferability. Credibility ↔ internal validity; transferability ↔ external validity; dependability ↔ reliability; confirmability ↔ objectivity. Member checking: participant verification. Audit trail: documented decisions. If an option pairs transferability with reliability, it is wrong; reliability’s counterpart is dependability.

p: Qualitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Ethnography studies a culture through prolonged participation (Malinowski, Geertz). Grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss, 1967; Strauss and Corbin; Charmaz’s constructivist version) generates theory from data. Phenomenology (Husserl) describes lived experience and uses bracketing (epoché) to set aside presuppositions. Narrative inquiry studies stories, and case study gives an in-depth account of a bounded case. The emic–etic distinction (Kenneth Pike) separates the insider’s categories from the outsider’s analytic categories. Ethnography → culture; grounded theory → theory from data; phenomenology → lived experience; bracketing → Husserl. Thick description → Geertz. Phenomenology describes experience; grounded theory builds theory. Do not interchange them.

p: Quantitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Quantitative research expresses phenomena in numbers and analyses them statistically. It is deductive (it starts with theory and hypotheses), uses structured instruments such as tests and questionnaires, draws large and preferably random samples, aims at objectivity and generalisation, and can be replicated. Its designs include descriptive surveys, correlational studies and experimental or quasi-experimental studies. Its strength is precision and the ability to test hypotheses; its weakness is limited attention to context and meaning. Numbers, structured tools, large samples, statistical tests, generalisation. Philosophical base: positivism and post-positivism. Quantitative studies still need valid and reliable tools; numbers do not guarantee objectivity.

p: Quantitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: S. S. Stevens (1946) classified measurement into four levels, remembered as NOIR. A nominal scale only classifies into categories (gender, religion); the mode and chi-square are suitable. An ordinal scale ranks (first, second, third) without equal gaps; the median, percentiles and rank correlation fit. An interval scale has equal intervals but an arbitrary zero (Celsius temperature, IQ, calendar year), so differences are meaningful but ratios are not; the mean, standard deviation and Pearson’s r are suitable. A ratio scale has equal intervals and a true zero (height, weight, income, age), so ratios are meaningful and every statistic can be used. 40 °C is not twice as hot as 20 °C because Celsius is interval; Kelvin is ratio. Likert items are ordinal in strict terms though often treated as interval. Scale Property Example Suitable average Nominal Classification Religion, blood group Mode Ordinal Order Rank, grade Median Interval Equal intervals, arbitrary zero Temperature in °C, IQ Mean Ratio True zero Weight, income Mean, geometric mean

p: Quantitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Measures of central tendency are the mean, median and mode; measures of dispersion are the range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation. In a perfectly normal distribution the curve is bell-shaped and symmetrical, mean = median = mode, and about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of cases lie within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean. In a positively skewed distribution mean > median > mode, and in a negatively skewed one mean \< median \< mode. Karl Pearson’s empirical relation for moderate skew is mode = 3 median − 2 mean. The correlation coefficient r ranges from −1 to +1; its square, r², is the proportion of variance shared. Spearman’s rho is used for ranks. Normal curve: 68–95–99.7 rule; mean = median = mode. Positive skew: tail to the right; mean is pulled highest. r = −1 perfect negative; 0 no linear relation; +1 perfect positive. Correlation is not causation, and r = 0 means no linear relation, not necessarily no relation.

t: 2E.4 Errors and Significance in Hypothesis Testing
p: Quantitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: A Type I error (alpha) is rejecting a null hypothesis that is true, a false positive. A Type II error (beta) is failing to reject a null hypothesis that is false, a false negative. Power (1 − beta) is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null. The significance level (commonly 0.05) is the maximum Type I risk the researcher accepts. The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true; if p is less than alpha, H0 is rejected. For a fixed sample size, lowering alpha raises beta. Type I = false alarm (alpha). Type II = missed effect (beta). Power = 1 − beta. p \< alpha → reject H0; a smaller p means stronger evidence against H0. The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

t: 2E.5 Statistical Tests: t-test, ANOVA and Chi-square
p: Quantitative Method · Research Aptitude
x: Parametric tests assume interval or ratio data, approximate normality and equal variances. The t-test (William Gosset, writing as “Student”, 1908) compares means of one sample, two independent groups or paired observations, especially with small samples; the z-test is used with large samples. ANOVA (Fisher) compares three or more means through the F-ratio of between-group to within-group variance. The chi-square test (Pearson) analyses frequencies in categories, for goodness of fit or independence. Non-parametric alternatives include the Mann–Whitney U test (for the independent t-test), the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (for the paired t-test) and the Kruskal–Wallis test (for one-way ANOVA). t-test: two means; ANOVA: three or more means; chi-square: categorical frequencies. Mann–Whitney U → independent t; Wilcoxon → paired t; Kruskal–Wallis → ANOVA. F = between-group variance ÷ within-group variance. Running many t-tests instead of one ANOVA inflates Type I error.

t: 3A.1 Sources and Criteria for Selecting a Problem
p: Identifying and Selecting a Research Problem · Research Aptitude
x: Identifying the problem is the first and most important step because every later decision depends on it; a problem well stated is half solved. Problems arise from personal experience and observation, gaps and recommendations in the literature, theories that need testing, practical or policy needs, discussions with supervisors and experts, and new technologies. A suitable problem is researchable (it can be investigated with data), significant and original, feasible in time, money, access and skill, interesting to the researcher, ethical and clearly delimited. Topics that are too broad cannot be completed; topics that are too narrow lack significance. The usual movement is from a general area to a narrowed, specific problem. Sources: experience, literature gaps, theory, previous recommendations, experts, social needs. Criteria: researchable, significant, original, feasible, ethical, interesting. First step of research = selecting and defining the problem. “Suggestions for further research” at the end of earlier studies are a rich source of problems.

t: 3A.2 Statement of the Problem, Objectives and Variables
p: Identifying and Selecting a Research Problem · Research Aptitude
x: The problem statement says what is to be studied in clear, specific and researchable terms, naming the variables, the population and the relationship of interest. It usually moves from background to gap to purpose and may be written as a question or a declarative sentence. Objectives convert the problem into achievable aims, begin with action verbs (to examine, to compare, to determine) and are often written to be specific, measurable and realistic. Research questions or hypotheses then follow from the objectives. Concepts in the statement must be operationalised so that they can be measured. Good statement: clear, specific, researchable, variables named. Objectives: action verbs, measurable, linked to the problem. Objectives describe what the study will do; hypotheses predict what the study will find.

p: Identifying and Selecting a Research Problem · Research Aptitude
x: Delimitations are the boundaries the researcher deliberately sets on the study, such as the geographical area, population, time period and variables included; they are choices within the researcher’s control. Limitations are weaknesses or constraints that the researcher cannot fully control, such as small sample size, limited time, imperfect tools, self-report bias and restricted generalisability. Assumptions are things taken to be true without proof. Stating all three honestly lets readers judge how far the findings apply. Delimitations = chosen scope. Limitations = unavoidable weaknesses. Assumptions = accepted without testing. If a restriction was a deliberate choice (only urban schools), it is a delimitation; if it was forced (low response rate), it is a limitation.

t: 3B.1 Purpose and Qualities of a Literature Review
p: Review of Literature · Research Aptitude
x: A literature review surveys and critically evaluates what is already known about the topic. It helps the researcher avoid duplication, discover the research gap, sharpen the problem and hypotheses, build the theoretical framework, learn which methods and tools worked, and compare later findings with earlier ones. A good review is relevant, current, organised thematically or chronologically, critical rather than merely descriptive, and ends by showing what is missing. It begins early but continues throughout the study. A research gap is a question that earlier studies left unanswered or answered inadequately. Purposes: avoid duplication, find gap, refine problem, frame theory, choose methods. Good review: critical synthesis, not a list of summaries. Citing many studies is not a review; synthesis and critique are what count.

t: 3B.2 Primary and Secondary Sources of Literature
p: Review of Literature · Research Aptitude
x: Primary literature reports original research or ideas for the first time: research articles, theses, conference papers, patents and technical reports. Secondary literature interprets or summarises primary work: review articles, textbooks, encyclopaedias, handbooks and yearbooks. Tertiary sources help you find the others: indexes, abstracts, bibliographies, directories and databases. Grey literature includes reports, working papers and theses that are not commercially published. Primary: original research. Secondary: reviews, textbooks. Tertiary: indexes, bibliographies. Grey literature: outside commercial publishing. A review article is secondary even if it appears in a journal.

p: Review of Literature · Research Aptitude
x: Effective searching starts with keywords and their synonyms. Boolean operators combine terms: AND narrows the search (both terms must appear), OR broadens it (either term, useful for synonyms), and NOT excludes a term. Truncation (for example educat*) finds word endings, wildcards replace single characters, and quotation marks search an exact phrase. Field searching, filters for date and type, and controlled vocabulary or thesaurus terms (such as MeSH in medicine) refine results. Citation chaining follows references backward and citations forward from a good paper. AND narrows; OR widens; NOT excludes. Truncation (*) for word stems; quotes for exact phrases. Snowballing = following references and citing papers. If you want more results, use OR; if you want fewer and more precise results, use AND.

p: Review of Literature · Research Aptitude
x: Shodhganga is the national repository of Indian electronic theses and dissertations (ETDs), maintained by the INFLIBNET Centre, Gandhinagar, an inter-university centre of the UGC. UGC regulations require universities to deposit the electronic copy of every approved doctoral thesis there. Shodhgangotri holds synopses of research topics from registered scholars. Other INFLIBNET services include e-ShodhSindhu , the consortium for electronic resources, and Vidwan , the database of experts. Searching Shodhganga shows what Indian doctoral work already exists on a topic. Shodhganga = theses; Shodhgangotri = synopses; INFLIBNET Centre, Gandhinagar (UGC). e-ShodhSindhu = e-resources consortium; Vidwan = experts database. Shodhganga holds completed theses, whereas Shodhgangotri holds synopses of ongoing research.

t: 3B.5 Types of Reviews and Journal Metrics
p: Review of Literature · Research Aptitude
x: A narrative review summarises a field selectively. A systematic review follows an explicit protocol, searches comprehensively, applies stated inclusion criteria and appraises quality, often reported by PRISMA guidelines. A meta-analysis statistically pools effect sizes across studies. A scoping review maps the extent of literature. Journal quality is often judged by metrics. The impact factor (Clarivate’s Journal Citation Reports) is the number of citations in a year to items published in the previous two years divided by the number of citable items in those years. CiteScore (Scopus) uses a four-year window. The h-index (Hirsch, 2005) is the largest number h such that the author has h papers each cited at least h times; the i10-index counts papers with at least ten citations. Impact factor: two-year window, Clarivate. CiteScore: four-year window, Scopus. h-index: Hirsch, 2005. Systematic review: protocol; meta-analysis: statistical pooling. Impact factor measures a journal, h-index measures an author; mixing them is a typical trap.

p: Formulating Hypotheses · Research Aptitude
x: Hypotheses can be classified in several ways. A research (scientific) hypothesis states the expected relationship in substantive terms; a statistical hypothesis restates it in terms of population parameters, such as μ1 = μ2. A null hypothesis denies any difference or relationship, and an alternative hypothesis asserts one. A directional (one-tailed) hypothesis predicts the direction of the difference (group A will score higher than group B) and is tested with a one-tailed test; a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis predicts only that a difference exists. A simple hypothesis links one independent and one dependent variable, whereas a complex hypothesis involves several variables. A working hypothesis is a provisional guess used to guide early investigation. Directional → one-tailed test; non-directional → two-tailed test. Simple = one IV and one DV; complex = more than one of either. Null (H0) and alternative (H1/Ha) are statistical forms. The wording “is greater than” or “is lower than” signals a directional hypothesis; “is different from” signals a non-directional one.

p: Formulating Hypotheses · Research Aptitude
x: The null hypothesis states that there is no significant difference or relationship, for example “there is no significant difference in the achievement of boys and girls”. It is the starting assumption of statistical testing, because it is easier to find evidence against a precise statement than to prove a vague one. The researcher computes a test statistic and its p-value; if p is smaller than the chosen significance level, H0 is rejected in favour of H1, otherwise we fail to reject it. Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true, only that the data did not provide enough evidence against it. Typical forms are H0: μ1 = μ2 against H1: μ1 ≠ μ2 (two-tailed) or H1: μ1 > μ2 (one-tailed). “No significant difference/relationship” = null hypothesis. Decision words: reject H0 or fail to reject H0 (not “prove”, not “accept”). p \< alpha → reject H0. An option that says the null hypothesis is proved true by a non-significant result is wrong.

p: Formulating Hypotheses · Research Aptitude
x: Hypotheses come from theory (deduced consequences), earlier research findings, everyday observation and experience, analogy with other fields, cultural beliefs and insight. Goode and Hatt list sources such as science itself, analogies, culture and personal experience. Formulating a hypothesis involves reviewing the literature, identifying the variables, stating the expected relationship, checking that it can be tested with available methods, and operationalising the terms. A good hypothesis is clear, specific, testable, consistent with known facts, simple, and stated before data are collected. Sources: theory, past research, observation, analogy, culture, experience. Qualities: testable, specific, simple, consistent with existing knowledge. A hypothesis built after looking at the data and then “tested” on the same data is poor practice.

t: 3D.1 Purpose and Principles of Research Design
p: Research Design · Research Aptitude
x: The research design is the plan that connects the research questions to the data and the analysis; it specifies the type of study, the sample, the tools, the timing and the analytical procedures. Its purpose is to obtain valid answers economically and to control variance. Kothari groups designs as exploratory (flexible, to formulate a problem), descriptive and diagnostic (accurate description, little flexibility) and experimental (hypothesis testing). Fisher’s three principles of experimental design are replication , randomisation and local control , and Kerlinger’s MAX-MIN-CON principle guides variance control. A research proposal or synopsis sets out the design in advance: title, background, review, objectives, hypotheses, methodology, sampling, tools, analysis plan, schedule and references. Design = blueprint. Fisher: replication, randomisation, local control. Exploratory = flexible; descriptive = structured; experimental = tests causal hypotheses. Design is decided before data collection; it is not the same as the report structure.

p: Research Design · Research Aptitude
x: Exploratory designs are used to formulate a problem or hypotheses when knowledge is limited. Selltiz and colleagues named three common methods: a literature survey, an experience survey of knowledgeable people, and the analysis of insight-stimulating examples (case studies). Mixed-methods designs, as classified by Creswell, include the convergent parallel design (both strands collected together and merged), the explanatory sequential design (quantitative first, qualitative to explain), and the exploratory sequential design (qualitative first, then a quantitative test). Notation such as QUAN → qual shows the order and the priority of the strands. Exploratory methods: literature survey, experience survey, insight-stimulating cases. Explanatory sequential = QUAN then qual; exploratory sequential = qual then QUAN. In “explanatory” sequential, the qualitative strand explains numbers, which is the reverse of the exploratory sequence.

p: Research Design · Research Aptitude
x: In quasi-experimental designs the researcher manipulates a treatment but cannot randomly assign participants, as in the non-equivalent control group design, the interrupted time-series design and the regression-discontinuity design. True experimental designs use random assignment. Fisher’s formal designs include the completely randomised design (units assigned wholly at random), the randomised block design (units grouped into homogeneous blocks and randomised within blocks), the Latin square (two blockings) and factorial designs (several factors studied together with their interactions). Notation: R for random assignment, X for the treatment and O for an observation. Quasi-experiment: treatment but no randomisation. CRD, RBD, Latin square, factorial: formal experimental designs. If groups were formed by existing classrooms rather than random assignment, the design is quasi-experimental.

t: 3D.4 Construct Validity and Types of Variables
p: Research Design · Research Aptitude
x: Construct validity asks whether the study’s measures and treatments really represent the theoretical constructs intended; it is threatened by vague definitions of the construct, relying on a single measure (mono-operation bias) or a single method (mono-method bias). Variables can be further classified: latent variables are not directly observable (intelligence, attitude) and are inferred from manifest or observed indicators such as test scores; dichotomous variables have two categories (pass/fail); dummy variables code categories as 0 and 1 for regression; composite variables combine several items into one score. Latent = unobserved construct; manifest = observed indicator. Dummy variable: 0/1 coding of categories. Construct validity concerns meaning of measures, not the size of the sample.

t: 3E.1 Basic Concepts: Sample, Statistic and Errors
p: Sampling · Research Aptitude
x: The population (universe) is the complete set of units that the researcher wants to describe; the sampling frame is the actual list from which the sample is drawn; a sample is the subset studied. A parameter describes the population (written with Greek letters, such as μ and σ) and a statistic describes the sample (x̄ and s). Sampling is used because it saves time and cost and is the only possible option when testing is destructive. Sampling error is the difference between a sample statistic and the population parameter that arises by chance because only a part is studied; it falls as the sample grows and can be estimated in probability samples through the standard error (σ/√n). Non-sampling errors , such as non-response, measurement and coverage errors, occur in censuses as well and do not shrink with a larger sample. Parameter = population; statistic = sample. Standard error = σ/√n; to halve it, the sample must be four times larger. Census has no sampling error but may have large non-sampling error. A very large but biased sample is still biased; size cannot cure bad selection.

p: Sampling · Research Aptitude
x: Sample size depends on the variability of the population, the precision (margin of error) required, the confidence level, the number of subgroups to be analysed, the expected response rate and the resources available. For a proportion, a common formula is n = Z²pq / e²; with p = 0.5, 95% confidence (Z = 1.96) and a 5% margin of error it gives about 384. Yamane’s simple formula is n = N / (1 + Ne²). Beyond a moderately large population, the population size matters little; what matters is the absolute sample size. About 30 observations are often cited as the minimum for the central limit theorem to begin to apply. 95% confidence → Z = 1.96; 99% → Z = 2.58. Greater variability or tighter precision → larger sample. Increasing n reduces sampling error, not bias. Sample size does not need to be a fixed percentage of the population.

p: Sampling · Research Aptitude
x: In simple random sampling each unit has an equal and independent chance, drawn by lottery or random number tables. Systematic sampling picks every k-th unit after a random start, where k = N/n; it is convenient but risky if the list has a hidden pattern. Stratified sampling divides the population into internally homogeneous strata and draws randomly from each, proportionately or disproportionately; it improves precision. Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups (schools, villages) that are internally heterogeneous, saving cost but usually with higher error than simple random sampling of the same size. Multistage sampling selects in successive stages (state, district, village, household), as national surveys do. Non-probability methods include convenience , purposive (judgemental) , quota and snowball sampling; their selection probabilities are unknown, so sampling error cannot be calculated. Stratified: homogeneous within strata. Cluster: heterogeneous within clusters. Quota = non-random equivalent of stratified; snowball = chain referral for hidden populations. Sampling with replacement: a unit may be chosen more than once. Stratified draws from every stratum; cluster draws only some clusters and studies all or many units in them.

p: Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: A good questionnaire is short, clear, logically ordered (easy and non-sensitive items first) and free from jargon, ambiguity, leading, loaded and double-barrelled questions. Closed-ended items (dichotomous, multiple-choice, rating, ranking) are easy to score; open-ended items give rich detail but are harder to code. Contingency or filter questions direct only some respondents to follow-up items. Pre-testing and a cover letter explaining the purpose improve quality and response. Online surveys are fast and cheap but suffer from self-selection, coverage bias (people without internet are excluded) and low control over who answers. Avoid double-barrelled questions (two ideas in one item). Closed = easy to analyse; open = depth. Online survey limits: coverage and self-selection bias. A question such as “Is the teacher knowledgeable and friendly?” is double-barrelled.

p: Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Test–retest reliability correlates scores from the same people on two occasions; practice and memory effects can distort it. Parallel-forms reliability correlates two equivalent versions. Split-half reliability correlates two halves of one test (often odd and even items); because the halves are shorter, the coefficient is stepped up with the Spearman–Brown formula, r(full) = 2r / (1 + r). KR-20 suits dichotomous items and Cronbach’s alpha (Cronbach, 1951) suits multi-point items such as Likert scales. Inter-rater agreement is shown by percentage agreement or Cohen’s kappa. Longer tests, clearer items and uniform administration raise reliability. Test–retest → stability; parallel forms → equivalence; split-half, KR-20, alpha → internal consistency. Spearman–Brown: corrects split-half; Cohen’s kappa: agreement between raters. Alpha ≥ 0.70 acceptable. Matching each method to the type of reliability is the usual question pattern.

p: Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Content validity is judged by experts who check that items represent the whole domain, often guided by a table of specifications; face validity is only the surface impression. Criterion-related validity compares scores with an external criterion, either measured at the same time (concurrent) or later (predictive). Construct validity is shown by convergent evidence (correlation with measures of the same construct), discriminant evidence (low correlation with unrelated constructs), known-groups comparison and factor analysis; Campbell and Fiske (1959) proposed the multitrait–multimethod matrix. A test’s validity cannot exceed the square root of its reliability. Concurrent = now; predictive = future. Convergent and discriminant belong to construct validity. Maximum validity = √ reliability.
