Content validity is a matter of judgement, not a correlation coefficient.

p: Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Observation may be participant or non-participant, structured or unstructured, overt or covert, and uses tools such as checklists, rating scales, anecdotal records, time sampling and event sampling. Rating errors include the halo effect (a general impression colours all ratings), leniency or severity error, central tendency error and the logical error . Interviewer bias can also distort answers. Projective techniques present ambiguous stimuli so that people project hidden feelings: the Rorschach inkblot test (1921), the Thematic Apperception Test (Murray and Morgan, 1935), word association, sentence completion and draw-a-person tests. They are used mainly for personality assessment and are open to subjective scoring. Halo effect: one trait influences ratings of others. Rorschach = inkblots; TAT = pictures and stories. Projective tests: disguised purpose, ambiguous stimuli. Halo effect is a rating error, not a sampling error.

p: Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: A standardised test has fixed content, uniform administration and scoring procedures, and norms obtained from a representative sample, so that an individual’s score can be interpreted against others. Norm-referenced tests compare a person with the norm group using percentiles, stanines or T-scores; criterion-referenced tests compare performance with a set standard. Examples are intelligence tests (Binet–Simon 1905, Stanford–Binet, Wechsler scales), aptitude and achievement tests, personality inventories (MMPI, Cattell’s 16PF) and interest inventories (Strong, Kuder). Speed tests stress time, whereas power tests stress difficulty. Norms → interpretation against a reference group. Binet–Simon: first intelligence test (1905). A teacher-made test is not standardised, even if it is reliable.

t: 3G.1 Processing of Data: Editing, Coding and Tabulation
p: Data Analysis and Interpretation · Research Aptitude
x: Processing prepares raw data for analysis, and Kothari lists the order as editing, coding, classification and tabulation. Editing checks completed instruments for errors, omissions and inconsistencies, either in the field or centrally. Coding assigns numerical or symbolic labels to responses, guided by a codebook. Classification groups data by attributes or by class intervals. Tabulation arranges the classified data in rows and columns; the parts of a table are the title, caption (column headings), stub (row labels), body, footnotes and source note. Data cleaning also deals with missing values and outliers. Order: editing → coding → classification → tabulation. Table parts: title, stub, caption, body, footnote, source. Stub refers to the row headings; caption refers to the column headings.

p: Data Analysis and Interpretation · Research Aptitude
x: The mean uses all values but is pulled by extremes; the median is the middle value and is best for skewed data or open-ended classes; the mode is the most frequent value and is the only average for nominal data. The geometric mean suits growth rates and the harmonic mean suits rates such as speed. In a symmetrical distribution all three coincide; in positive skew (long right tail) mean > median > mode; in negative skew mean \< median \< mode. Karl Pearson’s coefficient of skewness is (mean − mode) / SD. Kurtosis describes peakedness: leptokurtic (peaked), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat). The coefficient of variation (SD / mean × 100) compares variability between series with different units. Positive skew: mean is highest. Negative skew: mean is lowest. Median for skewed data; mode for nominal data; SD is the most reliable measure of dispersion. In skewed income data the median represents the typical person better than the mean.

p: Data Analysis and Interpretation · Research Aptitude
x: Inferential statistics draw conclusions about a population from a sample, through estimation (point and interval estimates, with confidence intervals) and hypothesis testing . Parametric tests (t, z, F) assume interval or ratio data and approximately normal distributions; non-parametric or distribution-free tests (chi-square, Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis, sign test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Spearman) suit nominal or ordinal data, small samples and non-normal data. Degrees of freedom: for a chi-square test of independence df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1), so a 3 × 4 table has 6; for goodness of fit df = k − 1; for an independent-samples t-test df = n1 + n2 − 2. Chi-square works on frequencies, not percentages. df (independence) = (r − 1)(c − 1); df (goodness of fit) = k − 1. Non-parametric tests: fewer assumptions but usually less power. Chi-square is non-parametric even though it is widely used with large samples.

p: Data Analysis and Interpretation · Research Aptitude
x: Pearson’s product-moment r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between interval or ratio variables; Spearman’s rank correlation and Kendall’s tau serve ordinal data; point-biserial and phi coefficients handle a dichotomy. Partial and multiple correlation add control for or combine variables. Regression predicts one variable from another by the least-squares line y = a + bx, where b is the slope. The two regression lines intersect at the means, r² equals the product of the two regression coefficients (so r is their geometric mean, with the common sign), and r² is the coefficient of determination. Correlation, however high, does not prove cause, and spurious correlations arise from a third variable. b(yx) × b(xy) = r²; both coefficients carry the sign of r. Regression lines meet at (x̄, ȳ); r² = variance explained. Correlation measures association; regression is used for prediction.

p: Data Analysis and Interpretation · Research Aptitude
x: Interpretation draws meaning from analysed results by linking them to the hypotheses, earlier findings and theory, and by stating what they imply. It is the bridge between analysis and the report. Kothari’s precautions are to avoid generalising beyond the population studied, to check that the sample and tools were sound, not to infer cause from correlation alone, to keep extraneous factors and limitations in view, and to avoid selective reporting. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance, so effect sizes (for example Cohen’s d) and confidence intervals should accompany p-values. Statistical significance ≠ practical significance. Do not generalise beyond the data; do not infer cause from correlation. A result can be significant with a huge sample and still be trivial in size.

p: Report Writing · Research Aptitude
x: A research report has three parts. The preliminary pages include the title page, certificate, declaration, acknowledgements, abstract, table of contents and lists of tables, figures and abbreviations. The main body contains the introduction, review of literature, methodology, results and analysis, discussion, conclusions, recommendations and limitations with suggestions for further research. The end matter contains the bibliography or references, appendices (questionnaires, raw data, tools, supplementary tables) and, where used, a glossary or index. Technical reports serve scholars and funders, while popular reports serve the general public with simpler language. Preliminary pages → body → end matter. Appendix: supporting material kept out of the body. Abstract: short summary, typically 150–300 words. Tools and raw data belong in appendices, not in the main chapters.

p: Report Writing · Research Aptitude
x: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page and an endnote at the end of a chapter or document. A bibliography lists all works consulted, whereas a reference list lists only works cited, usually in alphabetical order by author’s surname. Latin abbreviations save space: ibid. (ibidem, in the same place) refers to the immediately preceding source; op. cit. (opere citato) refers to a work already cited; loc. cit. (loco citato) refers to the same passage; et al. means and others; cf. means compare; viz. means namely; passim means here and there; sic means thus, as in the original. Ibid. = same as the immediately preceding reference. Op. cit. = work cited earlier; loc. cit. = same place cited earlier. Bibliography = all consulted; references = only cited. Ibid. cannot be used if another source has intervened since the one it refers to.

p: Report Writing · Research Aptitude
x: Research writing should be clear, precise, objective and formal, usually impersonal and in the past tense for methods and results, and free of jargon, emotive words and padding. Conclusions must follow from the findings, answer the objectives and state whether hypotheses were supported, without claiming more than the data allow and without introducing new data. Recommendations should be practical and linked to specific findings, and the report should also state limitations and suggest directions for further research. Careful revision and proofreading complete the work. Conclusions: derived from results, not beyond them. Recommendations: practical, specific, evidence-based. A conclusion that introduces new results is a flaw; new results belong in the results section.

t: 4A.1 Meaning and Organisation of a Thesis
p: Format and Structure of a Thesis · Research Aptitude
x: A thesis is a long, formally written document submitted for a degree, presenting the candidate’s original research, the method used and the conclusions reached. In India and the United Kingdom “thesis” usually denotes the doctoral work and “dissertation” the shorter master’s work, while in the United States the usage is often reversed. Before the thesis comes the synopsis , a concise research plan submitted at registration. The work is carried out under a supervisor, monitored by a research advisory or doctoral committee, and finally examined by external evaluators and defended in an open viva voce . A thesis must show an original contribution to knowledge, a mastery of the literature, and a sound method. Its parts follow a standard order: preliminary pages, main chapters and end matter. Synopsis → research plan; thesis → completed doctoral document; viva voce → oral defence. Standard order: preliminary pages → chapters → end matter. Original contribution is the central requirement for a doctoral thesis. A thesis differs from a term paper or project report by its originality and depth; a synopsis is a plan, not a summary of finished work.

p: Format and Structure of a Thesis · Research Aptitude
x: The preliminary (front) pages come before the first chapter. They normally include the title page (title, candidate’s name, degree, supervisor, institution, month and year), the supervisor’s certificate stating that the work is original and was done under guidance, the candidate’s declaration of originality, the acknowledgements , the abstract , the table of contents , and the lists of tables, figures and abbreviations . A preface is written by the author about the purpose and scope of the work, whereas a foreword is written by someone else. These pages are numbered in lower-case Roman numerals (i, ii, iii), and the main text restarts with Arabic numeral 1. Certificate: by the supervisor. Declaration: by the candidate. Preface: by the author; foreword: by another person. Front matter in Roman numerals; text in Arabic numerals. If the question asks who certifies originality of guidance, the answer is the supervisor, not the candidate.

p: Format and Structure of a Thesis · Research Aptitude
x: The typical chapters are: Introduction (background, statement of the problem, objectives, hypotheses, significance, scope and delimitations, definitions of terms); Review of Related Literature (what is known, the gap and the theoretical framework); Methodology (design, population, sample, tools, procedure and the plan for analysis); Results or Data Analysis (findings in tables and figures, with minimal interpretation); Discussion (meaning of the findings, comparison with earlier studies); and Summary, Conclusions and Recommendations (what was found, what follows, limitations and suggestions for further research). Some theses merge results and discussion; qualitative theses may arrange chapters by theme. Chapter order: introduction → literature → methodology → results → discussion → conclusions. Results report; discussion interprets. Delimitations and objectives belong in the introduction. Putting interpretation into the results chapter, or new data into the conclusion chapter, are standard faults.

p: Format and Structure of a Thesis · Research Aptitude
x: The end matter follows the last chapter. The bibliography or reference list gives full details of sources, alphabetically by author. Appendices hold supporting material that would interrupt the text: questionnaires, tests, raw data, permission letters and extra tables, each labelled Appendix A, B and so on and mentioned in the text. A glossary is an alphabetical list of specialised terms with meanings. An index is an alphabetical list of subjects and names with page numbers, mostly used in books. In Indian practice the term annexure is used for official documents or material from other sources attached to the thesis, although appendix and annexure are often used loosely. References before appendices in most styles (APA). Appendix = supporting material; glossary = terms; index = subjects with page numbers. An index is not a table of contents: the table of contents lists the thesis’s own headings in order of appearance, while an index is alphabetical.

p: Format and Structure of a Thesis · Research Aptitude
x: The UGC regulates the doctoral degree through its Ph.D. regulations (a 2016 version, later revised in 2022), which cover admission, course work, supervisors, research advisory committees, duration, evaluation and submission. The thesis is evaluated by external examiners, followed by an open viva voce. Earlier regulations required scholars to make presentations and publish a paper before submission, so check the current rules. A soft copy of the approved thesis must be deposited with INFLIBNET for hosting on Shodhganga, and under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018 the thesis must carry an undertaking of originality and be checked with plagiarism-detection software. Thesis soft copy → INFLIBNET → Shodhganga. Plagiarism regulations: UGC 2018; undertaking of originality is mandatory. Evaluation: external examiner(s) and open viva. Do not mix up the Ph.D. regulations (degree process) with the 2018 plagiarism regulations (academic integrity).

t: 4B.1 IMRaD and Sections of an Article
p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: Most scientific articles follow the IMRaD structure: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, preceded by the title, abstract and keywords and followed by the conclusion, acknowledgements and references. The Introduction tells why the study matters (background, gap, objective); the Methods section tells how it was done in enough detail for replication; the Results section reports what was found without interpretation; the Discussion explains what the results mean, compares them with earlier work, admits limitations and states implications. The overall shape is like an hourglass, moving from the general field to the specific study and back to general significance. Abstracts and conclusions are usually written last. IMRaD: Introduction (why), Methods (how), Results (what), Discussion (so what). Methods must allow replication. Results state findings; discussion interprets them. Interpretation inside the results section, or new data in the discussion, indicates a structural error.

p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: A good title is concise, specific and informative, contains the key variables, and avoids unexplained abbreviations. The abstract is a stand-alone summary of the purpose, method, main results and conclusion, usually 150 to 300 words, containing no citations and no new information. It may be informative (structured under headings) or descriptive (indicating what the paper covers). Keywords , usually three to eight, are the terms by which indexing services and search engines retrieve the paper, so they should be standard terms rather than the title’s words alone. Some journals also ask for a graphical abstract or highlights. Abstract: self-contained, no citations, written last. Keywords: for indexing and retrieval. Structured abstract: Background, Methods, Results, Conclusions. An abstract that cites references or introduces material absent from the paper is faulty.

p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: An original research article reports new data and is the main type. A short communication or brief report publishes preliminary or limited findings quickly. A review article summarises and critiques existing literature, and may be narrative or systematic; a meta-analysis pools results statistically. A case report describes a single case in detail. Other items include letters to the editor, commentaries and editorials (opinion pieces), perspectives, technical notes, conference papers and book reviews. Original article = new data; review article = synthesis of existing work. Short communication = brief, preliminary. Editorial and commentary = opinion, not primary research. A review article does not report new empirical data.

p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: Peer review is the evaluation of a manuscript by independent experts before publication, to check validity, originality and significance. The usual path is submission, editorial screening (a weak paper may be “desk rejected”), assessment by reviewers, an editorial decision (accept, minor revision, major revision or reject), revision with a response letter, and proofs. In single-blind review the reviewers know the authors but the authors do not know the reviewers; in double-blind review both are anonymous; in open review identities (and sometimes reports) are public. Its weaknesses are delay, reviewer bias and inconsistency, and the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) provides guidelines for editors and reviewers. Single-blind: authors unaware of reviewers. Double-blind: both anonymous. Open: identities disclosed. Decisions: accept, minor revision, major revision, reject. COPE: ethics guidance for publishers and editors. Double-blind protects against bias toward author identity, but it is not a guarantee of quality.

p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: Identifiers make scholarly output traceable. The ISSN (International Standard Serial Number) is an eight-digit number identifying a periodical, with separate numbers for print and electronic forms; the ISBN identifies a book and has thirteen digits since 2007; the DOI (Digital Object Identifier) is a permanent link to a particular article; and ORCID is a persistent sixteen-digit identifier for an individual researcher. Metrics rate journals and authors: the impact factor (Clarivate, two-year window), CiteScore (Scopus, four-year window), SJR (weights citations by the prestige of the citing journal), SNIP (normalises for field differences), the h-index and i10-index . In India the UGC-CARE list (Consortium for Academic and Research Ethics) identifies quality journals. ISSN = 8 digits, serials. ISBN = 13 digits, books. ORCID = 16 digits, researchers. DOI = permanent article link. Impact factor: Clarivate; CiteScore, SJR, SNIP: Scopus-based. UGC-CARE: quality-journal list. ISSN is for journals; ISBN is for books. DOI points to an item; ORCID points to a person.

t: 4B.6 Predatory Journals, Duplicate Submission and Authorship
p: Format and Structure of a Research Article · Research Aptitude
x: Predatory journals exploit the author-pays model: they charge fees, provide little or no genuine peer review, make false claims about indexing or impact factor, spam researchers with invitations and promise very quick acceptance; the term is linked with Jeffrey Beall’s lists. Safeguards include checking indexing in databases, membership of DOAJ and COPE, and the “Think. Check. Submit.” checklist. Duplicate submission means sending the same manuscript to several journals at once; redundant publication means publishing the same findings twice; salami slicing splits one study into several thin papers. Authorship should reflect substantial contribution: the ICMJE criteria require substantial contribution to the work, drafting or critical revision, final approval and accountability. Ghost authors contribute but are not named; guest or gift authors are named without contributing. Predatory journal: fees without real review; false indexing claims. Salami slicing: splitting one study into many papers. Ghost author: unnamed contributor; gift author: named non-contributor. Submitting one manuscript to two journals simultaneously is unethical even if the journals are reputable.

t: 4C.1 APA Style: Reference List and Editions
p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: APA style, from the American Psychological Association, is used in psychology, education and the social sciences. It uses author–date citation and a References list that is alphabetical, double-spaced and has a hanging indent. The current edition is the seventh (published in 2019); the sixth appeared in 2009. In a journal reference the article title is in sentence case, the journal title and volume are italicised and the DOI is given as a URL. Book titles are in sentence case and italic, and the publisher’s location is no longer included. The seventh edition lists up to twenty authors and cites works by three or more authors with et al. from the first citation. APA 7th edition: 2019; 6th: 2009. Author–date; hanging indent; alphabetical references list. Sentence case for article and book titles; italic for journal and book titles. APA uses “References”, whereas MLA uses “Works Cited”.

t: 4C.2 APA Style: In-text Citations and Quotations
p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: In-text citations give the author and year: (Smith, 2020) or Smith (2020). With two authors both names are given with an ampersand inside brackets: (Smith & Jones, 2020); with three or more, use (Smith et al., 2020). A direct quotation needs a page number, (Smith, 2020, p. 15), and a quotation of fewer than forty words is put in quotation marks within the text, while one of forty words or more is set as an indented block quotation without quotation marks. A source cited through another is shown as (Smith, 2000, as cited in Jones, 2015). A work without a date uses n.d.; personal communications are cited only in the text. Under 40 words: inline quotation marks. 40 words or more: block quote, no marks. Three or more authors: et al. from first citation. Secondary source: “as cited in”. The forty-word threshold for block quotations is APA’s; MLA uses a different rule (more than four lines of prose).

p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: The Modern Language Association style is used mainly in literature, languages and the humanities. It uses author–page in-text citation with no comma and no “p.”, for example (Smith 45), and a Works Cited list in alphabetical order with a hanging indent. The ninth edition appeared in 2021. Entries follow a template of core elements: author, title of source, title of container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, publication date and location. Titles of independent works such as books are italicised, and titles of shorter works such as articles are put in quotation marks. A block quotation is used for prose of more than four lines and is indented from the left margin. MLA: author–page, e.g. (Smith 45); Works Cited; 9th edition (2021). Containers: the larger work holding a source (a journal, a website). Block quotation: more than four lines of prose. No year appears in MLA in-text citations, unlike APA.

t: 4C.4 Other Styles: Chicago, Harvard, Vancouver, IEEE, AMA, OSCOLA, Turabian, ACS
p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: Different disciplines prefer different styles. Chicago (the Chicago Manual of Style ; the 17th edition of 2017 is widely cited and a newer edition appeared in 2024) offers a notes-and-bibliography system with footnotes or endnotes, used in history and the humanities, and an author–date system. Harvard is a generic author–date style with no single official manual, common in the UK and Australia. Vancouver uses numbers in order of first citation and is used in medicine. IEEE uses numbers in square brackets, such as [1], for engineering and computing. AMA uses superscript numbers for medical writing (11th edition, 2020). OSCOLA is the Oxford style for legal citation with footnotes. Turabian is a student adaptation of Chicago (9th edition, 2018). ACS serves chemistry. Numbered styles list references in order of citation, not alphabetically. Style Discipline Citation form APA Psychology, education, social sciences Author–date MLA Literature, humanities Author–page Chicago / Turabian History, humanities Footnotes or author–date Harvard General Author–date Vancouver, AMA Medicine Numbered IEEE Engineering, computing Numbered in brackets OSCOLA Law Footnotes

t: 4C.5 Latin Abbreviations: Ibid., Op. cit., Loc. cit.
p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: Footnote conventions use Latin shorthand. Ibid. (ibidem) refers to the work cited in the immediately preceding note; op. cit. (opere citato) refers to a work already fully cited earlier, with the author’s name and page; loc. cit. (loco citato) refers to the same place (same page or passage) in a work already cited; idem means the same author; et al. means and others; cf. (confer) means compare; q.v. (quod vide) means which see; viz. means namely; e.g. (exempli gratia) means for example; i.e. (id est) means that is; passim means throughout; ff. means and the following pages. Modern manuals, including recent Chicago editions, discourage ibid. and op. cit. in favour of shortened citations. Ibid. = immediately preceding source. Op. cit. = earlier cited work. Loc. cit. = same passage. e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is. Do not swap e.g. and i.e.: e.g. gives examples, while i.e. restates or clarifies.

p: Styles of Referencing and Citation · Research Aptitude
x: A citation acknowledges a source inside the text and is matched by an entry in the reference list. A primary citation gives the original source, and a secondary citation cites a source through another. Citation indexing, pioneered by Eugene Garfield through the Science Citation Index, allows tracing who cites whom and led to the impact factor. Bibliometrics (the term is credited to Alan Pritchard, 1969) measures publications and citations, with classic laws: Lotka’s law on author productivity, Bradford’s law on scattering of articles across journals, and Zipf’s law on word frequency. Altmetrics measure online attention. Reference managers such as Zotero, Mendeley and EndNote store sources and format citations in many styles. Garfield: citation indexing and impact factor. Lotka: authors. Bradford: journals. Zipf: words. Citation Style Language (CSL) underlies many reference-manager styles. Citing a source you have not read, through another author, should be shown as a secondary citation.

p: Research Paper, Article, Workshop, Seminar, Conference and Symposium · Research Aptitude
x: These academic events differ in purpose and format. A seminar is a gathering, usually small, where participants present papers or prepared views on a topic under expert guidance and discuss them. A workshop is practice-oriented: participants learn skills or methods by doing, with hands-on exercises. A symposium is a formal meeting in which several experts deliver short papers on different aspects of one theme. A conference is a larger formal gathering, often periodic, with many papers in parallel sessions and opportunities for networking. A colloquium is a more informal academic discussion, often a departmental talk. Faculty development programmes and refresher courses train teachers; a webinar is a web-based seminar. Seminar = presentation + discussion. Workshop = hands-on skills. Symposium = several experts, one theme. Conference = large, many sessions. Colloquium = informal academic talk and discussion. If the stem stresses learning by doing, it is a workshop; if it stresses several speakers on aspects of one theme, it is a symposium.

p: Research Paper, Article, Workshop, Seminar, Conference and Symposium · Research Aptitude
x: A conference starts with a call for papers ; authors submit abstracts, which are reviewed and accepted, after which full papers are prepared in a final (camera-ready) form. The inaugural session opens the event, the keynote address by an invited expert sets the theme, a plenary session is attended by all participants with no parallel sessions, technical sessions are parallel sessions where papers are presented, and a poster session displays work visually with authors standing by to answer questions. The accepted papers are often published as conference proceedings , sometimes with an ISBN or ISSN. The event ends with a valedictory session . Keynote: sets theme. Plenary: everyone together. Technical sessions: parallel paper presentations. Poster session: visual presentation, authors present at the poster. Proceedings: published collection of conference papers. Plenary sessions have no parallel sessions, while technical sessions do.

p: Research Paper, Article, Workshop, Seminar, Conference and Symposium · Research Aptitude
x: The chairperson presides over a session, introduces speakers, manages time and keeps discussion orderly. The convener or organising secretary arranges the event. The rapporteur records the proceedings of a session and prepares a summary report with recommendations. A discussant is a prepared respondent who comments critically on papers. A moderator guides the discussion, particularly in panels and webinars. A resource person is an expert invited to deliver a talk or conduct a session, and the keynote speaker delivers the principal address. Chair presides; rapporteur records; discussant critiques; moderator facilitates; convener organises. The person who prepares the session report is the rapporteur, not the chair.

p: Research Paper, Article, Workshop, Seminar, Conference and Symposium · Research Aptitude
x: A panel discussion brings a small group of experts, commonly three to six, before an audience to discuss a topic under a moderator; it presents different viewpoints and usually includes audience questions, and it is spontaneous rather than based on read papers. A round table gives equal status to all participants around an issue. A webinar is a seminar delivered over the internet using video platforms, with interactive features such as chat and polls, and it can be recorded for later viewing. MOOCs, such as those on SWAYAM in India, are open online courses and differ from a single-event webinar. Panel: experts + moderator + audience interaction. Webinar: online seminar; interactive and often recorded. A webcast is mainly one-way, while a webinar is interactive.

t: 4D.5 Research Papers, Monographs and Book Reviews
p: Research Paper, Article, Workshop, Seminar, Conference and Symposium · Research Aptitude
x: A research paper presents original findings in a journal or conference. A monograph is a detailed scholarly work on a single, specialised subject, usually by one or a few authors. A treatise is a systematic, comprehensive discussion of a subject. A book review is a critical evaluation of a book, combining a summary with an assessment. An edited volume collects chapters by different authors under an editor, and a festschrift is a collection of essays in honour of a scholar. Handbooks and encyclopaedias are reference works, and an annotated bibliography lists sources with short evaluative notes. Monograph: one specialised subject in depth. Edited volume: many authors, one editor. Book review: summary plus critical assessment. Festschrift: essays honouring a scholar. A monograph is not a collection of papers by many authors; that is an edited volume.

p: Digital Tools for Literature Search · Research Aptitude
x: ICT stands for information and communication technology: the computers, networks, software and media used to create, store, retrieve and share information. In research, ICT lets a scholar locate literature, collect and analyse data, manage references and publish. A search engine crawls and indexes the open web (Google, Bing), whereas a database contains curated, indexed records (Scopus, PubMed), so a database search is usually more precise for scholarly work. Boolean logic, named after George Boole, combines terms: AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes. Truncation (educat*) retrieves word endings, quotation marks fix an exact phrase, and filters limit by date, language, subject or document type. In Google, a minus sign excludes a word and operators such as site: and filetype: restrict the search. ICT = information and communication technology. Boolean: AND (narrow), OR (broaden), NOT (exclude); quotes = phrase; * = truncation. Google: -word excludes; site: restricts domain; filetype: restricts format. Adding more AND terms reduces results; adding more OR terms increases them.

t: 5A.2 Scholarly Search Engines and Citation Tracking
p: Digital Tools for Literature Search · Research Aptitude
x: Google Scholar (launched 2004) is a free search engine for scholarly articles, books, theses and patents; its “Cited by” link lets you follow later work, and it offers alerts, a personal library and author profiles with h-index and i10-index. It is broad but not curated, so quality control is the user’s job. Semantic Scholar (Allen Institute for AI) uses AI to rank and summarise papers. BASE (Bielefeld) and CORE aggregate open-access content. Dimensions and OpenAlex provide open or freemium bibliographic data, and visual tools such as Connected Papers and ResearchRabbit map citation networks. Microsoft Academic was shut down in 2021. Scopus and Web of Science provide curated citation tracking by subscription. Google Scholar: free, broad, “Cited by”, alerts, profile metrics. Semantic Scholar: AI-based. BASE and CORE: open-access aggregators. Scopus and Web of Science: curated, subscription citation databases. Wide coverage is not the same as quality: Google Scholar includes non-peer-reviewed items.

p: Digital Tools for Literature Search · Research Aptitude
x: The INFLIBNET Centre at Gandhinagar, an inter-university centre of the UGC, runs most national scholarly infrastructure. Shodhganga hosts doctoral theses; Shodhgangotri hosts synopses; Vidwan is the database of experts; IRINS is the Indian Research Information Network System for institutional research profiles; and ShodhShuddhi provides plagiarism-detection access to institutions. E-resource consortia included the UGC-INFONET Digital Library Consortium (universities), N-LIST (colleges) and INDEST-AICTE (technical institutions), later brought together as e-ShodhSindhu . The National Digital Library of India (NDLI) , run from IIT Kharagpur under the Ministry of Education, is a single-window learning repository, and e-PG Pathshala offers postgraduate content. From 2025 the One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) scheme aims to give government-funded institutions access to thousands of international journals through a single national arrangement. Shodhganga = theses; Shodhgangotri = synopses; Vidwan = experts; IRINS = research profiles. N-LIST = colleges; INFONET = universities; INDEST = technical institutions; e-ShodhSindhu = merged consortium. ONOS = One Nation One Subscription (2025 onward). NDLI belongs to the Ministry of Education (IIT Kharagpur), not to the UGC’s INFLIBNET.

p: Digital Tools for Literature Search · Research Aptitude
x: Open access (OA) means free online access to scholarly work with permission to reuse under open licences such as Creative Commons. The gold route publishes in an OA journal, often funded by an article processing charge; the green route deposits a version in a repository, sometimes after an embargo; hybrid journals make selected articles OA in a subscription journal; diamond or platinum OA charges neither author nor reader. The movement rests on the Budapest (2002), Bethesda and Berlin (2003) declarations. The DOAJ lists vetted OA journals, OpenDOAR lists repositories, and SHERPA/RoMEO records publishers’ self-archiving policies. Preprints are manuscripts shared before peer review on servers such as arXiv (1991, Paul Ginsparg), bioRxiv, medRxiv, SSRN and ChemRxiv. Plan S (cOAlition S, 2018) requires publicly funded research to be published in OA form. Gold = OA journal; green = repository self-archiving; diamond = no fees for anyone. DOAJ = OA journals; OpenDOAR = repositories. Preprints are not peer reviewed. Free to read is not necessarily free to reuse; licences define reuse rights.

p: Digital Tools for Literature Search · Research Aptitude
x: Current awareness services keep researchers informed of new publications without repeated searching. Table-of-contents (TOC) alerts email the contents of new journal issues, saved-search alerts notify when new results match a query, citation alerts tell you when your paper is cited, and RSS feeds deliver headlines to a reader. A library-based version is Selective Dissemination of Information (SDI) , which matches new documents to a user’s interest profile. Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed and publishers’ sites all offer alerts. SDI = profile-based delivery of new information. Alerts: TOC, search, citation; RSS = feed. An alert informs you about new items; it does not evaluate their quality.

p: Digital Tools for Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Online survey platforms let researchers build questionnaires, distribute links and collect responses automatically. Google Forms is free and sends results to Google Sheets; Microsoft Forms is similar within Microsoft 365; SurveyMonkey and Qualtrics offer advanced features and academic licences; LimeSurvey is open source; KoboToolbox , ODK and SurveyCTO support offline mobile collection in the field; REDCap serves clinical and academic research with strong data-security features. Useful functions include skip logic (branching), randomisation of items, validation rules, multilingual forms and export to CSV, Excel or SPSS. Limitations are self-selection bias, coverage bias, low response and duplicate or bot responses. Google Forms: free, links to Sheets. Qualtrics: advanced. KoboToolbox/ODK: offline field use. REDCap: clinical research. Skip logic shows questions according to earlier answers. An online survey cannot represent people without internet access.

t: 5B.2 Computer-assisted Interviewing and Mobile Data Collection
p: Digital Tools for Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Computer-assisted methods replace the paper questionnaire. CAPI (computer-assisted personal interviewing) means an interviewer asks questions face to face and enters answers on a tablet or laptop; CATI is the telephone version; CAWI is web-based self-completion; CASI is computer-assisted self-interviewing; IVR is interactive voice response; PAPI is the traditional pen-and-paper personal interview. Built-in skip patterns, range checks, GPS and time stamps reduce entry errors and speed up processing. Large national surveys in India, such as the recent rounds of the National Family Health Survey, have used tablet-based CAPI. CAPI = in person; CATI = telephone; CAWI = web; PAPI = paper. Advantages: fewer errors, faster data, built-in checks, geo-tagging. CAPI is interviewer-administered, whereas CAWI is respondent self-administered.

p: Digital Tools for Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Video platforms such as Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams allow interviews and focus groups across distance, with recording only after informed consent. Transcription may be manual or automatic (Otter, Trint, Whisper-based tools and similar), but automatic transcripts must be checked against the audio for errors, names and dialect. Crowdsourcing platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk, Prolific and CloudResearch recruit participants quickly for surveys and experiments; researchers must pay fairly and use attention checks to guard against careless or automated responses. Citizen-science sites such as Zooniverse crowdsource data classification by volunteers. Consent is required before recording. MTurk, Prolific: online participant pools. Zooniverse: citizen science. Always verify automatic transcripts. Crowdsourced samples are convenience samples and may not represent the general population.

t: 5B.4 Web Data, APIs and Big Data
p: Digital Tools for Data Collection · Research Aptitude
x: Researchers can gather data from the web by scraping (extracting content from pages with tools such as BeautifulSoup, Scrapy or Selenium) or, more cleanly, through an API (application programming interface) offered by a platform. Other sources are Google Trends (relative search interest), web analytics, social-media analytics, sensors and Internet-of-Things devices, satellite imagery and open government data such as data.gov.in. Big data is classically defined by three Vs: volume, velocity and variety, with veracity and value often added, and it is handled with tools such as Hadoop and Spark. Problems include representativeness, platform rules and API limits, and privacy and consent. Three Vs: volume, velocity, variety. API = structured access permitted by the platform; scraping = extracting pages directly. Respect robots.txt, terms of service and privacy law. Social media users are not a random sample of the population, so conclusions need caution.

p: Digital Tools for Data Analysis · Research Aptitude
x: SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, now IBM SPSS) is menu-driven and popular in social science and education. SAS is strong in business and pharmaceutical analytics; Stata in economics and epidemiology; Minitab in quality control; EViews in time-series econometrics; AMOS and LISREL in structural equation modelling; SmartPLS in PLS-SEM. R is a free, open-source language for statistics with thousands of packages on CRAN and the RStudio environment, and Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn) serves data science. PSPP is a free SPSS-like program, and JASP and jamovi are free graphical programs built on R. Excel handles basic statistics through its Data Analysis ToolPak. SPSS = social sciences; SAS = business/pharma; Stata = economics; R = free and open source. PSPP, JASP and jamovi = free alternatives with menus. AMOS/LISREL = SEM. R and Python need code; SPSS, JASP and jamovi can be used through menus.

t: 5C.2 Qualitative Analysis Software and Text Tools
p: Digital Tools for Data Analysis · Research Aptitude
x: CAQDAS (computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software) helps organise, code and retrieve text, audio, video and images. Leading packages are NVivo , ATLAS.ti , MAXQDA , Dedoose (web-based and suited to mixed methods), QDA Miner and the free Taguette . Typical functions are coding (called nodes in NVivo), queries, word-frequency counts, word clouds and matrix comparisons. Voyant Tools is a web-based text-analysis tool, AntConc supports corpus linguistics, and sentiment analysis and topic modelling (such as LDA) apply computational text mining. The software stores and retrieves codes; the researcher still decides what the codes and themes mean. CAQDAS: NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, Dedoose, Taguette. Voyant Tools: text analysis in the browser; word cloud shows word frequency. A word cloud displays frequency, not meaning or themes.

t: 5C.3 Visualisation, Data Mining and Computational Tools
p: Digital Tools for Data Analysis · Research Aptitude
x: Tableau , Power BI and Looker Studio build interactive dashboards; Datawrapper and Flourish produce web charts; Gephi analyses networks; VOSviewer (from Leiden University) and CiteSpace map bibliometric networks. For mining and machine learning, WEKA (University of Waikato), Orange , KNIME and RapidMiner offer visual workflows. Jupyter Notebook is an interactive document that combines code, output and text for Python, R and Julia, and Google Colab provides Jupyter-style notebooks in the cloud. Python’s Matplotlib, Seaborn and Plotly and R’s ggplot2 are common plotting libraries. VOSviewer: bibliometric maps. Gephi: networks. WEKA: data mining. Jupyter: code + text notebooks. Colab: cloud notebooks. ggplot2: R graphics. Tableau and Power BI are for visualisation, not for storing or collecting data.

t: 5C.4 Collaboration and Writing Tools: Git, Overleaf and LaTeX
p: Digital Tools for Data Analysis · Research Aptitude
x: Git , created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, is a distributed version-control system that tracks changes to files, and GitHub and GitLab host Git repositories for collaboration. LaTeX (based on TeX by Donald Knuth and developed by Leslie Lamport) is a typesetting system favoured for mathematical and technical documents, with BibTeX handling references, and Overleaf is an online collaborative LaTeX editor. Google Docs and Microsoft 365 allow real-time co-editing. The Open Science Framework (OSF) supports project management and pre-registration, Zenodo (from CERN) and Figshare issue DOIs for data and code, and protocols.io shares methods. Git: version control (Torvalds, 2005). LaTeX: typesetting. Overleaf: online LaTeX. OSF: open-science projects and pre-registration. Zenodo and Figshare: DOIs for datasets. Git tracks versions of files; it is not a word processor.

p: Digital Tools for Data Analysis · Research Aptitude
x: A Geographic Information System (GIS) captures, stores, analyses and displays spatial data in layers. ArcGIS (Esri) is commercial, QGIS is free and open source, and Google Earth Engine handles large satellite archives; in India Bhuvan is ISRO’s geoportal. Data cleaning detects and corrects errors, duplicates, inconsistent labels, missing values and outliers before analysis. OpenRefine (formerly Google Refine) clusters and standardises messy data, and Excel Power Query and R’s tidyverse also support data wrangling. Cleaning decisions must be documented so the analysis stays reproducible. QGIS = free GIS; ArcGIS = commercial; Bhuvan = ISRO. OpenRefine = data cleaning. Cleaning is a step before analysis, not after interpretation.

p: Online Databases and Repositories · Research Aptitude
x: Scopus (Elsevier, 2004) is a large abstract and citation database that supplies CiteScore, SJR, SNIP and author profiles. Web of Science (Clarivate, formerly the Institute for Scientific Information) has the Core Collection of SCIE, SSCI, AHCI and the Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI), and publishes the Journal Citation Reports with the impact factor. Google Scholar is free but not curated. Dimensions links publications with grants and patents. In India, INFLIBNET’s IndCat is a union catalogue of library holdings, and the UGC-CARE list (Consortium for Academic and Research Ethics, introduced around 2018–19) was created to identify quality journals, though UGC’s journal-quality policy has been revised, so check the current position. Scopus = Elsevier; Web of Science = Clarivate; impact factor = JCR. WoS Core Collection: SCIE, SSCI, AHCI, ESCI. Google Scholar = free, not curated. CiteScore belongs to Scopus; impact factor belongs to Journal Citation Reports.

p: Online Databases and Repositories · Research Aptitude
x: Subject databases give deeper coverage in a field. PubMed/MEDLINE (National Library of Medicine) covers biomedicine; ERIC covers education; PsycINFO (APA) covers psychology; EconLit covers economics; IEEE Xplore covers engineering and electronics; the ACM Digital Library covers computing; MathSciNet covers mathematics; SciFinder covers chemistry; and the Cochrane Library holds systematic reviews in health. JSTOR is an archive of humanities and social science journals with older issues. ProQuest Dissertations and Theses collects theses, and EBSCOhost and ProQuest are platforms hosting many databases. arXiv (physics, mathematics, computer science), SSRN (social sciences) and RePEc (economics) provide preprints and working papers. PubMed = medicine; ERIC = education; PsycINFO = psychology; EconLit = economics; JSTOR = archive of journals. IEEE Xplore = engineering; ACM DL = computing; arXiv = physics, maths, CS preprints. EBSCOhost is a platform that hosts databases, not itself a subject database.

t: 5D.3 Identifiers, Quality Lists and Access Initiatives
p: Online Databases and Repositories · Research Aptitude
x: ORCID gives each researcher a persistent identifier that distinguishes them from others with the same name and links to their works. Other profiles are Web of Science ResearcherID, Scopus Author ID, Google Scholar profile and INFLIBNET’s Vidwan. Crossref is the main registration agency for scholarly DOIs and DataCite registers DOIs for datasets. The Directory of Open Access Journals vets OA journals, and the UGC-CARE list was India’s quality list. Access initiatives include e-ShodhSindhu , NDLI , IRINS and, from 2025, ONOS (One Nation One Subscription), which seeks a single national subscription to major international journals for public institutions. ORCID = researcher ID. Crossref = DOI registration for scholarly content. DataCite = DOIs for data. ONOS = national subscription scheme; Vidwan = Indian experts database. ORCID identifies a person; DOI identifies a work.

p: Online Databases and Repositories · Research Aptitude
x: Research data repositories store datasets and make them citable. Examples are Zenodo , Figshare , Dryad , Harvard Dataverse , OSF , Mendeley Data and ICPSR for social science data; in India the Open Government Data platform is data.gov.in , working under the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy of 2012. The FAIR principles (Wilkinson and colleagues, 2016) say that data should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. Good practice includes a data management plan, rich metadata (for example Dublin Core), a persistent identifier such as a DOI, and a clear licence (CC0 or CC BY). FAIR = Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (2016). Data repositories: Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, Dataverse, ICPSR. India: data.gov.in; NDSAP 2012. FAIR does not always mean open; data can be FAIR yet access-controlled.

p: Online Databases and Repositories · Research Aptitude
x: Metrics operate at three levels. Journal-level measures are the impact factor, CiteScore, SJR, SNIP and Eigenfactor. Author-level measures include the h-index (Hirsch, 2005), the g-index (Leo Egghe) and the i10-index (Google Scholar). Article-level measures include citation counts, field-weighted citation impact and altmetrics (online attention such as news, social media and policy mentions, shown by Altmetric and PlumX). Misuse of metrics is criticised in the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA, 2012) and the Leiden Manifesto (2015), which urge that research be judged on its content and not on journal metrics alone. h-index: Hirsch, 2005. i10: Google Scholar. g-index: Egghe. DORA (2012) and Leiden Manifesto (2015): responsible use of metrics. Altmetrics: online attention. A high journal impact factor does not guarantee that a given article is good.

p: Reference Managers · Research Aptitude
x: A reference manager collects bibliographic records and PDFs, organises them in a library and formats citations and bibliographies automatically. Zotero is free and open source, developed at George Mason University’s Center for History and New Media (2006), and captures records through a browser connector. Mendeley (owned by Elsevier) combines reference management with PDF reading and annotation. EndNote (Clarivate) is a commercial desktop-based manager. JabRef works natively with BibTeX, Paperpile integrates with Google Docs, RefWorks is from ProQuest and Citavi is popular in Europe. They save time and reduce citation errors, but the captured metadata must still be checked. Zotero: free, open source. Mendeley: Elsevier. EndNote: Clarivate, commercial. JabRef: BibTeX. Functions: capture, store, organise, cite, format bibliography. A reference manager does not guarantee correct citations; auto-captured data can contain errors.

p: Reference Managers · Research Aptitude
x: The cite while you write feature inserts citations into Word, LibreOffice or Google Docs through a plug-in and builds the bibliography in a chosen style. Styles are stored in Citation Style Language (CSL) files, which makes it possible to switch between APA, MLA, Chicago, Vancouver and others in one click. Common exchange formats are RIS , BibTeX (.bib) and EndNote XML . Further features include duplicate detection, full-text search, annotation of PDFs, tagging, group libraries for collaboration and synchronisation across devices. Cite While You Write (CWYW) = plug-in citing. Formats: RIS, BibTeX, EndNote XML; styles: CSL. Group libraries enable shared reading lists. Changing the style in a reference manager changes only the formatting, not the accuracy of the underlying data.

p: Plagiarism-checking Tools · Research Aptitude
x: Detection software compares a submitted text with large databases of web pages, journals and previously submitted papers, then highlights matching passages and produces a similarity report. Turnitin is widely used for student work; iThenticate , also from Turnitin, is used by researchers and publishers and powers Crossref Similarity Check . Urkund (now part of Turnitin as Ouriginal) was supplied to Indian institutions through INFLIBNET’s ShodhShuddhi initiative, and India’s DrillBit has also been adopted, so check the current vendor. Grammarly , Copyscape , Unicheck and PlagScan offer other checks. The software finds matching text; it does not decide whether plagiarism has occurred, which needs human judgement. Turnitin: students. iThenticate: researchers and publishers. ShodhShuddhi: INFLIBNET’s service for Indian institutions. Output: similarity report highlighting matches. A similarity report is evidence for review, not a verdict.

t: 5F.2 Similarity Index and Limitations of Checkers
p: Plagiarism-checking Tools · Research Aptitude
x: The similarity index is the percentage of the text that matches other sources; it is not the same as a plagiarism percentage, because matches can be properly quoted or cited. Under the UGC 2018 regulations, matches in quoted material with attribution, references, bibliography, table of contents, preface, acknowledgements, and generic terms, laws, standard symbols and common knowledge are excluded from the similarity count. Checkers give false positives (common phrases, correctly cited text) and false negatives : paraphrased plagiarism, translated plagiarism, copied ideas and figures, and sources absent from their database are missed. Detectors for AI-generated text are unreliable and should not be used as sole proof. Similarity index ≠ plagiarism percentage. Excluded in UGC 2018 counting: quotes with attribution, references, bibliography, preface, acknowledgements, common knowledge. Software misses paraphrase, translation and idea plagiarism. A zero similarity index does not prove originality, and a high one does not prove plagiarism.

t: 5F.3 Avoiding Plagiarism and Use of Generative AI
p: Plagiarism-checking Tools · Research Aptitude
x: To avoid plagiarism, acknowledge every source for words, data, figures and ideas; put exact words in quotation marks; paraphrase by restating in your own structure and still cite; keep careful notes that separate your ideas from sources; use a reference manager; run a self-check before submission; and obtain permission for reused material, including your own earlier published text. Generative AI tools can produce fluent text but may invent references and reproduce source material, so the researcher remains responsible for accuracy and originality. Journals and bodies such as COPE and ICMJE hold that an AI tool cannot be an author, and its use should be disclosed as the journal or institution requires. Presenting AI-written text as your own work is treated as misconduct in many policies. AI cannot be listed as an author; disclose AI assistance. Verify every AI-supplied reference against the source. Paraphrasing still needs citation. Changing a few words of a source is patchwriting, not paraphrasing, and still counts as plagiarism.

t: 6A.1 Meaning and Purpose of Research Ethics
p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Ethics is the study of moral principles that distinguish right from wrong conduct, and research ethics applies them to the design, conduct and reporting of research. It protects the dignity, rights, safety and privacy of participants, protects animals and the environment, and safeguards the integrity of knowledge so that the public can trust science. David Resnik lists its purposes as promoting the aims of research (truth and avoidance of error), supporting values needed for collaboration (trust, fairness, accountability), keeping researchers answerable to the public, and upholding wider moral and social values such as human rights, animal welfare and legality. Research ethics applies to all fields, not just medicine, and it is wider than the law: an act may be legal and still be unethical. Responsible conduct of research rests on honesty, objectivity, carefulness, openness, confidentiality and respect for colleagues and intellectual property. Research ethics covers participants, animals, data, authorship and the public interest. Core integrity values: honesty, objectivity, carefulness, openness, accountability. Ethics ≠ law; ethics applies in social sciences and humanities as well. A statement that ethics applies only to medical or clinical research is wrong.

t: 6A.2 Historical Codes: Nuremberg, Helsinki and Belmont
p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Modern research ethics grew from abuses. The Nuremberg Code (1947) came from the trial of Nazi doctors; its first principle is that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. The Declaration of Helsinki , adopted by the World Medical Association in 1964 and revised several times since, is the central statement for medical research and requires ethics committee review, informed consent and a favourable risk–benefit balance. The Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972), in which poor Black men in Alabama were left untreated to observe the disease, led to the US National Research Act (1974) and then to the Belmont Report (1979) with its three principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice. The CIOMS guidelines (from 1982, revised in 2016) apply these principles internationally, and ICH-GCP governs clinical trials. Nuremberg 1947 (voluntary consent); Helsinki 1964 (WMA); Belmont 1979 (three principles). Tuskegee: 1932–72; led to the National Research Act and Belmont Report. CIOMS: international ethical guidelines. Keep the order: Nuremberg (1947) → Helsinki (1964) → Belmont (1979).

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: The Belmont Report’s principles are respect for persons (autonomy and protection of those with diminished autonomy, giving rise to informed consent), beneficence (maximise benefits and minimise possible harm) and justice (fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research and fair selection of participants). Beauchamp and Childress, in Principles of Biomedical Ethics , name four principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence (do no harm, primum non nocere ) and justice. A risk–benefit assessment must show that risks are justified by the expected benefit. The Tuskegee study violated all three Belmont principles, notably justice, because a vulnerable group bore the burden. Belmont: respect for persons, beneficence, justice. Beauchamp and Childress: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice. Justice = fair selection and fair sharing of burdens and benefits. Belmont has three principles and Beauchamp–Childress has four; non-maleficence is the extra one.

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Before a study involving people starts, an independent committee reviews the protocol, the consent documents and the safeguards: an Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) in India, an Institutional Review Board (IRB) in the United States and a Research Ethics Committee (REC) in the UK. Such committees are multidisciplinary and include scientists, a clinician, a legal expert, a social scientist and a lay member, and they monitor studies after approval. In India the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017) set the standards, with general principles such as essentiality, voluntariness, non-exploitation, social responsibility, privacy and confidentiality, risk minimisation, professional competence, maximisation of benefit, transparency and accountability, and totality of responsibility. Clinical trials are governed by the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, and registered in the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI). IEC (India), IRB (US), REC (UK): independent protocol review. ICMR National Ethical Guidelines: 2017. CTRI: trial registry. Committee includes a lay person and a legal expert. Ethics approval must come before data collection, not after.

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Vulnerable groups include children, prisoners, pregnant women, people with mental illness or cognitive impairment, the elderly, the economically or educationally disadvantaged, refugees, and people in dependent relationships such as students or employees. They need extra safeguards, such as parental consent plus the child’s assent, or a legally authorised representative. Minimal risk means harm no greater than in ordinary daily life. Deception is acceptable only when the study has real value, no non-deceptive alternative exists, the risk is minimal and participants are debriefed afterwards. Classic cases are Milgram’s obedience experiments (deception and distress), Zimbardo’s Stanford prison experiment (psychological harm) and Humphreys’ covert observation study, Tearoom Trade . Minimal risk = no greater than daily life. Deception needs justification, minimal risk and debriefing. Right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Consent from a parent does not replace the child’s own assent, where the child is able to give it.

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: A conflict of interest arises when a researcher’s personal, financial or professional interest could, or could appear to, compromise judgement or objectivity. Financial examples are sponsor funding, consultancy fees, shares and patents; non-financial examples include rivalry, close personal relationships and academic competition. Conflicts are not always wrong, but they must be managed: disclose them to the institution, ethics committee, funder and journal; step aside from decisions where they apply (recusal); and arrange independent oversight. Reviewers and editors with a conflict should decline to handle the paper. Manage conflict by disclosure, recusal and oversight. Journals require a conflict-of-interest statement from authors. The perceived conflict matters as well as the actual one; hiding a conflict is the real offence.

t: 6A.7 Research Misconduct: Fabrication, Falsification and Plagiarism
p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Research misconduct is conventionally summed up as FFP. Fabrication is making up data or results; falsification is manipulating materials, equipment, processes or data, or changing or omitting results so that the record is not accurate; plagiarism is taking another’s ideas, words or results without credit. Honest error and genuine differences of opinion are not misconduct. Related questionable research practices are p-hacking, HARKing (hypothesising after results are known), selective reporting and cherry-picking. Terms sometimes used for data abuse are cooking (selecting data that fit), trimming (smoothing outliers) and forging . Consequences range from retraction to dismissal. FFP = fabrication, falsification, plagiarism. HARKing = presenting a post-hoc hypothesis as if it were pre-planned. Honest error ≠ misconduct. Fabrication invents data that never existed; falsification alters data that did exist.

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Authorship credit should follow contribution and responsibility. The ICMJE (Vancouver) criteria require all four: substantial contribution to conception, design, data or analysis; drafting or critically revising the work; final approval of the version published; and agreement to be accountable for the work. Contributors who do not qualify are thanked in the acknowledgements. Ghost authorship hides a real contributor; guest or gift (honorary) authorship credits someone who did not contribute. The corresponding author handles communication with the journal. Publication ethics also forbids duplicate and redundant publication, salami slicing, image manipulation and breach of confidentiality in peer review, and the CRediT taxonomy describes fourteen contributor roles. COPE guides editors on dealing with misconduct. ICMJE: four criteria, all required. Ghost = unnamed contributor; guest or gift = named without contributing. CRediT: 14 contributor roles; COPE: publication ethics body. Holding a senior position or providing funding does not by itself qualify for authorship.

p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: A whistleblower reports suspected misconduct in good faith through proper channels; institutions must protect them from retaliation and keep their identity confidential as far as possible. In India the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 covers disclosures about public servants. For animal research the guiding framework is the 3Rs of Russell and Burch (1959): Replacement (use non-animal methods where possible), Reduction (use the fewest animals) and Refinement (minimise suffering). The Five Freedoms come from the Brambell Report (1965). In India the CPCSEA (Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals), set up under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, regulates animal experiments through Institutional Animal Ethics Committees, and the ARRIVE guidelines govern reporting of animal studies. 3Rs: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement (Russell and Burch, 1959). CPCSEA and IAEC: India’s animal-experiment oversight. Whistleblower must act in good faith and be protected. Reduction means fewer animals, not fewer experiments of poor design; poor design wastes animals.

t: 6A.10 Research Integrity, Open Science and Questionable Practices
p: Ethical Principles in Research · Research Aptitude
x: Research integrity statements set shared standards. The Singapore Statement (2010) names four principles: honesty, accountability, professional courtesy and fairness, and good stewardship; the Montreal Statement (2013) addresses collaboration across borders; the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity lists reliability, honesty, respect and accountability. Open-science practices support integrity: sharing data and materials, pre-registration, registered reports and replication. Publication bias (the file drawer problem , a term from Robert Rosenthal) is the tendency to publish only significant results. The reproducibility crisis refers to the low rate at which many published findings can be replicated. Replicability means getting similar results with new data; reproducibility means getting the same results from the same data and code. Singapore Statement 2010: honesty, accountability, courtesy and fairness, stewardship. File drawer problem = unpublished negative results. Reproducibility = same data and code; replicability = new data. Do not interchange reproducibility and replicability; the data source is what differs.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: The word comes from the Latin plagiarius , a kidnapper. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, ideas, data or creative work as one’s own, without proper acknowledgement. The UGC regulations of 2018 describe it as taking someone else’s work or ideas and passing them off as one’s own. Forms include verbatim copying, mosaic plagiarism or patchwriting (stitching together phrases from sources with small changes), paraphrasing without credit , self-plagiarism (reusing one’s own published text without disclosure), translation plagiarism , idea plagiarism , plagiarism of data or images , secondary-source plagiarism (citing a source one has not read), and contract cheating or ghostwriting . It can be intentional or accidental, but carelessness is not a defence. Presenting a junior colleague’s results as one’s own is also plagiarism. Common knowledge need not be cited. Plagiarism = using others’ work without credit; applies to words, ideas, data, images. Mosaic/patchwriting: stitched phrases with minor changes. Self-plagiarism: reusing your own published text without disclosure. Changing a few words in a copied sentence is still plagiarism; accidental plagiarism is still plagiarism.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: There are three legitimate ways to use a source: quote (exact words in quotation marks, with citation and page), paraphrase (restate the idea in your own words and sentence structure, still with citation) and summarise (condense the main points, with citation). Direct quotations should be rare and short; long ones are set as block quotes. Statistics, theories, findings, figures and unusual ideas must be cited, while widely known facts do not need citation. Keep notes that clearly separate your words from source words, cite as you write, and match every in-text citation to a reference-list entry. A paraphrase that keeps the original structure and merely swaps synonyms is inadequate. Quote: exact words + quotation marks + citation. Paraphrase: new wording + citation. Even a perfect paraphrase needs a citation. Removing quotation marks while keeping the wording is plagiarism even if a citation is given.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: In India copyright is governed by the Copyright Act, 1957 (amended in 2012). It arises automatically when an original literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, film or sound recording is created; registration is optional. It protects the expression of ideas, not the ideas themselves. For literary works the term is the author’s life plus sixty years. Under fair dealing (Section 52) limited use for private study, research, criticism, review, reporting and teaching is allowed, a narrower idea than the US doctrine of fair use. Authors also hold moral rights of paternity and integrity. Creative Commons licences (CC BY, BY-SA, BY-NC, BY-ND, CC0) state what reuse is allowed. Plagiarism is an ethical offence against academic norms, whereas infringement is a legal offence; one can plagiarise public-domain work, which is free from copyright, without breaking copyright law. Copyright Act, 1957; term: life + 60 years for literary works; arises without registration. Fair dealing (Section 52): research, criticism, review, teaching. CC BY requires attribution; CC0 waives rights. Copyright protects expression, not ideas; plagiarism and copyright infringement are different wrongs.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: The UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018 apply to students, researchers, faculty and staff. They require an undertaking of originality, use of plagiarism-detection software, and institutional bodies for academic integrity (a Departmental Academic Integrity Panel and an Institutional Academic Integrity Panel). They exclude from similarity counting quotations with attribution, references and bibliography, table of contents, preface and acknowledgements, and generic terms, laws, standard symbols and standards. Penalties depend on the similarity level. For students: Level 0 up to 10% (no penalty); Level 1 above 10% to 40% (a revised script must be submitted within six months); Level 2 above 40% to 60% (debarred from submitting a revised script for one year); Level 3 above 60% (registration for that programme cancelled). For faculty and staff the levels lead to withdrawal of the manuscript and, at higher levels, denial of increments and exclusion from supervision, and repeat offences attract severe action. Levels 0–3 at 10%, 40%, 60% thresholds. Exclusions: quotes with attribution, references, preface, acknowledgements, common knowledge. Bodies: DAIP and IAIP. The thresholds define where each level begins; check whether the question says “above” or “up to”. Level Similarity Student consequence 0 Up to 10% None 1 10–40% Revise within six months 2 40–60% Barred from submitting revised version for one year 3 Above 60% Registration cancelled

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: The International Center for Academic Integrity names the fundamental values of academic integrity as honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and, added later, courage. Breaches include cheating (unauthorised aid), collusion (unauthorised collaboration), contract cheating (paying someone to produce work, as through essay mills), ghostwriting , impersonation, fabrication of data or citations, facilitating others’ dishonesty and multiple submission of the same work for credit more than once. Institutions respond with honour codes, education, clear policies and fair procedures. ICAI values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility, courage. Contract cheating = paying for work; collusion = improper collaboration. Collaboration that the instructor allows is not collusion; unauthorised collaboration is.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: Beyond plain plagiarism, several practices damage integrity. Image manipulation (splicing, duplicating or selectively adjusting blots and micrographs) distorts evidence. Padding the reference list adds irrelevant sources to look scholarly. Coercive citation is when editors or reviewers pressure authors to cite their journal or their own work to raise metrics, and citation cartels are groups citing each other to inflate counts; excessive self-citation has a similar effect. Paper mills are commercial services that sell fabricated papers or authorship. Peer-review rings use fake reviewers, and predatory journals accept papers for a fee without genuine review. Such journals typically promise very quick acceptance and make false claims about indexing. Coercive citation: demanded by editors or reviewers. Paper mill: sells papers or authorship. Predatory journal: fee, no real review, quick acceptance, false claims. Image manipulation is misconduct, not mere “enhancement”. Quick acceptance guaranteed within days is a red flag, not a feature.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: Authorship disputes are best prevented by agreeing contributions and author order at the start of the project against the ICMJE criteria and institutional rules. When a dispute arises, the first step is a discussion among the authors using those criteria, then referral to the institution or the journal, whose editor may consult COPE guidance. People who contributed but do not meet authorship criteria (technical help, language editing, general supervision, funding access) are named in acknowledgements with their permission, and funding sources are stated. The CRediT roles are conceptualisation, data curation, formal analysis, funding acquisition, investigation, methodology, project administration, resources, software, supervision, validation, visualisation, writing the original draft, and writing (review and editing). First step in an authorship dispute: discuss within the team against agreed criteria. Acknowledge non-author contributors and funders. CRediT: 14 roles. Honorary authorship damages credibility; acknowledgement is the correct recognition for minor help.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: Consequences of misconduct include retraction of papers, rejection or withdrawal of a thesis, cancellation of registration or degree, loss of funding and employment, debarment, reputational damage and sometimes legal action. Well-known cases include Hwang Woo-suk (fabricated stem-cell papers in Science , 2005), Diederik Stapel (fabricated data in many social-psychology papers, 2011), Jan Hendrik Schön (fabricated physics results at Bell Labs, 2002), Andrew Wakefield (the retracted 1998 Lancet paper linking MMR vaccine to autism), Haruko Obokata (retracted STAP cell papers, 2014) and the Piltdown Man hoax (exposed in 1953). Retraction Watch , founded in 2010, tracks retractions, and COPE gives retraction guidelines. Hwang: stem cells. Stapel: social psychology. Schön: physics. Wakefield: MMR and autism. Obokata: STAP. Retraction Watch: database of retractions. A retraction does not always mean fraud; it can follow honest error, but the reason must be stated.

p: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity · Research Aptitude
x: Detection combines software (see 5F) with human judgement: sudden shifts in style, anachronisms, inconsistent terminology and unusual fluency can signal copying. Software cannot catch everything, such as translated text, paraphrase and unavailable sources. Generative AI adds new problems: tools can invent references, reproduce source text and produce paraphrase that evades checkers, and “tortured phrases” from paraphrasing tools can reveal machine-spun text. Journals and COPE advise that AI cannot be an author, that its use must be disclosed, and that the human authors remain responsible for accuracy. AI-text detectors are unreliable and should not be used alone to accuse anyone. AI cannot be an author; disclose use; humans are accountable. Check every AI-generated citation against a real source. An AI-detection score is not proof of misconduct.

t: 6C.1 Informed Consent: Meaning, Elements and Rights
p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: Informed consent is a participant’s voluntary agreement to take part after being told what the research involves. It is a process , not just a signature on a form. Its elements are disclosure (purpose, procedures, duration, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality arrangements and whom to contact), comprehension (language and wording the person understands, in their own language), voluntariness (no coercion or undue influence), competence (capacity to decide) and authorisation (signature, thumbprint or witnessed agreement). The information is given in a participant information sheet and recorded in a consent form. Participants may withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits, and the form must not ask them to give up legal rights. In India the consent process in regulatory clinical trials is audio-visually recorded, and participants who suffer trial-related injury are entitled to free medical care and compensation under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019. Elements: disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, competence, authorisation. Consent is a continuing process; withdrawal is allowed at any time without penalty.
