Nuremberg Code: voluntary consent is essential. A signed form obtained without real understanding is not valid informed consent.

p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: Where a person cannot legally consent, a legally authorised representative (parent, guardian or other) gives permission, and the participant’s own assent is sought as far as they can understand. In the ICMR 2017 guidelines, children aged about 7 to 12 years give oral assent and those aged about 12 to 18 years give written assent, in addition to parental consent. For people who cannot read, an impartial witness is present during the consent process. Participants with mental illness, pregnant women, prisoners, students and employees need extra protection because of limited autonomy or power relationships. When new information emerges that may affect willingness to continue, participants are informed and consent is renewed. Child: parental consent + child assent. Illiterate participant: impartial witness. Authorised representative consents for those lacking capacity. Re-consent when significant new information appears. Assent is not a legal substitute for consent; it adds respect for the child’s own wishes.

p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: An ethics committee may waive informed consent for minimal-risk studies when obtaining consent is impracticable, such as research on anonymised records. Reasonable compensation for time, travel and inconvenience is acceptable, but a payment so large that it clouds judgement is undue inducement . Coercion is the threat of harm or penalty for refusing, as when a teacher requires students to take part or a doctor implies that care depends on participation. Exploitation means taking unfair advantage of vulnerable people. The therapeutic misconception occurs when participants wrongly believe that the research is designed for their personal benefit. In community studies, permission from community leaders does not replace individual consent. Waiver: minimal risk + impracticable + committee approval. Undue inducement = excessive reward; coercion = threat or penalty. Therapeutic misconception: mistaking research for treatment. Paying participants is not unethical in itself; the amount and the pressure created are what matter.

p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: Anonymity means that nobody, including the researcher, can link data to a participant. Confidentiality means that the researcher knows the identity but promises not to disclose it. Privacy is a person’s right to control access to personal information and to be free from intrusion. Techniques include removing direct identifiers, assigning codes (pseudonymisation) with the key stored separately, encryption, password protection, locked storage and limited access. Small samples or unusual details can make a person re-identifiable even without a name, so reports should aggregate data and alter identifying details. Confidentiality has limits: researchers may have to disclose when someone is at risk of serious harm or when the law requires it, and participants should be told so in advance. In focus groups, confidentiality cannot be guaranteed because other participants hear the discussion, so ground rules are agreed. Anonymity: identity unknown even to the researcher. Confidentiality: identity known but protected. Pseudonymisation: codes with a separate key. Focus groups: confidentiality cannot be fully guaranteed. A study using names on the questionnaire cannot call itself anonymous, though it may be confidential.

t: 6C.5 Data Protection Laws and Use of Data
p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: In India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the processing of digital personal data. It speaks of the data principal (the individual) and the data fiduciary (the entity deciding the purpose and means of processing), requires notice and consent for stated purposes, limits use to those purposes, and gives principals rights to access, correction and erasure. It provides conditional exemptions for research, archiving and statistical use when safeguards are in place, and it requires verifiable parental consent for children; check the status of its implementing rules. Earlier, the Information Technology Act, 2000 and its rules covered sensitive data. Abroad, the EU GDPR (2018) and US HIPAA (1996, for health information) are leading models. Secondary use of data should stay within the scope of the original consent or be approved by an ethics committee, and publicly posted online material still raises privacy and terms-of-service questions. DPDP Act 2023: data principal (individual), data fiduciary (processor of purpose). GDPR 2018 (EU); HIPAA 1996 (US health data). Reuse of data must respect the original consent. “Public” online posts are not automatically free to use without ethical review.

p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: Honest reporting means describing the methods, the results and the limitations accurately, including negative and non-significant findings. It excludes fabrication and falsification, and it also excludes subtler distortions: selective reporting of outcomes, cherry-picking of data, p-hacking (trying analyses until one is significant), HARKing and unplanned post-hoc subgroup analysis presented as planned. Publication bias (the file drawer problem) arises when only positive results are published, and outcome-reporting bias when only some measured outcomes are reported. Images must be adjusted uniformly and any adjustment disclosed. Reporting guidelines improve completeness: CONSORT for randomised trials, PRISMA for systematic reviews, STROBE for observational studies, ARRIVE for animal studies and COREQ or SRQR for qualitative work, catalogued by the EQUATOR Network. CONSORT = trials; PRISMA = systematic reviews; STROBE = observational; ARRIVE = animals; COREQ/SRQR = qualitative. p-hacking, HARKing, cherry-picking = distortions of reporting. Honest error is corrected, not concealed. Leaving out inconvenient results that were measured is a form of bias even if no number was changed.

p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: Pre-registration means recording the hypotheses, design and analysis plan in a time-stamped public registry before collecting data, so that later choices cannot be disguised as plans. Registries include OSF Registries, AsPredicted, ClinicalTrials.gov, the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI) and PROSPERO for systematic reviews. In registered reports a journal reviews the protocol first and commits to publishing the paper whatever the result. Transparency also covers sharing data, code and materials, following the FAIR principles and the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) guidelines, and including a data-availability statement. The reproducibility crisis , highlighted when a large replication project in psychology (2015) reproduced fewer than half of the studies, drives these reforms. Sharing must still respect consent and confidentiality, so the aim is data “as open as possible, as closed as necessary”. Pre-registration: plan recorded before data collection. Registered report: protocol is peer-reviewed first; publication does not depend on results. Registries: OSF, AsPredicted, ClinicalTrials.gov, CTRI, PROSPERO. Pre-registration does not forbid exploratory analysis; it requires that exploratory work be labelled as such.

t: 6C.8 Correcting Errors: Errata, Retractions and Honest Error
p: Informed Consent, Confidentiality and Honesty in Reporting Data · Research Aptitude
x: When an error is found after publication, the proper response is a published correction. An erratum corrects an error made by the publisher, and a corrigendum corrects an error made by the author; both leave the paper standing when the conclusions are unaffected. An expression of concern is a notice from editors that questions about a paper are under investigation. A retraction withdraws a paper because of serious error or misconduct (fabrication, plagiarism, duplicate publication or unethical research); the paper remains accessible but is marked as retracted, following COPE guidelines. Retraction is not always a finding of fraud, since honest error can lead to it, and researchers who discover their own honest error are expected to report it promptly to the journal. Erratum = publisher’s error; corrigendum = author’s error. Expression of concern = investigation in progress. Retraction = withdrawal for serious problems. Honest error ≠ misconduct; concealing it is the wrong. A retracted paper is still visible, marked as retracted, so that readers know its status.

p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: The word education is traced to three Latin roots, and examiners like to ask which root carries which meaning. Educare means to bring up, to nourish or to train; educere means to lead out or to draw out; educatum means the act of teaching or training. The “drawing out” sense ( educere ) is the one that fits the Indian and progressive view that the child already holds potential which education brings to the surface, whereas the “putting in” view treats the child as an empty vessel to be filled. This is the single most useful distinction in the whole subject: almost every thinker below can be placed on one side or the other. Education is a lifelong, purposeful and social process. It has a narrow meaning (schooling, instruction in an institution) and a broad meaning (everything that shapes a person from birth to death). It is also described as a bipolar process (John Adams: teacher and learner) and a tripolar process (John Dewey: teacher, learner and society, because the curriculum and the aims come from society). Educational agencies are classed as formal (schools, universities, with planned curriculum and certification), informal (family, peer group, media, with no planning) and non-formal (open schools, adult literacy centres, planned but outside the formal system, with flexible timing).

t: 1.2 Definitions of Education You Must Know
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Mahatma Gandhi: education is “an all-round drawing out of the best in child and man: body, mind and spirit.” Note the three-part (body, mind, spirit) structure. Swami Vivekananda: education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man. This is the classic statement of the educere view. Rabindranath Tagore: the highest education is that which does not merely give information but makes our life harmonious with all existence. Associated with Shantiniketan and Visva-Bharati. Aristotle: education is the creation of a sound mind in a sound body. Plato: education is the development in the body and soul of all the beauty and perfection of which the individual is capable. Pestalozzi: education is the natural, harmonious and progressive development of man’s innate powers. Froebel: education is the unfoldment of what is already enfolded in the germ. He is the father of the kindergarten (“garden of children”). Rousseau: advocated negative education and a return to nature in his book Emile ; the child should not be forced into adult moulds and should learn from natural consequences. John Locke: the mind at birth is a tabula rasa (blank slate), which supports the “filling in” view. John Dewey: education is a continuous reconstruction of experience; education is not preparation for life, it is life; the school is a miniature (embryonic) society. Detailed in 1.5.

p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching is a deliberate, planned and interactive activity in which a more knowledgeable person arranges conditions that help another person learn. It is not the same as lecturing, telling or merely covering the syllabus. The most important conceptual idea is Dewey’s analogy: teaching is to learning what selling is to buying. A shopkeeper who has not sold anything has not really been selling, and a teacher whose students have not learned has not really taught. Teaching is therefore judged by its results in learning , not by the amount said. Key definitions, with the logic examiners test: B. O. Smith: teaching is “a system of actions intended to induce learning.” The word intended matters: the actions are goal-directed, and the word system tells you teaching is organised, not random. This is the most frequently tested definition. N. L. Gage: teaching is a form of interpersonal influence aimed at changing the behaviour potential of another person. John Brubacher: teaching is the arrangement and manipulation of a situation in which there are gaps and obstructions which an individual will seek to overcome and from which he will learn in the course of doing so. H. C. Morrison: teaching is an intimate contact between a more mature personality and a less mature one, designed to further the education of the latter. Edmund Amidon: teaching is an interactive process, primarily involving classroom talk, which takes place between teacher and pupil during certain definable activities. This is the basis of interaction analysis ( Topic 6 ). Thomas Green: teaching is a set of activities that may include telling, showing, demonstrating and questioning, and it need not always be formal lecturing.

t: 1.4 Teaching, Instruction, Training, Conditioning and Indoctrination
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Questions often ask which word fits which situation. Instruction is the narrower, content-focused part of teaching, concerned mainly with the cognitive domain (imparting knowledge and skills). Teaching is broader: it includes instruction but also develops attitudes, values and thinking, and is concerned with the whole person. Training aims at a specific skill or habit through practice (typing, driving, surgery). Conditioning builds automatic responses through repetition and reinforcement without necessarily involving understanding (the behaviourist model). Indoctrination transmits beliefs in a way that does not allow the learner to question or examine them, and is regarded as the opposite of genuine teaching because it closes the mind. A useful test: if the learner’s reason and choice are respected, it is teaching; if they are bypassed, it is conditioning or indoctrination.

t: 1.5 Dewey and the Pragmatic View of Education
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: John Dewey (1859 to 1952), an American philosopher and the leading figure of pragmatism , argued that knowledge arises from experience and is tested by its consequences. His Laboratory School at the University of Chicago (1896) tried out his ideas. Four ideas dominate the exam: (1) education as growth and reconstruction of experience : each experience should leave the learner better able to handle the next; (2) learning by doing : activity, not passive listening, is the route to understanding; (3) the school as a miniature society : the school should be a simplified, purified and balanced community life, not a place cut off from real life; and (4) democratic education , with shared decision-making and respect for the learner’s interests. Dewey also described reflective thinking in How We Think (1910) as five phases: (i) a felt difficulty , (ii) location and definition of the problem, (iii) suggestion of possible solutions (hypotheses), (iv) reasoning out the consequences of each suggestion, and (v) observation and experiment leading to acceptance or rejection. The sequence “felt difficulty first, testing last” is a very common memory question. His ideas were converted into classroom practice by his follower W. H. Kilpatrick as the project method .

t: 1.6 Characteristics and Basic Requirements of Teaching
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching is purposeful (aimed at objectives), interactive (a two-way process), planned yet flexible, a science (because it uses research-based principles) and an art (because it needs creativity, expression and personal style), a continuous improvement process, and a social act with moral responsibility. The three variables of teaching are the independent variable (the teacher, teaching style and strategies), the dependent variable (the learner’s learning outcomes) and the intervening variable (learner’s motivation, ability, attention and readiness, which cannot be seen directly but affect results). The basic requirements for effective teaching are: clear objectives; mastery of content; knowledge of learner characteristics; suitable methods and materials; a healthy classroom climate; two-way communication; reinforcement and feedback; and proper evaluation. Phases of teaching (Philip Jackson): the pre-active phase (planning: setting objectives, selecting content and methods), the interactive phase (actual classroom delivery and student interaction) and the post-active phase (evaluation, feedback, reflection and re-planning).

p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Maxims are time-tested rules that make teaching natural and psychological: known to unknown; simple to complex; concrete to abstract; whole to part; analysis to synthesis; induction to deduction; psychological to logical order; empirical to rational; actual to representative. The one that trips candidates most is psychological to logical : begin from what is natural and interesting to the child, and only later arrange knowledge in the logical order of the subject. Induction to deduction means moving from examples to the rule first, and then using the rule on new cases.

t: Memory Capsule: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: Educare = to nourish; educere = to lead out; educatum = act of teaching. Bipolar = John Adams (teacher, learner). Tripolar = Dewey (teacher, learner, society). “System of actions intended to induce learning” = B. O. Smith . “Interpersonal influence” = Gage . “Intimate contact of mature with less mature” = Morrison . “Classroom talk” = Amidon . Teaching : learning :: selling : buying = Dewey . Jackson’s phases: pre-active, interactive, post-active. Dewey’s reflective thinking starts with a felt difficulty and ends with testing the hypothesis. Kindergarten = Froebel; negative education / Emile = Rousseau; tabula rasa = Locke.

t: Analysis Angle: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements
p: Education and Teaching: Meaning, Nature and Requirements · Teaching Aptitude
x: When a question describes a teaching situation, first ask: is the learner’s reasoning being engaged or bypassed? A teacher who dictates notes and tests recall is operating closer to instruction; one who poses a problem and lets students reason is teaching in the fuller sense. When an option claims that “teaching is complete once the syllabus is covered”, it is almost always wrong because teaching is defined by its effect on learning (Dewey, Smith). In matching questions, anchor on the key word in each definition (system, interpersonal influence, intimate contact, talk). In assertion-reason questions on Dewey, the correct reason for “school is a miniature society” is that education is life and not a preparation for it.

p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: These three words differ in scope, and the difference is tested. An aim is a broad, long-term, general direction of education (for example, “the development of good citizenship”). A goal is narrower and tied to a programme or stage (for example, “the school will achieve 100 percent functional literacy”). An objective is specific, short-term and observable , stated in terms of what the learner will be able to do after instruction. An instructional (behavioural) objective is the most specific form. A learning outcome is the programme- or course-level statement of what a learner will know and be able to do at the end, and is the unit of Outcome-Based Education (OBE), which is central to NEP 2020 and NAAC accreditation. A badly written objective uses vague verbs such as “know”, “understand” or “appreciate”; a good one uses a measurable action verb such as “define”, “classify”, “calculate” or “design.”

p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Ralph Tyler (1949) gave the objectives-centred curriculum model and insisted that objectives should state both the behaviour and the content. Benjamin Bloom (1956) led a group that classified educational objectives into three domains. Robert Mager (1962) popularised precise behavioural objectives with three components: the performance (what the learner will do), the conditions under which it is done, and the criterion (the standard of acceptable performance). The ABCD format (Audience, Behaviour, Condition, Degree) is a later classroom-friendly formulation of the same idea. The RCEM (Regional College of Education, Mysore) scheme, developed in India on Bloom’s model, groups cognitive objectives as Knowledge, Understanding, Application and Skill . A question asking “which of Tyler, Mager and Bloom contributed to objective-writing?” has the answer “all, at different stages.”

p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Bloom’s taxonomy is a hierarchy : each level builds on the one below it, from simple recall to complex judgment. The 1956 categories, from lowest to highest, are: Knowledge: recalling facts, terms, dates, definitions, sequences. Verbs: define, list, name, recall, state. Comprehension: understanding meaning; interpreting, translating, summarising, explaining in one’s own words. Verbs: explain, describe, summarise, paraphrase. Application: using learned rules, methods or principles in a new situation. Verbs: apply, solve, demonstrate, use. Analysis: breaking material into parts and seeing relationships and organisation. Verbs: analyse, compare, differentiate, examine. Synthesis: putting parts together to form a new whole; originality. Verbs: design, compose, construct, formulate. Evaluation: judging value against criteria. Verbs: judge, critique, justify, appraise. A useful way to see the logic: knowledge and comprehension are lower-order thinking; application is the bridge; analysis, synthesis and evaluation are higher-order thinking. An item that asks a student to “critique the methodology of a research paper” is evaluation, one that asks them to “explain why objects fall at the same rate” is comprehension, and one that asks them to “use the law to calculate” is application.

p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: A group led by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl (Bloom’s former student) revised the taxonomy in 2001. Three changes are repeatedly tested: (1) nouns were replaced by verbs (Knowledge → Remember, Comprehension → Understand, Application → Apply, Analysis → Analyse); (2) Synthesis was renamed Create and placed at the top ; (3) Evaluation moved below Create . So the new order is Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. The revision also added a second dimension, the knowledge dimension , with four types: factual, conceptual, procedural and metacognitive knowledge. A learning objective is therefore a combination of a verb (cognitive process) and a noun (type of knowledge). Remember the difference in the order of the top two levels: in 1956 evaluation was the peak, in 2001 creation is the peak.

t: 2.5 The Affective Domain (Krathwohl, Bloom and Masia, 1964)
p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: The affective domain deals with feelings, attitudes, interests and values. Its five levels run from simple awareness to a value that governs one’s whole behaviour: Receiving (willingness to attend), Responding (active participation or reacting), Valuing (attaching worth to something, showing commitment), Organisation (arranging values into a system and resolving conflicts between them) and Characterisation by a value or value complex (behaviour becomes consistent with the internalised value system, becoming part of one’s character). Mnemonic: R-R-V-O-C. Example mapping: a student who listens to a talk on honesty (receiving), discusses it (responding), declares honesty important (valuing), balances honesty against loyalty (organisation) and lives consistently by it (characterisation). “Appreciating classical music” is an affective objective, not a cognitive one.

p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: The psychomotor domain concerns physical skills and coordination. Three taxonomies are named in exams. Dave (1970) has five levels: Imitation, Manipulation, Precision, Articulation, Naturalisation (mnemonic: I-M-P-A-N). Simpson (1972) has seven: Perception, Set, Guided Response, Mechanism, Complex Overt Response, Adaptation and Origination. Harrow (1972) has six: Reflex movements, Basic fundamental movements, Perceptual abilities, Physical abilities, Skilled movements and Non-discursive communication. In every scheme the movement goes from conscious, clumsy copying to automatic, fluent and finally creative performance.

t: Memory Capsule: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy
p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Cognitive (Bloom 1956): Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis, Evaluation. Revised (2001): Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. Affective (Krathwohl 1964): Receiving, Responding, Valuing, Organisation, Characterisation (R-R-V-O-C). Psychomotor: Dave (5, I-M-P-A-N), Simpson (7), Harrow (6). Knowledge dimension (2001): factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive. Mager: performance, conditions, criterion. RCEM: knowledge, understanding, application, skill. Tyler = objectives-centred curriculum; Bloom = taxonomy; Mager = behavioural objectives.

t: Analysis Angle: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy
p: Objectives of Teaching and Bloom's Taxonomy · Teaching Aptitude
x: To classify a test item or objective, ignore the topic and look at the verb and demand . “List five causes of the French Revolution” sounds historical but only asks for recall, so it is the lowest level. “Debate the pros and cons of liberalisation” asks for judging, so it is evaluation. “Design an alternative economic model” asks for producing something new, so it is synthesis or creation. Questions that combine levels (“analyse and then judge”) are placed at the highest level involved. For objective-quality questions, the poorly written objective is always the vague one (“the student will understand photosynthesis”) and the well-written one has an observable verb, a condition and a standard. For Bloom vs revised Bloom, the safest trap check is: if an option says “Evaluation is at the top” it describes the 1956 version, not the 2001 version.

t: 3.1 The Three Levels at a Glance
p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching can be conducted at three levels of increasing depth, each linked to a thinker and a type of learning. Memory level (Herbart) aims at retention and recall of facts. Understanding level (Morrison) aims at grasping meaning, principles and relationships. Reflective level (Hunt) aims at independent thinking, problem-solving and critical judgment. They form a hierarchy: understanding includes memory, and reflection includes both.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: The memory level is the lowest, often called “thoughtless” teaching because the learner reproduces information without grasping its meaning. Its objective is knowledge acquisition and retention (corresponding to the knowledge category of Bloom). The teacher is the active transmitter and the learner a passive receiver, so it is highly teacher-centred and rooted in the “empty vessel” view. Learning here is rote , reproductive and often uses drill, repetition, mnemonics and cramming. It is evaluated by recall-type or objective tests. It is suitable for facts that must simply be remembered (tables, formulae, vocabulary, dates), and it is a necessary foundation, but if teaching stops here, students cannot apply what they know. Herbart’s five formal steps are the lesson-plan model associated with this level: Preparation, Presentation, Association (comparison), Generalisation and Application.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: At this level the learner must see the relationship between facts and the principles behind them, so that knowledge can be used in new situations. Morrison’s mastery approach is built on insight: the learner can explain, generalise and apply in his or her own words. It is reconstructive rather than reproductive learning. The teacher’s role changes from a mere transmitter to a guide who explains with examples, uses questions and builds scaffolding, and the learner is more active than at the memory level but still depends on the teacher for direction. It is assessed with essay and short-answer tests that demand explanation, and with objective tests that require application. Morrison’s teaching cycle has five steps: Exploration, Presentation, Assimilation, Organisation and Recitation.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: The reflective level is the highest and most demanding. The learner is placed in a problem situation and must use analysis, imagination and judgment to find a solution, so learning is problem-centred , active, independent and creative . The teacher is a facilitator or co-inquirer who creates the problem situation and supports reasoning without giving the answer, and the learner is the main actor. Because the outcomes are higher-order (analysis, synthesis, evaluation), assessment uses essay-type questions, projects and open-ended problems. This level is closest to Dewey’s reflective thinking ( Topic 1 ) and to the project and problem-solving methods ( Topic 6 ). It cannot be reached without a solid base of memory and understanding, so a teacher should treat the levels as cumulative stages of the same unit, not as rival choices.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Aim: retention (memory); insight and application (understanding); independent problem solving and critical thinking (reflective). Teacher’s role: transmitter (memory); guide (understanding); facilitator or co-inquirer (reflective). Learner’s role: passive receiver; active participant under direction; independent, self-directed investigator. Learning type: rote and reproductive; insightful and reconstructive; creative and problem-based. Motivation: extrinsic (rewards, marks) can be enough at the memory level; at the understanding level interest and meaning are needed; at the reflective level intrinsic motivation is essential. Test type: recall and objective items; short-answer, essay and application items; essay, project and open-ended problem items. Bloom link: knowledge; comprehension and application; analysis, synthesis and evaluation. Vygotsky link: memory is mostly what the child already can do; understanding works inside the ZPD with scaffolding; reflective teaching pushes toward independent performance at the upper edge of the ZPD.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Memory = Herbart = thoughtless, rote, lowest, teacher-centred. Understanding = Morrison = insight, rules, principles, mastery, guide. Reflective = Hunt = problem-centred, highest, creative, facilitator, intrinsic motivation. Herbart: Preparation, Presentation, Association, Generalisation, Application. Morrison: Exploration, Presentation, Assimilation, Organisation, Recitation.

p: Levels of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Scenario questions give a classroom picture and ask which level it shows. Decide by the student’s cognitive task . Students reciting the preamble or reproducing a definition: memory. Students explaining why a principle works or giving a new example: understanding. Students judging pros and cons of a policy or designing a model to solve a problem: reflective. Questions on teacher roles are consistent: transmitter, guide, facilitator in that order. “Which level is most important?” is a trap because the correct view is that all three are needed and build on one another, with reflective teaching being the highest aim but resting on memory and understanding. Watch for options claiming that “motivation is irrelevant at all three levels”, which are always wrong.

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching is only effective when it is matched to who is learning. Learner characteristics are the attributes that learners bring into a classroom: age and developmental stage, prior knowledge, intelligence and aptitude, motivation, interests, learning style, self-concept, emotional state, social and cultural background, language and special needs. Two principles run through the whole chapter. First, individual differences exist in every class, so one method for all will fail some learners (this is why differentiated instruction is recommended). Second, what the learner already knows is the single strongest factor in what he or she will learn next (Ausubel: “the most important single factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows; ascertain this and teach accordingly”).

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Jean Piaget saw the child as an active little scientist who builds knowledge by interacting with the world. His main terms are schema (a mental framework or structure for organising knowledge), assimilation (fitting new information into an existing schema), accommodation (changing the schema to fit new information), adaptation (the combined process of assimilation and accommodation) and equilibration (the balancing force that drives development when there is a conflict between what is known and what is experienced). Development proceeds through four invariant stages, and each stage is qualitatively different: Sensorimotor (0 to 2 years): knowledge comes through senses and actions. Key achievement: object permanence (understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight), at about 8 to 12 months. Early reflexes give way to goal-directed action. Preoperational (2 to 7 years): use of symbols, language and pretend play grows, but thinking is intuitive and illogical. Characteristics: egocentrism (cannot see from another person’s viewpoint), animism (believing objects are alive), centration (focusing on one feature), irreversibility, and failure of conservation . The classic experiment is three mountains for egocentrism. Concrete operational (7 to 11 years): logical thinking about concrete, real objects. The child masters conservation (quantity stays the same despite change in shape), reversibility , classification (grouping by categories) and seriation (arranging in an ordered series, such as by size). Abstract and hypothetical thinking is still difficult. Formal operational (about 12 years and above, some books say 11+): abstract, hypothetical and hypothetico-deductive reasoning ; systematic thinking about possibilities, ideals and “what if” problems, and use of scientific logic. Teaching implications: give concrete materials and hands-on activities in the primary years; arrange tasks that cause cognitive conflict so that learning pushes development; do not teach abstract ideas before the child is ready ( readiness ); respect that children learn in different time frames. Critics note that Piaget underestimated children’s abilities and understated the role of social and cultural factors, which is Vygotsky’s point.

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Lev Vygotsky argued that cognitive development is a social process: higher mental functions begin between people (interpsychological) and are then internalised (intrapsychological). Language is the main cultural tool for thought. The key concepts are: Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): the gap between what a learner can do independently and what he or she can do with the guidance of a more capable person . Good teaching targets the ZPD, so tasks should be slightly beyond current ability, neither too easy nor impossibly hard. More Knowledgeable Other (MKO): anyone with a better understanding or higher ability in a task: a teacher, peer, parent, coach or even software. Scaffolding: temporary support (hints, modelling, questioning, breaking a task into steps) that is gradually withdrawn as the learner grows competent. The term was introduced by Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976), not by Vygotsky himself, though it fits his theory. Private speech: children talking to themselves while working is not a mental disorder; it is a cognitive self-regulation tool that gradually becomes silent inner speech. Piaget vs Vygotsky: Piaget emphasised individual discovery and the idea that development precedes learning; Vygotsky emphasised social interaction and the idea that learning leads development. Piaget focused on stages; Vygotsky did not propose fixed stages.

t: 4.4 Other Theorists Useful for Learner Characteristics
p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Jerome Bruner described three modes of representation: enactive (action), iconic (images) and symbolic (language), and proposed the spiral curriculum (revisiting ideas at increasing depth) and discovery learning . Erik Erikson gave eight psychosocial stages, each with a crisis: trust vs mistrust, autonomy vs shame and doubt, initiative vs guilt, industry vs inferiority (6 to 12 years, the school years), identity vs role confusion (adolescence), intimacy vs isolation, generativity vs stagnation and integrity vs despair. Lawrence Kohlberg described moral development at three levels: preconventional (obedience and self-interest), conventional (approval of others and law-and-order) and postconventional (social contract and universal ethical principles). Abraham Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is a pyramid in which lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones can motivate: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation . A hungry, frightened or neglected student cannot concentrate on learning; this is the main teaching implication. Albert Bandura proposed observational (social) learning (Bobo doll experiment) and self-efficacy , which is a person’s belief in his or her own capacity to carry out a task, not the actual ability and not an intelligence score. High self-efficacy predicts effort and persistence. Julian Rotter’s locus of control distinguishes learners who believe outcomes depend on their own effort (internal) from those who attribute outcomes to luck or others (external). Metacognition (John Flavell) is “thinking about one’s own thinking”: planning, monitoring and evaluating one’s own learning.

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Howard Gardner’s Multiple Intelligences include linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, bodily-kinaesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic (added later). The teaching implication is to present content in several ways. David Kolb’s experiential learning cycle has four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation , and four learning styles: diverger, assimilator, converger and accommodator. The VARK model (Visual, Aural, Read/write, Kinaesthetic) is a popular classification. Evidence for matching teaching strictly to a “style” is weak, so the wise teacher uses varied methods rather than labelling learners.

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Malcolm Knowles contrasted pedagogy (teaching children) with andragogy (teaching adults). Adult learners (a) have a self-concept of being independent and self-directed , (b) bring a rich reservoir of prior experience that is a resource, (c) have readiness to learn linked to life roles , (d) want problem-centred, immediately applicable learning , (e) are driven mainly by internal motivation and (f) need to know why they are learning something. Therefore adult education prefers discussion, case studies, projects and self-directed learning, and teachers act as facilitators. The common error is to think that adults rely only on concrete operations or have no capacity for abstract thinking, which is false.

t: 4.7 Special Groups: Gifted, Slow, Differently Abled; Inclusive Education
p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Gifted learners (IQ commonly taken as above 130, or exceptional talent) need enrichment, acceleration and challenge . Slow learners (IQ roughly 70 to 90) need more repetition, simpler steps, concrete material and patience, but they are not mentally disabled and are not necessarily less motivated. Differently abled learners require accessible materials and assistive technology. Inclusive education means the education system includes all learners in the common classroom, regardless of disability, gender, caste or economic background; it is backed by the Salamanca Statement (1994), the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009), the RPwD Act (2016) and NEP 2020. It is not education only for gifted learners, not education only for differently abled learners, and not education for economically weaker sections alone.

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Piaget: Sensorimotor (0 to 2, object permanence), Preoperational (2 to 7, egocentrism, animism), Concrete operational (7 to 11, conservation, seriation), Formal operational (12+, abstract, hypothetico-deductive). Vygotsky: ZPD, MKO, scaffolding (Wood, Bruner and Ross), private speech, social constructivism. Bruner: enactive, iconic, symbolic; spiral curriculum. Erikson: school age = industry vs inferiority; adolescence = identity vs role confusion. Maslow: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. Bandura: observational learning, self-efficacy. Rotter: locus of control. Flavell: metacognition. Kolb: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation. Gardner: multiple intelligences. Knowles: andragogy (self-directed, experience, internal motivation, problem-centred).

p: Learner Characteristics · Teaching Aptitude
x: Most application questions here give a learner behaviour and ask for the concept. A child who says that a taller glass holds more water: preoperational, no conservation. A student working a maths problem aloud to himself: private speech as self-regulation. A teacher who gives a hint and then withdraws it as the student improves: scaffolding within the ZPD. A student who believes “I can do this if I work at it”: high self-efficacy (not locus of control, which is about causes of outcomes ). A learner who cannot focus because of hunger: Maslow, a lower need unmet. When two thinkers are compared, anchor on the central contrast: individual vs social; stages vs no stages; development leads learning vs learning leads development. For adult learners, the correct option is nearly always the one that stresses prior experience and self-direction. For special groups, reject options that treat slow learners as unmotivated or inclusive education as limited to one group.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching effectiveness is not decided by the teacher alone; it emerges from the dynamic interaction of four sets of factors: teacher-related, learner-related, content and method-related, and institutional or environmental . Questions in this area usually reward the option that sees teaching as a system and reject options such as “teacher factors alone determine quality” or “institutional factors override all others.”

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Subject knowledge and pedagogical skill: a teacher must know the content and how to teach it. Communication ability: clarity, voice, language, questioning and listening. Personality and attitude: enthusiasm, warmth, patience, fairness and sense of humour create a climate of trust. Professional commitment and motivation: a motivated teacher motivates learners. Experience and reflective practice: the teacher who reflects on lessons improves. Teacher expectations: high expectations tend to raise performance, low ones lower it. This is the Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect : in the 1968 study by Rosenthal and Jacobson at an elementary school, teachers were told that certain randomly chosen children were “bloomers” about to show intellectual gains; those children actually improved more, showing that expectation changes teacher behaviour and thereby student outcomes. The reverse is the Golem effect. Adaptive teaching , the ability to adjust methods to learners’ needs, is a major teacher quality.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Prior knowledge, intelligence, readiness (physical, mental, emotional), motivation (intrinsic vs extrinsic), interest, attention, learning style, self-efficacy, health, emotional state, family background, language proficiency, and peer influence. The principle is that the learner is an active partner: teaching can only create conditions for learning, not force it.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: The nature and difficulty of the content (abstract vs concrete), the logical organisation of material, the match between the method and the objective, availability of teaching aids and technology, appropriate evaluation and sufficient time. A method that suits a psychomotor objective (demonstration) may be useless for a reflective objective (discussion or project).

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Infrastructure (classroom, library, laboratory, internet), class size (very large classes reduce interaction), school climate and leadership, administrative support, curriculum flexibility, examination pressure, policy and regulation, community and parental involvement, and socio-economic conditions. The classroom climate (emotionally safe, democratic, respectful) strongly affects participation and learning. Studies of classroom climate include Lippitt and White’s experiment on authoritarian, democratic and laissez-faire leadership, which found democratic climates the most productive in the long run.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Modern thought views the teacher as a facilitator, guide, mentor, motivator, evaluator, researcher and reflective practitioner , not a mere transmitter. Characteristics of effective teaching: clear objectives, organised content, variety of methods, active involvement, regular feedback, high expectations, positive climate and efficient use of time. Reflective teaching (Donald Schon: reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action) and action research are tools for improving practice.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Four groups: teacher, learner, content and method, institutional and environmental. Pygmalion effect = Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968), “bloomers”: teacher expectation changes student performance. Adaptive teaching = a key teacher-related quality. Climate study: Lippitt and White (authoritarian, democratic, laissez-faire). Teacher roles: facilitator, guide, mentor, motivator, reflective practitioner.

p: Factors Affecting Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: The correct answer in “factor” questions is generally the interactive one. If a question describes a teacher who behaves differently towards students believed to be bright and the results follow the expectation, the concept is the Pygmalion effect (a teacher-related factor that works through the learner). If a question asks what makes a class improve, look for options that combine teacher quality, learner readiness and a supportive environment. Beware of absolute words such as “alone”, “only”, “never” and “overtide all”: these usually mark wrong options.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Methods are best understood by who is active . Teacher-centred methods (lecture, demonstration, narration, recitation) emphasise transmission and suit large groups, factual content and the memory level. Learner-centred methods (discussion, project, problem solving, heuristic, inquiry, cooperative learning) emphasise activity and suit understanding and reflective levels. Technology-mediated methods (programmed instruction, computer-assisted learning, blended learning, flipped classroom, online learning) personalise and scale learning. No single method is best; selection depends on objectives, content, learner characteristics, time and resources .

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Lecture method: the teacher explains orally. Advantages: economical, covers a lot, suits large groups, gives structure. Limits: passive learners, little feedback, memory-level outcomes, attention declines after about 15 to 20 minutes. Lecture-cum-demonstration improves it by adding visual proof. Demonstration method: the teacher shows a process, experiment or skill while students observe; ideal for psychomotor skills , science experiments and where apparatus is costly or dangerous. Narration (story-telling), description and recitation are used for history, literature and moral education.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Discussion method: guided exchange of ideas; builds thinking and communication. Seminar: a participant (or group) presents a paper and the group discusses it, led by an expert; it is not a lecture or drill. Symposium: several experts speak on different aspects of one theme. Panel discussion: a small group of experts discusses a topic in front of an audience, with a moderator. Workshop: hands-on, skill-based group work on a practical problem. Conference: large gathering to share research. Brainstorming (Alex Osborn): group generates many ideas without criticism; stimulates creativity. Project method (W. H. Kilpatrick, based on Dewey): learners plan and carry out a purposeful activity in a real-life setting; learning by doing. Steps: providing a situation, choosing, planning, executing, evaluating, recording. Problem-solving method: follows the reflective thinking steps of Dewey. Heuristic method (H. E. Armstrong): the student acts as a discoverer; the word comes from the Greek heurisko , I find out. Inductive and deductive methods: moving from examples to rule, and from rule to examples. Socratic method: disciplined questioning to draw out knowledge and expose contradictions. Case method (Harvard): analysis of real or simulated cases, popular in management and law. Role play and simulation: acting out situations to learn behaviour and empathy. Cooperative and collaborative learning: small heterogeneous groups work for a shared goal with individual accountability. Jigsaw (Elliot Aronson, 1971): each member becomes an expert on one part and teaches the group. Think-Pair-Share (Frank Lyman): think alone, discuss with a partner, share with the class. Montessori method: didactic materials, freedom within limits and the prepared environment for young children. Kindergarten: Froebel. Dalton Plan: Helen Parkhurst, individual contracts and self-pacing. Peer tutoring and mentoring , team teaching (two or more teachers share a class) and inquiry-based learning .

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Programmed instruction was developed from Skinner’s operant conditioning. Linear programming (Skinner): small steps, active response, immediate feedback, self-pacing; every learner follows the same sequence. Branching programming (Norman Crowder): learner’s response decides the next frame, with remedial branches for errors. Mathetics (Thomas Gilbert) emphasises mastery of behaviour chains. Pressey built an early teaching machine in the 1920s. The Keller Plan (Personalised System of Instruction, 1968) uses self-paced modules with mastery tests and proctors. Computer-assisted instruction offers drill, tutorials, simulation and games. Blended learning combines face-to-face and online teaching (not technology-only, not traditional-only, not multilingual teaching). Flipped classroom: learners study content (video) at home and use class time for discussion and problem-solving. E-learning and MOOCs are discussed in Topic 7 .

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Microteaching, developed by Dwight Allen at Stanford University (1963) , is a scaled-down teaching encounter (small class of 5 to 10 students, a single skill, 5 to 10 minutes) used to train teachers. The cycle is Teach, Feedback, Re-plan, Re-teach, Re-feedback ; in the commonly cited Indian model the timings are roughly 6, 6, 12, 6, 6 minutes (36 minutes in all). Skills practised include set induction (introducing a lesson), stimulus variation, probing questioning, explaining, illustrating with examples, reinforcement, fluency in questioning, silence and non-verbal cues, using the blackboard, recognising attending behaviour and closure . The purpose is to master one skill at a time in a safe setting with immediate feedback.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Ned Flanders’ Interaction Analysis Categories (FIAC) record classroom talk every three seconds using ten categories. Teacher talk, indirect influence (1 to 4): accepts feeling, praises or encourages, accepts or uses students’ ideas, asks questions. Teacher talk, direct influence (5 to 7): lecturing, giving directions, criticising or justifying authority. Student talk (8 and 9): student response, student initiation. Category 10: silence or confusion. The results are shown in a matrix; the I/D ratio (indirect to direct influence) indicates the teacher’s style. A higher I/D ratio signifies a more democratic and student-centred classroom.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Behaviourism (Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Watson): learning is a change in observable behaviour produced by conditioning and reinforcement; its methods are drill, programmed instruction and reward. Cognitivism (Gestalt, Bruner, Ausubel, Gagne): learning is mental information processing and insight; its methods are advance organisers, concept mapping and discovery. Constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner): learners actively construct knowledge; its methods are inquiry, projects and cooperative learning. Humanism (Rogers, Maslow): learning is self-directed growth in a supportive climate. Gagne’s nine events of instruction are: gain attention, inform objectives, stimulate recall of prior learning, present stimulus, provide learning guidance, elicit performance, provide feedback, assess performance, enhance retention and transfer. Thorndike’s laws are readiness, exercise and effect.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Project method = Kilpatrick; Heuristic = Armstrong; Dalton = Helen Parkhurst; Kindergarten = Froebel; Brainstorming = Osborn; Jigsaw = Aronson; Think-Pair-Share = Lyman; Keller Plan = PSI. Linear programming = Skinner; branching = Crowder; mathetics = Gilbert. Microteaching = Dwight Allen (Stanford, 1963); cycle = teach, feedback, re-plan, re-teach, re-feedback. Flanders: 10 categories; 1 to 4 indirect, 5 to 7 direct, 8 and 9 student talk, 10 silence. Seminar = paper presentation and discussion. Symposium = several experts, one theme. Panel = experts in front of an audience.

p: Methods of Teaching · Teaching Aptitude
x: Match the objective to the method. Teaching a skill with apparatus: demonstration. Teaching a large body of factual content to a large class: lecture. Developing critical thinking about a social issue: discussion, seminar or case study. Developing independent problem-solving: project or heuristic method. For efficient use of class time with mixed ability: cooperative learning or the flipped model. A question that offers “teacher lectures for the full session” as the best way to develop reflection is wrong. In Flanders questions, calculate by category: praising and asking questions are indirect ; lecturing and giving directions are direct . When a scenario shows a teacher who accepts and builds on student ideas, the I/D ratio rises.

p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching support systems are the resources that help a teacher make instruction clearer, more interesting and more lasting: teaching aids, libraries, laboratories, technology and digital platforms. Teaching aids are classified as audio (radio, audio recordings, podcasts), visual (charts, models, maps, flash cards, blackboard, projected slides), audio-visual (television, films, video, multimedia) and activity-based (field trips, experiments, role play). Their purpose is to make abstract ideas concrete, raise attention and interest, support different learning styles and improve retention. A critical caution: aids support a teacher, they never replace one, and the wrong aid at the wrong time is a distraction. Educational technology has three strands: hardware (devices, projectors, computers), software (programmed material, courseware, apps) and the systems approach (planning inputs, process and outputs scientifically). ICT (Information and Communication Technology) refers to the whole family of digital tools used for teaching, learning and administration.

p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: Edgar Dale, in Audio-Visual Methods in Teaching , arranged learning experiences on a cone from most concrete at the bottom to most abstract at the top . The levels, from base to apex, are: Direct purposeful experiences; Contrived experiences (models, mock-ups); Dramatised experiences (role play, plays); Demonstrations; Field trips; Exhibits (and museums); Television; Motion pictures; Recordings, radio and still pictures; Visual symbols (charts, maps); Verbal symbols (spoken and written words). The cone shows the increasing abstraction as one moves up, and it recommends that teachers choose a mix of experiences, generally beginning with concrete and moving up to abstract. A common misunderstanding to avoid: the popular percentages attached to the cone (“we remember 10 percent of what we read”, etc.) were not given by Dale and have no research basis. Dale’s cone is about concreteness vs abstraction , not about retention figures. A question asking which sits in the middle (exhibits, television) or at the top (verbal symbols) is a pure memory item; a question asking why direct experience is placed at the bottom is a concept item (it is the most concrete and involves the most senses).

t: 7.3 ICT, Digital Repositories and Government Initiatives
p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: India has built a large public digital learning ecosystem. The ones worth knowing: NPTEL (National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning, begun 2003 by IITs and IISc): video and web courses in engineering and sciences. SWAYAM and SWAYAMPRABHA: discussed below. e-PG Pathshala: postgraduate e-content (non-technical) developed by UGC through INFLIBNET. CEC (Consortium for Educational Communication) produces undergraduate content; its Educational Multimedia Research Centres (EMRCs) produce videos. Shodhganga: repository of Indian PhD theses (INFLIBNET). Shodhgangotri: repository of research synopses. e-ShodhSindhu: consortium for e-journals and e-books for higher education. National Digital Library of India (NDLI): a single window to educational resources. DIKSHA: digital infrastructure for school education and teachers (NCERT/MoE). NISHTHA: teacher training programme. PM eVidya: umbrella programme for multi-mode digital education. e-Pathshala (NCERT) gives textbooks and resources. National Academic Depository (NAD): digital storage of academic awards and certificates, linked to DigiLocker. Academic Bank of Credits (ABC): see Topic 8 . Virtual Labs, Vidwan (expert database), NIRF (ranking framework, 2015) and NAAC (accreditation) are related quality and access tools.

p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: Meaning of the letters: Massive (very large enrolment, sometimes lakhs of learners), Open (accessible to anyone without entry requirements, often free to learn), Online (delivered over the internet), Course (a structured learning programme with a defined outcome). The term was coined in 2008 (credited to Dave Cormier and Bryan Alexander) for the course Connectivism and Connective Knowledge (CCK08) taught by George Siemens and Stephen Downes at the University of Manitoba. The 2011 Stanford online AI course by Sebastian Thrun and Peter Norvig attracted about 160,000 learners, and 2012 was called the “Year of the MOOC” when Coursera, edX and Udacity launched. Two types. cMOOC (connectivist MOOC) is based on connectivism (learning as building networks of connections); it is open, learner-driven and based on blogs, forums and social media; Siemens and Downes. xMOOC (extended MOOC) is institution-led, with video lectures, quizzes, assignments and certificates, in the style of Coursera and edX. Further forms include SPOCs (Small Private Online Courses) and hybrid or blended MOOCs , which combine online content with face-to-face support (this is what the word hybrid signifies). Features and limitations. Strengths: scale, flexibility of time and place, low cost, access to expert teachers, self-paced learning, support for lifelong learning. Limitations: very high dropout rates (often 90 percent or more), the digital divide, limited personal interaction, doubts about assessment authenticity, language barriers and uneven quality. A MOOC does not replace the university; it is supplementary and helps learners who could not otherwise attend.

t: 7.5 SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active-learning for Young Aspiring Minds)
p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: SWAYAM is India’s national MOOC platform, launched on 9 July 2017 , and it is built on the three cardinal principles of education policy: access, equity and quality. Its mission is to take the best teaching to every learner, including the economically disadvantaged. Course delivery uses a four-quadrant approach: Quadrant 1: video lecture ; Quadrant 2: specially prepared reading material (downloadable and printable); Quadrant 3: self-assessment through tests and quizzes ; Quadrant 4: online discussion forum to clear doubts. Cost: courses are free of cost for learning; a nominal fee is charged only for the certificate when the learner chooses to take the proctored examination. Certification: requires appearing in and passing a proctored examination at an assigned centre; watching videos alone does not earn a certificate. Credit transfer: under UGC regulations (2016, later amended) a university may allow students to earn credits through SWAYAM courses, up to 40 percent of the courses in a programme in a semester (originally 20 percent). The credits are recorded in the Academic Bank of Credits. National coordinators who prepare and deliver the courses: AICTE (self-paced and international courses), NPTEL (engineering), UGC (non-technical postgraduate education), CEC (undergraduate education), NCERT (school education), NIOS (school education, open schooling), IGNOU (out-of-school and bridge courses), IIM Bangalore (management) and NITTTR (teacher training). Courses are also offered in regional languages , which reduces the language barrier that keeps many learners out of English-medium online content. SWAYAM vs IGNOU: SWAYAM is a MOOC platform offering free online courses for learners, supplementing the formal system; IGNOU is an open and distance learning university that awards its own degrees. SWAYAM is not only for school students.

p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: SWAYAMPRABHA is a group of Direct-to-Home (DTH) educational television channels , started in 2017 with 32 channels , broadcast through the satellite GSAT-15 , free to air, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week . Fresh content is telecast for about four hours daily and repeated several times so that learners can watch at a convenient slot. The channels are run by IITs, UGC, CEC, IGNOU, NCERT, NIOS and NITTTR; the satellite uplink is done by BISAG and the web portal is maintained by INFLIBNET. Its purpose is to reach learners who have no internet connection or computer , so it extends education to rural and remote areas using a technology (television) that most homes have. SWAYAMPRABHA is not a mobile app, not a scholarship scheme, not an examination portal and does not award certificates (it is supplementary, and certification is available through SWAYAM, the internet-based platform). The two platforms together (SWAYAM for online + SWAYAMPRABHA for DTH) cover both connected and unconnected learners.
