x: Dale’s cone: Direct purposeful experiences (bottom) → Contrived → Dramatised → Demonstrations → Field trips → Exhibits → Television → Motion pictures → Recordings/radio/still pictures → Visual symbols → Verbal symbols (top). MOOC term: 2008, CCK08; Siemens and Downes = cMOOC; Coursera, edX, Udacity = xMOOC (2012). SWAYAM: 9 July 2017; access, equity, quality; four quadrants (video, reading material, self-assessment, discussion forum); free learning, nominal exam fee; proctored exam; up to 40 percent credit transfer. SWAYAM coordinators: AICTE, NPTEL, UGC, CEC, NCERT, NIOS, IGNOU, IIMB, NITTTR. SWAYAMPRABHA: 32 DTH channels, GSAT-15, 24x7, free to air, no certificate. NPTEL 2003; Shodhganga = theses; e-PG Pathshala = PG content; NAD = academic awards depository.

t: Analysis Angle: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM
p: Teaching Support Systems, Aids, MOOCs and SWAYAM · Teaching Aptitude
x: Questions here test whether you can separate look-alike items. Which platform for which problem? A learner without internet or a computer: SWAYAMPRABHA. A learner who wants a credit-bearing course with an exam: SWAYAM. A researcher looking for earlier theses: Shodhganga. Which statement about SWAYAM is correct? Pick the one that mentions four quadrants, free access, proctored exams and the multi-coordinator structure, and reject options that say “only for school students”, “very high fee”, or “certificate for only watching videos.” For “MOOC” scenario items, the cMOOC is the one tied to connectivism and networks, while the xMOOC resembles a traditional course delivered at scale. For Dale’s cone, always remember the direction: bottom = concrete, top = abstract , so any option that puts verbal symbols at the base is wrong.

p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: CBCS, introduced by UGC guidelines in 2015 , gives students the freedom to choose courses from a prescribed list, to learn at their own pace, and to combine disciplines. It rests on three ideas: a semester structure, a credit for every course and a grade instead of marks. The course types are: Core courses: compulsory papers of the chosen discipline that form the foundation of the programme. Elective courses: chosen by the student; they are Discipline Specific Electives (DSE) (from the same discipline but giving specialisation), Generic Electives (GE) (chosen from other disciplines to broaden knowledge) and Project or Dissertation . Ability Enhancement Compulsory Courses (AECC): Environmental Science and English or Modern Indian Language communication . Skill Enhancement Courses (SEC): value-based or skill-based courses (for example, computer skills or soft skills). Credit definition (UGC): 1 credit = 1 hour of lecture or tutorial per week per semester, or 2 hours of practical or laboratory work per week per semester. A semester is about 15 to 18 weeks (roughly 90 teaching days). The usual idea of CBCS is flexibility, interdisciplinarity, uniform standards across universities, easier mobility and a shift from rote learning toward continuous assessment. It does not mean that every student takes identical courses, and it does not eliminate internal assessment.

p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: UGC’s ten-point scale is: O (Outstanding) = 10, A+ (Excellent) = 9, A (Very Good) = 8, B+ (Good) = 7, B (Above Average) = 6, C (Average) = 5, P (Pass) = 4, F (Fail) = 0, Ab (Absent) = 0. SGPA (Semester Grade Point Average) = Σ(credit × grade point) ÷ Σ(credits) for one semester. CGPA (Cumulative Grade Point Average) = Σ(credit × SGPA) ÷ Σ(credits) across all semesters. Worked example: Course 1 has 4 credits and grade A (8), Course 2 has 4 credits and grade B+ (7), Course 3 has 2 credits and grade O (10). Total credit points = (4 × 8) + (4 × 7) + (2 × 10) = 32 + 28 + 20 = 80. Total credits = 10. SGPA = 80 ÷ 10 = 8.0. The rule is to weight each grade by its credit , never to take a simple average of grade points. A student who fails a course can usually carry it forward and clear it later without repeating the whole semester.

t: 8.3 Credit Transfer, Academic Bank of Credits and NAD
p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: Credit transfer means that credits earned at one institution (or through SWAYAM) are recognised by another, and it is what makes mobility possible. The Academic Bank of Credits (ABC) , launched in 2021 under NEP 2020, is a digital repository in which a learner’s credits from recognised institutions are stored in an account, much like money in a bank, and can be redeemed toward a degree; credits stay valid for a period of seven years . It is not a financial bank, not a scholarship fund and not a database of question papers. Related are the National Credit Framework (NCrF) and the National Higher Education Qualifications Framework (NHEQF) , which define levels and credit values across school, higher and vocational education.

t: 8.4 NEP 2020: Key Points for Teaching Aptitude
p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: The 5+3+3+4 structure replaces the 10+2 structure in school education (Foundational, Preparatory, Middle, Secondary stages). Target: Gross Enrolment Ratio of 50 percent in higher education by 2035. Multidisciplinary higher education institutions; flexibility of subjects; no rigid separation of arts, science and commerce. Four-year undergraduate programme with multiple entry and exit: exit after 1 year gives a Certificate, 2 years a Diploma, 3 years a Bachelor’s degree , and the 4-year programme gives a Bachelor’s degree with Honours or with Research. Credits are stored in the ABC. A single regulator for higher education (HECI) is proposed, the National Research Foundation (NRF) is to fund research, and the National Testing Agency (NTA) conducts common entrance tests. Emphasis on mother tongue and multilingualism , outcome-based education , continuous formative assessment , vocational education from school, a four-year integrated B.Ed. as the minimum teacher-preparation qualification by 2030, and public spending of 6 percent of GDP on education. The Ministry of Human Resource Development was renamed the Ministry of Education.

t: Memory Capsule: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020
p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: CBCS: UGC 2015; core, elective (DSE, GE, project), AECC (Environmental Science; English/MIL), SEC. 1 credit = 1 hour lecture or tutorial per week, or 2 hours practical per week. O = 10, A+ = 9, A = 8, B+ = 7, B = 6, C = 5, P = 4, F = 0. SGPA = Σ(credit × grade point) ÷ Σ credits. ABC = digital credit repository, credits valid seven years; NAD = academic awards depository. NEP 2020: 5+3+3+4; GER 50 percent by 2035; multiple entry and exit (1, 2, 3, 4 years); HECI; NRF.

t: Analysis Angle: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020
p: Higher Education Reforms: CBCS, Credits, Grading and NEP 2020 · Teaching Aptitude
x: Computation questions are easy marks if you apply the weighted formula. In concept questions about CBCS, choose the answer stressing choice, flexibility, credit-based and multidisciplinary learning , and reject answers stating that all students take identical courses or that internal assessment is abolished. When asked how SWAYAM supports CBCS and NEP, the link is credit transfer : courses taken online count toward the degree and are stored in the ABC. In “multiple exit” questions, memorise the ladder 1-2-3-4 years with Certificate-Diploma-Degree-Honours/Research, and reject options that say “only one exit at four years” or “no exit option.”

p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: These three words are used loosely in daily speech but are distinct in exams. Measurement is the process of assigning a number to a characteristic according to a rule (a student scored 62 out of 100); it is purely quantitative and says nothing about worth. Assessment is the broader process of gathering and interpreting evidence about learning, through tests, observation, projects and portfolios, usually to improve learning. Evaluation is the judgment of value or worth made by comparing the evidence with criteria or standards; it combines quantitative and qualitative information and leads to decisions (promotion, grading, programme change). The relationship is a ladder: measurement is the number, assessment is the evidence and interpretation, and evaluation is the value judgment. Evaluation is integral to teaching , not separate from it: it tells the teacher what to reteach, and tells the student where he or she stands. It is not a post-teaching activity only.

t: 9.2 Types of Evaluation by Purpose and Timing
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: Placement evaluation (before instruction): determines the appropriate level, group or course for a learner (the entry point). Diagnostic evaluation: identifies the specific causes of persistent learning difficulties; it goes deeper than formative testing. A student who keeps failing fractions should be diagnosed to find the exact sub-skill gap, not merely given a lower grade. Formative evaluation (term coined by Michael Scriven, 1967; applied to learning by Bloom): conducted during instruction to give feedback and improve teaching and learning; it is low-stakes and ongoing. Examples: quizzes, questioning, homework, observation. It is assessment for learning . Summative evaluation: conducted at the end of a unit, term or course to grade, certify or promote; it is high-stakes and gives a final judgment. It is assessment of learning . Annual and semester-end examinations are summative. Prognostic evaluation predicts future success (an aptitude test).

t: 9.3 Types of Evaluation by Frame of Reference
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: Norm-referenced evaluation compares a learner’s performance with that of a peer group (norm) ; the result is rank, percentile or standard score, and it spreads students along a normal distribution; it tells who is better, not whether a standard was achieved. Criterion-referenced evaluation (term from Robert Glaser, 1963) compares performance with a pre-set standard or criterion ; the result is mastery or non-mastery of defined outcomes, and in principle every student can achieve the standard. Self-referenced (ipsative) evaluation compares a learner with his or her own earlier performance and is useful for motivation and progress tracking. Use norm-referenced for selection and ranking (entrance tests), criterion-referenced for certification of competence (driving test, professional licensing) and self-referenced for personal growth.

p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: Tests can be objective (MCQ, true-false, matching: high objectivity, wide coverage, quick scoring, but poor at testing creativity), short answer and essay type (good for expression and reasoning, but lower objectivity and lower coverage). Non-test techniques: observation, checklist (presence or absence of a behaviour), rating scale (degree of a behaviour), anecdotal record (a short factual account of a significant incident), cumulative record card (complete developmental record over the years), sociometry (Moreno: mapping social relations in a group), interview and questionnaire , projects and assignments . A rubric is a scoring guide listing criteria with performance descriptors for different levels (it is not a grading curve or an answer sheet); analytic rubrics score each criterion separately and holistic rubrics give one overall score. A portfolio is a purposeful collection of a learner’s work over time that shows effort, progress and reflection, so it is not a single high-stakes exam and not a peer-assessment tool. Authentic assessment tests learners in real or realistic tasks (for example, a medical student examining a real patient), and it is considered highly valid for professional skills. 360-degree evaluation gathers feedback from multiple sources (teacher, peers, self, parents, sometimes administrators). Open-book examinations test application and reasoning more than memory.

p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: Validity: the test measures what it is intended to measure. Types: content validity (adequate sampling of the syllabus), construct validity (measures the intended trait), criterion-related validity ( concurrent when compared with an existing test, predictive when it predicts future performance). Validity is the most important quality. A reliable test need not be valid, but a valid test must be reliable. Reliability: consistency of scores. Methods: test-retest , parallel (equivalent) forms , split-half (corrected by the Spearman-Brown formula), Kuder-Richardson (KR-20, KR-21) and Cronbach’s alpha (internal consistency), and inter-rater reliability for subjective scoring. Objectivity: scoring does not depend on the scorer’s opinion. Usability (practicability): easy to administer, score and interpret; economical. Discriminating power and appropriate difficulty level. Norms for interpretation. Item analysis: the difficulty index (p) is the proportion of examinees who answer the item correctly (higher p = easier item; a good item typically lies between about 0.3 and 0.7). The discrimination index (D) compares the top and bottom groups (usually the upper and lower 27 percent): D = (number correct in upper group minus number correct in lower group) ÷ number in one group. It shows whether the item separates strong from weak students.

t: 9.6 Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE) and Internal Assessment
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: CCE assesses all aspects of a child’s development continuously (frequent formative checks through the year) and comprehensively (both scholastic , meaning academic, and co-scholastic , meaning life skills, attitudes, sports, arts and values). It was promoted by the Right to Education Act (2009) and adopted by CBSE in 2009, and it embodies the principle that evaluation should reduce the stress of a single final exam. In higher education the equivalent is a combination of internal assessment and semester-end examination , giving students grades on the basis of both. A modern assessment programme emphasises formative assessment, rubrics, portfolios and outcome-based evaluation.

t: 9.7 Computer-Based Testing (CBT) and Computerised Adaptive Testing (CAT)
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: CBT delivers a test on a computer; it permits instant scoring, randomised questions and option order, multimedia items, secure digital records and flexible scheduling. UGC NET has been a computer-based test conducted by the NTA since December 2018. Important terms: Item bank (question bank): a large pool of pre-tested, calibrated test items stored with statistics on difficulty and discrimination, from which tests are assembled. It is not a bank for exam fees, answer scripts or a storage room for paper. Computerised Adaptive Testing (CAT): the difficulty of each question is adjusted dynamically according to the candidate’s previous answers (a correct answer leads to a harder item, a wrong one to an easier item). It uses Item Response Theory (IRT) and estimates ability with fewer questions and greater precision. CBT in general merely delivers the test by computer; CAT adapts . Percentile: a percentile of 95 means the candidate scored better than (or equal to) 95 percent of the candidates ; it is not 95 percent marks, not rank 95 and not 95 questions answered. Percentile scores are used when a test is held in multiple shifts to normalise results, because the question papers differ slightly in difficulty. Remote proctoring: online examination with live invigilation through webcam and software, plus AI flagging of suspicious behaviour. Secure browsers and biometric verification reduce cheating. Mark for review (flagging) is a useful CBT feature: candidates can flag unsure questions and return to them. Equity issues: all candidates should use the same digital tools provided by the examination centre; digital divide and familiarity with computers can be concerns.

t: Memory Capsule: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: Measurement = number; assessment = evidence; evaluation = value judgment. Formative = during, feedback (Scriven, 1967). Summative = end, grading. Diagnostic = causes of difficulty. Placement = entry level. Norm-referenced = compared with peers (rank, percentile). Criterion-referenced = fixed standard (Glaser, 1963). Self-referenced = own earlier performance. Validity (most important) vs reliability (consistency); Spearman-Brown for split-half; KR-20, Cronbach’s alpha. Difficulty index p = proportion correct. Discrimination index = upper group minus lower group (27 percent). CCE: scholastic + co-scholastic; RTE Act 2009; CBSE 2009. CAT adjusts difficulty (IRT); item bank = calibrated question pool; percentile = share of candidates scored below.

t: Analysis Angle: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing
p: Evaluation Systems and Computer-Based Testing · Teaching Aptitude
x: To choose between formative and summative, ask what happens next : if the result is used to adjust teaching, it is formative; if it is used to grade or certify, it is summative. For norm vs criterion questions, look at the wording: “rank”, “percentile” and “selection” signal norm-referenced; “mastery”, “pass standard” and “achieving the objective” signal criterion-referenced. In scenarios where a student repeatedly makes the same error, the response is diagnostic testing followed by targeted remediation (not punishment or a lower grade). When asked which test is good, the answer is valid and reliable (validity first). For a question with a very high p-value, the item is too easy. For CBT questions, the distinguishing feature of CAT is that the question difficulty adapts to the test taker ; every other CBT feature (randomisation, instant result) is merely convenience.

p: Integration, Comparisons and Exam Strategy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching aptitude is not ten separate chapters but one connected story. Objectives ( Topic 2 , Bloom) decide what to teach and at which cognitive level. The levels of teaching ( Topic 3 ) tell you how deeply to teach it: memory for facts, understanding for principles, reflection for problem-solving. The learner’s characteristics ( Topic 4 ) decide how much a learner can handle (Piaget’s stage, Vygotsky’s ZPD, prior knowledge, motivation). The factors ( Topic 5 ) remind you that teacher, learner, content and environment interact. The methods ( Topic 6 ) are the vehicles, each suited to one level and one objective. Support systems ( Topic 7 ) enrich delivery from Dale’s concrete experiences to SWAYAM courses. Institutional frameworks ( Topic 8 ) like CBCS and NEP shape the programme. Evaluation ( Topic 9 ) closes the loop by checking whether the objectives were met and feeding back into planning, which is exactly Jackson’s pre-active, interactive and post-active cycle. The classic integrative question asks which statement best integrates Piaget, Vygotsky, Dewey, Bloom and Dale. The right answer reads like this: match content to the learner’s developmental stage (Piaget), support learners within the ZPD with scaffolding (Vygotsky), move from concrete to abstract experiences (Dale), engage learners in reflective inquiry around real problems (Dewey) and set objectives and tests at appropriate levels of thinking (Bloom). Wrong options always take one thinker and make it absolute: “focus only on examination preparation” or “standardise all methods regardless of learner characteristics.”

Knowles: andragogy. Flavell: metacognition. Rotter: locus of control. Erikson: psychosocial stages. Kohlberg: moral development. Dewey: reflective thinking, learning by doing, school as miniature society, pragmatism. Kilpatrick: project method. Froebel: kindergarten. Montessori: didactic materials. p: Integration, Comparisons and Exam Strategy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching vs instruction: teaching is broader (includes attitudes and values); instruction focuses on knowledge and skills. Teaching vs indoctrination: teaching respects reason; indoctrination bypasses it. Aim vs objective: aim is general and long-term; objective is specific and observable. Assimilation vs accommodation: fitting new information into an existing schema vs changing the schema. Piaget vs Vygotsky: individual vs social; development precedes learning vs learning leads development. Self-efficacy vs locus of control: belief in one’s ability vs belief about what causes outcomes. Seminar vs symposium vs panel: paper-and-discussion; several experts on aspects of one theme; experts discussing in front of an audience. Linear vs branching programme: one fixed path with small steps (Skinner) vs response-dependent path (Crowder). Formative vs summative; diagnostic vs formative: during vs end; diagnostic digs into causes. Norm-referenced vs criterion-referenced: compared with peers vs compared with a standard. Validity vs reliability: accuracy of what is measured vs consistency of scores. CBT vs CAT: test delivered by computer vs test whose difficulty adapts to the candidate. SWAYAM vs SWAYAMPRABHA: internet-based MOOC platform with certification vs DTH television channels without certification. cMOOC vs xMOOC: connectivist, network-based vs institution-led, content-based. Dale’s cone vs retention pyramid: concreteness-abstraction spectrum vs a myth about retention percentages.

t: 10.4 Reasoning Strategies for the Three Question Types
p: Integration, Comparisons and Exam Strategy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Memory questions: convert each list into a mnemonic or a story and revise it within 24 hours, then again after a week. Practise recall by writing, not re-reading: close the notes and list Bloom’s six levels, Piaget’s four stages, Dale’s eleven rungs and Flanders’ ten categories. Learn each name with its one distinctive idea (for example, “scaffolding term: Wood, Bruner and Ross”). Where two dates are possible, remember that SWAYAM and SWAYAMPRABHA are 2017, the CBCS guidelines 2015, NEP 2020, RTE 2009, microteaching 1963 and the MOOC term 2008. Concept questions: state the idea in your own sentence before looking at the options. If the definition has a key word (intended, interpersonal, intimate, interactive), find the option that carries it. Eliminate options with absolute words such as only , always , never , entirely and none unless the statement is a known fact. Be wary of options that contradict a core principle: that teaching is evidenced by learning, that learners are active, that evaluation guides teaching, that technology supplements and does not replace teachers. Analysis questions: read the scenario and identify the real variable being tested: the cognitive demand of a task (Bloom), the stage of the child (Piaget), the support provided (scaffolding), who is talking (Flanders), what happens after the test (formative or summative), or which learner is being served (SWAYAMPRABHA for the unconnected). For assertion-reason items, first test whether the assertion is true on its own, then whether the reason is true, then whether the reason explains the assertion. For matching items, solve the pairs you are sure of first and use elimination for the rest. For “EXCEPT” questions, mark each option as true or false and pick the false one. For “best integrates” or “most appropriate” questions, choose the option that is balanced and combines several principles rather than the one that overstates a single idea.

p: Integration, Comparisons and Exam Strategy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching: system of actions to induce learning (Smith). Three phases (Jackson). Levels: memory (Herbart) \< understanding (Morrison) \< reflective (Hunt). Methods: lecture (large group, memory), demonstration (skills), discussion and seminar (thinking), project (Kilpatrick), heuristic (Armstrong), programmed (Skinner, Crowder), microteaching (Allen, 1963), cooperative (Jigsaw). Flanders: 1 to 4 indirect, 5 to 7 direct, 8 to 9 student talk, 10 silence. Dale: concrete (bottom) to abstract (top); verbal symbols at the apex. Evaluation: formative (Scriven) vs summative; norm vs criterion (Glaser); validity first, then reliability; CAT adapts to the candidate; percentile = share of candidates scored below.

p: Integration, Comparisons and Exam Strategy · Teaching Aptitude
x: Teaching Aptitude rewards two habits: precise recall of a limited set of names, dates and sequences and calm reasoning about what a scenario is really testing . Revise the memory capsules daily in the last two weeks, attempt your 550 questions topic by topic, and for every wrong answer write one sentence that begins “I should have noticed that…”. The patterns you note (absolute words, mixed-up thinkers, level of cognition misjudged) will almost always repeat on exam day.
